# PocketOne

> PocketOne is a community fork of PocketBase (one Go binary: database, auth, files, realtime, admin UI) with extensions for point-in-time recovery, backups, mail, many instances on one server, deploys, tokens and OAuth, MCP, and server-rendered pages.

PocketOne takes the same commands and flags as PocketBase, plus its own; core PocketBase topics live at https://pocketbase.io/docs. Agent Skills for PocketOne: https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/agent (Claude Code: `/plugin marketplace add pocketonehq/pocketone`).


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/overview

# What is PocketOne?

PocketOne is a community fork of [PocketBase](https://pocketbase.io). It tracks upstream PocketBase and keeps its own
changes to the core small: only the hooks that let extensions extend and override PocketBase. Every feature lives in an
extension.

It's maintained by [Ben Allfree](https://github.com/benallfree) and contributors. Ben also created
[PocketHost](https://pockethost.io), which runs PocketOne in production, but PocketOne is its own project, open to
anyone who wants to help. PocketOne is not affiliated with or endorsed by the PocketBase project.

## Why a fork

PocketBase is a remarkable piece of software, and a lot of that comes from how it's made: one author, a deliberately
narrow scope, and a careful, steady pace. That focus is a big part of why it's so good, and how PocketBase is run is
Gani's call to make.

It also means PocketBase isn't set up to take larger contributions from the community, so ideas people want to build
have nowhere to land upstream: hooks that can do more, apps that run many instances, features anyone can write and
share. PocketOne is a different path for that work. It stays close to upstream and passes PocketBase's own tests, keeps
its changes to PocketBase small, and puts everything else in extensions that anyone can build on, improve and send
back.

## What it adds

Run `pocketone` the way you run `pocketbase`. These are the differences you'll notice; [New in PocketOne](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features) compares each one with PocketBase.

### Hooks with async, import and TypeScript

Your `pb_hooks` run on QuickJS with PocketBase's JS API, so they work unchanged, and they also get:
`async` handlers with `await` (the app keeps serving while one waits), ES module `import` and `node_modules` packages,
`.pb.ts` TypeScript files, globals shared by every handler, and memory and time limits.
[QuickJS hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs) walks through each one.

### Pages in TSX, TypeScript or EJS

Put `.tsx`, `.jsx`, `.ejs` or Markdown files in a `pb_pages` folder and they're server-rendered pages, with your
records a function call away. Components `import` each other, route files can be TypeScript, and every part of a
page can `await`. esbuild is built into
the binary, so there's no Node, no `npm install` and no build step. This site is one. `pocketone pages create myapp`
starts a new site from a starter kit. [Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/sites) shows a page in TSX.

### Hundreds of apps in one process

Add a `multisite` section to `pocketone.yaml` and one `pocketone` process runs hundreds of PocketBase apps as
isolates, routed by hostname. Each is a complete app with its own data, hooks and dashboard. It starts on its first
request in tens of milliseconds, costs about 3 MB while it runs, and is sandboxed from the others. No container per app.
[PocketBase isolates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/isolates) shows it running in a minute.

### Point-in-time restore, on by default

Your database is replicated with Litestream, so you can restore it to any moment from **Settings → Backups** or with
`pocketone pitr restore`. Turn it off with `--pitr=false`.

### Mail you can see in dev mode

In dev mode (`serve --dev`), an app with no SMTP settings doesn't send through the system's `sendmail`. The mail is
caught and shown at `http://127.0.0.1:8025`.

### A config file

Settings can live in `pocketone.yaml`, with secrets in a `.env` file beside it that your JS hooks never see. Without
the file, PocketOne behaves like stock PocketBase. `pocketone config` lists every section, and
`pocketone config check` checks a file. The [config reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference) lists every section.

### Commands for working with remote apps

- `pocketone login`, `remote` and `link`: save logins to your apps.
- `pocketone deploy`, `dev`, `pull` and `logs`: ship `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations` and `pb_public` to an app and
  watch it.
- `pocketone upgrade`: move to the latest release, keeping the old executable.
- `pocketone remote …`: every operation of every contract an app offers is a command, such as
  `pocketone remote restore to --at -2h`. The same operations are REST endpoints and MCP tools.
  [Remote CLI](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/remote) explains it, and the [CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli) lists every command.

### Agents and API tokens

- An MCP endpoint at `/mcp` lets agents such as Claude manage your app and call its tools.
- Long-lived API tokens (`pbt_…`) with scopes, for scripts and integrations.
- Your app can act as an OAuth provider; `pocketone login` and MCP sign-in use it.

### Extensions that fit together

PocketOne's extensions meet through contracts: named, versioned promises like `restore/v1` that any extension can
keep. The dashboard, the `pocketone` command, agents and your `pb_hooks` call the contract, so you can swap the
extension behind it without changing anything else. [How PocketOne fits together](https://pocketone.dev/docs/how-pocketone-fits-together) explains it.

### Everything else

Automatic TLS certificates, bulk mail to your own users, scheduled VACUUM, signed S3 download redirects, and more. See
[all extensions](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/all).

## What stays the same

The admin dashboard, collections, rules, the REST and realtime APIs, JS hooks and migrations all work as in PocketBase.
For those, the [PocketBase docs](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketbase) are the reference.

## How it's built

- **A small core.** PocketBase's own code changes only to add hooks. Each change is marked in the source, reviewed by
  someone who didn't write it, and kept minimal so upstream releases merge cleanly. You can review the complete core
  changes [here](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone#changes-we-made-to-pocketbase).
- **Everything else is an extension.** Extensions live in `ext/` in the repo. Each is its own Go module, with a README and a
  small example.
- **Off until you use it.** The extensions in the `pocketone` binary add no work to an app that doesn't use them.
- **One app or hundreds.** An extension written against the extension contract works the same on a single app and on every
  instance under a multi-instance host.

## Open to contributions

PocketOne is open to everyone. Ask questions and share ideas in
[GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/discussions), report bugs in
[Issues](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/issues), and send extensions as pull requests. Start with
[Writing an extension](https://pocketone.dev/docs/writing-an-extension).

## Where to next

- [Install PocketOne](https://pocketone.dev/docs/installation)
- [Browse the extensions](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/all)

# Installation

PocketOne is one executable, `pocketone`. It is built on PocketBase and takes the same commands and flags, plus its own.

- **Install:** [macOS](#macos) · [Windows](#windows) · [Linux](#linux)
- **Use:** [Run it](#run-it) · [Upgrade](#upgrade) · [Moving from PocketBase](#moving-from-pocketbase)

Another way to install (a release zip, Windows without Scoop, building from source, the install script's settings)?
See [Advanced installation](https://pocketone.dev/docs/guides/advanced-installation).

## macOS

With [Homebrew](https://brew.sh):

```bash
brew install pocketonehq/tap/pocketone
```

The formula lives in [pocketonehq/homebrew-tap](https://github.com/pocketonehq/homebrew-tap). Without Homebrew, use
the install script:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://pocketone.dev/install.sh | sh
```

It picks the newest release for your Mac, checks its checksum and puts `pocketone` in `/usr/local/bin` (asking for your
password through `sudo` when that folder isn't yours). Read it first if you like: [pocketone.dev/install.sh](/install.sh).

## Windows

With [Scoop](https://scoop.sh), in PowerShell:

```powershell
scoop bucket add pocketonehq https://github.com/pocketonehq/scoop-bucket
scoop install pocketone
```

The manifest lives in [pocketonehq/scoop-bucket](https://github.com/pocketonehq/scoop-bucket). Without Scoop, see
[Windows without Scoop](https://pocketone.dev/docs/guides/advanced-installation#windows-without-scoop).

## Linux

With [Homebrew](https://brew.sh), as on macOS:

```bash
brew install pocketonehq/tap/pocketone
```

Or with the install script, which suits a server:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://pocketone.dev/install.sh | sh
```

It finds your package manager (apt, dnf, yum, zypper or apk), downloads the newest release's `.deb`, `.rpm` or `.apk`
package for your system, checks its checksum and installs it with `sudo`. The package also sets PocketOne up as a
systemd service, stopped until you start it. With none of those package managers it puts the plain binary in
`/usr/local/bin` instead. To set the service up, see [Run PocketOne on a Linux server](https://pocketone.dev/docs/guides/linux-server).

## Run it

Create your first superuser before the first serve:

```bash
pocketone superuser upsert <email> <password>
pocketone serve
```

Opening `http://127.0.0.1:8090/_/` to create it also works, as in PocketBase.

To start a site with server-rendered pages:

```bash
pocketone pages create myapp
cd myapp
pocketone serve --dev --dir ./pb_data
```

In dev mode (`serve --dev`), an app with no SMTP settings doesn't send mail through the system's `sendmail`. PocketOne
catches the mail and shows it at `http://127.0.0.1:8025`.

## Upgrade

Upgrade the way you installed:

| Installed with | Upgrade with |
|---|---|
| Homebrew | `brew update && brew upgrade pocketone` |
| Scoop | `scoop update pocketone` |
| The install script | Run it again. |
| Anything else | `pocketone upgrade` |

`pocketone upgrade` replaces the executable with the latest release. The old one is kept beside it as
`pocketone-<version>` (`pocketone-<version>.exe` on Windows), never deleted, so you can go back. For a Homebrew, Scoop
or Linux package install it tells you the command above instead.

## Moving from PocketBase

PocketOne reads the same `pb_data`, `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations` and `pb_public` folders. Point it at your existing data
directory with `--dir`, as you would with `pocketbase`. Back up `pb_data` first.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/running

# Running PocketOne

PocketOne is your whole backend in one file. The `pocketone` executable is a database, a REST and realtime API, user
accounts and sign-in, file storage, an admin dashboard, a server for your pages and static files, and a JavaScript
runtime for your own code, plus PocketOne's extensions (deploys, restore, API tokens, AI models, MCP). There's nothing
else to install and nothing else to run.

An app is a folder. You start `pocketone` in it, and everything it keeps sits next to it.

## Start it

```bash
mkdir myapp && cd myapp
pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com 'a long password' --dir ./pb_data
pocketone serve --dir ./pb_data
```

```
Server started at http://127.0.0.1:8090
> Dashboard: http://127.0.0.1:8090/_/
> REST API:  http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/
```

- **`--dir`** is the app's data folder. Without it, `pocketone` uses `pb_data` next to the executable, so pass it (or
  set `dir:` in the [configuration](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml)'s `app:` section) to keep each app's data in its own folder.
- **`--http`** is where it listens (default `127.0.0.1:8090`); `--http 0.0.0.0:8090` listens on every address.
  `pocketone serve example.com` serves HTTPS for that domain, with a certificate it gets and renews itself.
- **`--dev`** prints every request and SQL statement, catches outgoing mail when no mail server is set (and shows it
  at http://127.0.0.1:8025), and skips a hook file with an error instead of stopping.
- Stop it with Ctrl-C. Nothing else is running: no database server, no queue, no worker.

`pocketone --help` lists every command; `pocketone serve --help` every flag. To keep it running on a server, see
[Run on a Linux server](https://pocketone.dev/docs/guides/linux-server).

## What's in the folder

| Folder | What it holds | Backed up | Deployed and synced | Safe to delete |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pb_data` | the database, uploaded files, logs | yes | never | no: it's your data |
| `pb_hooks` | your server code: [hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks) and [routes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/routes) (`*.pb.ts`), and `*.pb.wasm` modules | as code, in git | yes | no |
| `pb_pages` | your site's [pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages) | as code, in git | yes | no |
| `pb_migrations` | your [migrations](https://pocketone.dev/docs/migrations): collection changes and seed data | as code, in git | yes | no |
| `pb_public` | static files served as they are (a built single-page app, images) | as code, in git | yes | no |
| `pb_templates` | page templates you ejected (`pocketone template eject`) | as code, in git | yes | no |
| `pb_cache` | files extensions can rebuild, one folder each | never | never | yes, at any time |

Only `pb_data` is created for you; make the others when you need them. The app also writes `types.d.ts` and a
`tsconfig.json` next to them, so your editor knows the JavaScript API, and reads `pocketone.yaml` and `.env` from the
same folder if you add them ([Configuration](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml)). Add `pb_data/` and `pb_cache/` to your
`.gitignore`.

### `pb_data`

| In it | Is |
|---|---|
| `data.db` | the database: every collection and record, the settings |
| `auxiliary.db` | the logs |
| `storage/` | uploaded files, by collection and record (unless files are stored in S3) |
| `backups/` | backups you made (unless they're sent to S3) |
| `litestream/` | the change history for [point-in-time restore](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/restore) |

Never edit these by hand while the app runs, and never open the live database with another tool. Use the dashboard,
the API or your code.

### `pb_cache`

Each extension that keeps disposable files has its own folder, `pb_cache/<extension>/`. Everything in it can be
rebuilt, so deleting it is always safe: the app carries on, perhaps a little slower until the cache fills again.

```bash
pocketone cache                # each extension's folder, its file count and size
pocketone cache clear          # empty every folder
pocketone cache clear <name>   # empty one extension's folder
```

On a multisite host, each instance's `pb_cache` is kept by the host outside the instance's folder, so copies and moves
of an instance never carry it.

## The dashboard and superusers

The dashboard at `/_/` is where you manage the app: collections and records, settings, logs, backups, and the
screens extensions add (AI models, search, tokens, bulk mail).

![Settings in the dashboard: application, mail, files storage, backups, crons, LLM, SQL console and API tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/screenshots/dashboard-settings.jpg)

**Superusers** are the people who can open it. They're records of a built-in collection, `_superusers`, and they can do
everything: see and change every record, past every [API rule](https://pocketone.dev/docs/api-rules), and call the admin endpoints. Keep
them few.

```bash
pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com 'a long password' --dir ./pb_data   # create, or reset the password
pocketone superuser delete admin@example.com --dir ./pb_data
pocketone superuser otp admin@example.com --dir ./pb_data                       # a one-time password to sign in with
```

Create the first one before the first `serve`. Without any superuser, the app prints a link (and opens it in a
browser, on your own machine) to a page that creates one.

![The dashboard's superuser sign-in](https://pocketone.dev/docs/screenshots/dashboard-superuser-login.jpg)

![The _superusers collection, under System with the tables extensions keep](https://pocketone.dev/docs/screenshots/dashboard-superusers.jpg)

## Your app's users

Your app's own accounts are a different thing: records of an **auth collection** you control. Every app starts with
one, `users`, and you can add more (`customers`, `staff`). Users sign in through the [API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest/authentication)
or your [pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/authentication), never the dashboard, and what each may do is decided by your
collections' [API rules](https://pocketone.dev/docs/api-rules).

![The users collection: your app's accounts, with email, verified and name](https://pocketone.dev/docs/screenshots/dashboard-users.jpg)

| | Superusers | Users |
|---|---|---|
| Collection | `_superusers` (built in) | `users`, or any auth collection you add |
| Sign in at | the dashboard (`/_/`), the CLI, the admin API | your app: the [REST API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest/authentication), the SDK, your pages |
| May do | everything | what your API rules allow |
| Made by | `pocketone superuser upsert`, or another superuser | signing up, or you, in the dashboard or code |

See [Authentication](https://pocketone.dev/docs/authentication) for sign-in methods, and [API tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/tokens) for scripts
and other apps that call yours.

## Where a request goes

| Path | Served by |
|---|---|
| `/_/` | the dashboard |
| `/api/...` | the [REST API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest): records, auth, files, realtime, and your [custom routes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/routes) |
| `/api/_c/...` | the [extension APIs](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/apis) |
| `/mcp` | [MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/mcp), for AI agents |
| anything else | your [pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages) in `pb_pages` and the files in `pb_public` |

[Hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks) run on all of it: before and after records are saved, on requests, when mail goes out.

## Extension tables

Extensions that store records keep them in collections named `_<extension>_<table>` (`_bulkmail_campaigns`,
`_llm_calls`), so you can tell them from your own at a glance and see which extension owns each. They live in
`pb_data` with the rest of your data, so they're backed up with it. Extensions create and update them with their own
migrations, recorded apart from yours, so `pocketone migrate` never touches them:

```bash
pocketone extensions migrations              # every extension's migrations and when each was applied
pocketone extensions migrate down bulkmail   # revert bulkmail's last migration (its data goes with it)
```

## Next

- [Collections and fields](https://pocketone.dev/docs/collections): define your data.
- [Hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks): your first server code.
- [Starter kits](https://pocketone.dev/docs/starters): an app to begin from.
- [Deploy and live sync](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/deploy): put the folder on a server.

# Coming from PocketBase

PocketOne is PocketBase with more built in. Run `pocketone` the way you run `pocketbase`: the same commands and flags,
the same API, the same dashboard and the same `pb_data`, `pb_hooks` and `pb_migrations` folders.

## What stays the same

- **Your API and SDKs.** Collections, records, auth, files and realtime work as in PocketBase. The JS and Dart SDKs
  work unchanged.
- **Your hooks.** The JS API (`$app`, `routerAdd`, `onRecordCreate`, `cronAdd`, …) is PocketBase's, so existing
  `pb_hooks` run as they are. They run on [QuickJS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs), which adds imports, TypeScript and async handlers on
  top.
- **PocketBase's own tests.** PocketBase's test suite runs unmodified against PocketOne's core on every change and
  every day. See the live results on [PocketBase compatibility](https://pocketone.dev/docs/compatibility).

PocketOne is built on PocketBase v0.42. When pocketbase.io describes a newer release, some of it may not be in
PocketOne yet.

## What's added

Everything below is on by default. For each one, here's how you'd handle it in PocketBase and what PocketOne brings.

### Hooks

PocketBase runs `pb_hooks` on goja: CommonJS `require`, synchronous handlers, and a pool of runtimes that each load
your hook files. PocketOne runs the same JS API on QuickJS, so your hooks keep working, and adds `async`/`await`, ES
module `import` with `node_modules` packages, `.pb.ts` TypeScript, globals shared by every handler, and memory and time
limits. [QuickJS hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs)

### Sites

PocketBase serves static files and single-page apps from `pb_public`, and hooks can render HTML with `$template`.
PocketOne adds server-rendered pages: a `.tsx`, `.jsx`, `.ejs` or `.md` file in `pb_pages` becomes a route, with
`await` everywhere and no build step. [Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/sites)

### Many apps on one server

A PocketBase app is one process, and you host several by running a process, container or VM for each. PocketOne can
run hundreds of apps as isolates inside one process; each starts on its first request in tens of milliseconds, uses
about 3 MB and is sandboxed from the others. [PocketBase isolates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/isolates)

### Backups and restore

PocketBase makes backups on a schedule, to local disk or S3, and restores a whole backup. PocketOne also records every
change, so you can restore to any second in the last 72 hours, and undo the restore. [Point-in-time
restore](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/restore)

### Deploying

A PocketBase app is a folder you copy to the server; hooks reload when they change, and migrations run on the next
start. PocketOne adds `pocketone deploy`, which uploads only what changed, and `pocketone dev`, which keeps a local
folder and the running app in step both ways and streams the logs. [Deploy and live sync](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/deploy)

### Admin from anywhere

PocketBase's CLI runs on the machine that holds `pb_data`, and the dashboard and REST API work from anywhere. PocketOne
adds a remote CLI: sign in once, then run admin commands against any app from your terminal, a script or an agent.
[Remote CLI](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/remote)

### Tokens

A PocketBase auth token acts as its account, and changing the account's token key signs out all of its tokens at once.
PocketOne adds named, scoped API tokens that you revoke one by one, and makes your app an OAuth server that apps and
agents sign in through. [API tokens and OAuth](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/tokens)

### AI agents

PocketBase offers a REST API and realtime subscriptions, with official JavaScript and Dart SDKs. PocketOne also serves
MCP at `/mcp` on every app, with OAuth sign-in, so Claude and other agents work with your app as you, using your own
tools from `pb_hooks` too. [MCP for AI agents](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/mcp)

### Mail

PocketBase sends account mail (verification, password reset, email change, one-time codes), and your hooks can send any
message through its mailer. PocketOne adds campaigns from the dashboard, with unsubscribes, suppression and pacing
handled. [Bulk mail](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/bulk-mail)

### Desktop apps

A PocketBase app is a server: you host it, and people reach it from a browser. PocketOne can also build the same app
folder into a native desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux, with your hooks, migrations and public files inside one
executable and each user's data on their own machine. It's a preview. [Desktop apps](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/desktop)

### Configuration

In PocketBase, app settings live in the dashboard and `serve` takes its options as command-line flags. PocketOne adds
`pocketone.yaml`, one file next to your app for those options and every extension's, with a `.env` for secrets.
[pocketone.yaml](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml)

Smaller additions are listed under [Also built in](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features#also-built-in).

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/agents

# LLM skills for coding agents

PocketOne is new, so coding agents haven't seen much of it. Two things close that gap. Both are built from these docs, so they change when the docs change.

## Agent Skills

The `pocketone` plugin has two skills:

- **pocketone:** using PocketOne in an app: the `pocketone` binary and its commands, `pocketone.yaml`, deploying, every extension, and the app's pages in `pb_pages/` (routing, `ctx`, templates, layouts, auth).
- **pocketone-extensions:** writing your own extension and contributing it as a pull request: contracts, `extkit`, tests, and the README and changelog CI checks.

Each skill carries a copy of the docs in its `reference/` folder, so it works offline.

**Claude Code**

```
/plugin marketplace add pocketonehq/pocketone
/plugin install pocketone@pocketone
```

`/plugin marketplace update pocketone` picks up new versions.

**Other agents that read Agent Skills** (Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI and others)

```bash
npx skills add pocketonehq/pocketone
```

Or copy a skill folder into your project yourself. The skills live in [`agent/skills/`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/agent/skills).

## llms.txt

For agents and tools that read the web:

- [pocketone.dev/llms.txt](https://pocketone.dev/llms.txt) indexes every docs page with a one-line summary.
- [pocketone.dev/llms-full.txt](https://pocketone.dev/llms-full.txt) holds every docs page in one Markdown file.

# Collections and fields

A collection is a table of records with fields you define, plus its own [API rules](https://pocketone.dev/docs/api-rules) and a [REST
API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest). Every app starts with two: `_superusers` (who can open the dashboard) and `users` (your
app's accounts). You add the rest.

## Three kinds

| Kind | What it is | For |
|---|---|---|
| **Base** | a plain table | posts, orders, settings: anything |
| **Auth** | a table whose records can sign in, with email, password, verification and the sign-in methods you turn on | users, customers, staff; see [Authentication](https://pocketone.dev/docs/authentication) |
| **View** | a read-only table defined by a SQL `SELECT` over other collections | reports, joins, counts |

Every record has an `id` (15 characters, made for you unless you set one). Base and auth collections usually also get
`created` and `updated` (autodate fields, added by default in the dashboard).

## Create one in the dashboard

Open the dashboard (`/_/`), choose **New collection**, name it, add fields, and save. With automigrate on (the
default for `pocketone serve`), saving writes a migration file to `pb_migrations`, so the change goes with your code
when you [deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/deploy) it. See [Migrations](https://pocketone.dev/docs/migrations).

![The dashboard: collections in the sidebar, and the posts collection's records](https://pocketone.dev/docs/screenshots/dashboard-collection-records.jpg)

The gear next to a collection's name opens its settings: its fields, its API rules and, for an auth collection, its sign-in options.

![Editing the posts collection: its fields, each with its type and options](https://pocketone.dev/docs/screenshots/dashboard-collection-fields.jpg)

## Create one from code

The same collection as a migration, so it's created on every copy of your app:

```ts
// pb_migrations/1732300000_create_posts.ts
migrate((app) => {
  const posts = new Collection({
    type: "base",
    name: "posts",
    listRule: "",          // anyone can list
    viewRule: "",          // anyone can view
    createRule: "@request.auth.id != ''", // signed-in users can create
    updateRule: "author = @request.auth.id",
    deleteRule: "author = @request.auth.id",
    fields: [
      { type: "text", name: "title", required: true, max: 200 },
      { type: "text", name: "slug" },
      { type: "editor", name: "body" },
      { type: "relation", name: "author", collectionId: app.findCollectionByNameOrId("users").id, maxSelect: 1 },
      { type: "bool", name: "published" },
      { type: "autodate", name: "created", onCreate: true },
      { type: "autodate", name: "updated", onCreate: true, onUpdate: true },
    ],
    indexes: ["CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_posts_slug ON posts (slug)"],
  })
  app.save(posts)
}, (app) => {
  app.delete(app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts"))
})
```

```go
// migrations/1732300000_create_posts.go
func init() {
	m.Register(func(app core.App) error {
		users, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("users")
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		posts := core.NewBaseCollection("posts")
		posts.ListRule = types.Pointer("")
		posts.ViewRule = types.Pointer("")
		posts.CreateRule = types.Pointer("@request.auth.id != ''")
		posts.UpdateRule = types.Pointer("author = @request.auth.id")
		posts.DeleteRule = types.Pointer("author = @request.auth.id")
		posts.Fields.Add(
			&core.TextField{Name: "title", Required: true, Max: 200},
			&core.TextField{Name: "slug"},
			&core.EditorField{Name: "body"},
			&core.RelationField{Name: "author", CollectionId: users.Id, MaxSelect: 1},
			&core.BoolField{Name: "published"},
			&core.AutodateField{Name: "created", OnCreate: true},
			&core.AutodateField{Name: "updated", OnCreate: true, OnUpdate: true},
		)
		posts.AddIndex("idx_posts_slug", true, "slug", "")
		return app.Save(posts)
	}, func(app core.App) error {
		posts, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts")
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		return app.Delete(posts)
	})
}
```

A rule left unset (`null`, in Go `nil`) means only superusers may do that action; an empty string means anyone may.
[API rules](https://pocketone.dev/docs/api-rules) explains the rest.

Every field also has `name`, `hidden` (left out of API answers; superusers still see it) and `presentable` (shown in
the dashboard when another record points to this one). A field's value comes back from the API in its natural JSON
form: a number for `number`, an array of ids for a multi-relation, file names for `file`.

## Change a collection

Load it, change it, save it. Renaming a field keeps its data; removing one drops its column:

```ts
// pb_migrations/1732400000_posts_add_summary.ts
migrate((app) => {
  const posts = app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts")
  posts.fields.add(new TextField({ name: "summary", max: 300 }))
  posts.fields.getByName("body").required = true
  app.save(posts)
}, (app) => {
  const posts = app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts")
  posts.fields.removeByName("summary")
  posts.fields.getByName("body").required = false
  app.save(posts)
})
```

```go
m.Register(func(app core.App) error {
	posts, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	posts.Fields.Add(&core.TextField{Name: "summary", Max: 300})
	posts.Fields.GetByName("body").(*core.EditorField).Required = true
	return app.Save(posts)
}, func(app core.App) error {
	posts, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	posts.Fields.RemoveByName("summary")
	posts.Fields.GetByName("body").(*core.EditorField).Required = false
	return app.Save(posts)
})
```

Saving a collection checks it first (a relation must point at a real collection, an index must be valid SQL), and
fails with the reason if not.

## View collections

A view collection is a `SELECT` that the API serves like any other collection, read-only. Its fields come from the
query's columns, and it needs an `id` column:

```ts
migrate((app) => {
  app.save(new Collection({
    type: "view",
    name: "posts_per_author",
    listRule: "",
    viewQuery: "SELECT author AS id, COUNT(*) AS posts FROM posts GROUP BY author",
  }))
}, (app) => {
  app.delete(app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts_per_author"))
})
```

```go
m.Register(func(app core.App) error {
	view := core.NewViewCollection("posts_per_author")
	view.ListRule = types.Pointer("")
	view.ViewQuery = "SELECT author AS id, COUNT(*) AS posts FROM posts GROUP BY author"
	return app.Save(view)
}, func(app core.App) error {
	view, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts_per_author")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return app.Delete(view)
})
```

# Records

A record is one row of a [collection](https://pocketone.dev/docs/collections). Clients reach records through the [REST
API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest); this page is about your own code: a [hook](https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks), a [route](https://pocketone.dev/docs/routes), a cron
job or a migration. In JavaScript the app is `$app` (or `e.app` inside a handler, which is the right one inside a
transaction); in Go it's your `app`.

In the dashboard, a collection's records are a table you can search and filter; open one to edit it. Saving there runs the same validation and hooks as your code.

![Editing a posts record in the dashboard, with the slug a hook filled in](https://pocketone.dev/docs/screenshots/dashboard-record-edit.jpg)

## Find records

```ts
// one by id (throws a not-found error when it doesn't exist)
const post = $app.findRecordById("posts", "abc123def456ghi")

// many, by filter: collection, filter, sort, limit, offset, params
const recent = $app.findRecordsByFilter(
  "posts",
  "published = true && created > {:since}",
  "-created",
  20,
  0,
  { since: "2026-01-01 00:00:00" },
)

// the first match, or an error when there's none
const bySlug = $app.findFirstRecordByFilter("posts", "slug = {:slug}", { slug: "hello-world" })

// by one field's exact value
const sameSlug = $app.findFirstRecordByData("posts", "slug", "hello-world")

// how many
const drafts = $app.countRecords("posts", $dbx.hashExp({ published: false }))
```

```go
post, err := app.FindRecordById("posts", "abc123def456ghi")

recent, err := app.FindRecordsByFilter(
	"posts",
	"published = true && created > {:since}",
	"-created",
	20,
	0,
	dbx.Params{"since": "2026-01-01 00:00:00"},
)

bySlug, err := app.FindFirstRecordByFilter("posts", "slug = {:slug}", dbx.Params{"slug": "hello-world"})

sameSlug, err := app.FindFirstRecordByData("posts", "slug", "hello-world")

drafts, err := app.CountRecords("posts", dbx.HashExp{"published": false})
```

The filter is the same language as [API rules](https://pocketone.dev/docs/api-rules) and the API's `?filter=`. **Always pass values as
`{:name}` parameters**, never by building the string, so a value can't change the filter's meaning. The sort is a
comma list of fields, `-` for descending (`"-created,title"`). A limit of `0` means no limit.

Not finding a record is an error (`findRecordById`, `findFirstRecordBy...`), which a route turns into a 404. To check
without failing, catch it, or use `findRecordsByFilter` and look at the length.

## Read values

`get` returns a field's value as it is; the typed getters convert:

```ts
const title = post.getString("title")
const views = post.getInt("views")
const published = post.getBool("published")
const created = post.getDateTime("created") // a DateTime: .time(), .string(), .isZero()
const tags = post.getStringSlice("tags")   // multi-select, multi-relation, multi-file
const meta = post.get("meta")               // json: the parsed value
const id = post.id
```

```go
title := post.GetString("title")
views := post.GetInt("views")
published := post.GetBool("published")
created := post.GetDateTime("created")
tags := post.GetStringSlice("tags")
meta := post.Get("meta")
id := post.Id
```

An auth record also has `email()`, `verified()` and `validatePassword(password)` (in Go `Email()`, `Verified()`,
`ValidatePassword`).

## Create, change and delete

```ts
const posts = $app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts")
const post = new Record(posts)
post.set("title", "Hello")
post.set("author", userId)
$app.save(post) // validates, runs hooks, then inserts; post.id is set

post.set("title", "Hello again")
$app.save(post) // updates

$app.delete(post)
```

```go
posts, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts")
if err != nil {
	return err
}
post := core.NewRecord(posts)
post.Set("title", "Hello")
post.Set("author", userID)
if err := app.Save(post); err != nil {
	return err
}

post.Set("title", "Hello again")
if err := app.Save(post); err != nil {
	return err
}

if err := app.Delete(post); err != nil {
	return err
}
```

- **`save` validates first** (required fields, lengths, patterns, unique indexes) and fails with each field's problem.
  `saveNoValidate` skips that; use it only for data you've already checked.
- **Hooks run on every save,** whether the save came from the API, the dashboard or your code. Use
  `$app.unsafeWithoutHooks().save(record)` (Go `app.UnsafeWithoutHooks().Save`) to skip them, for example inside a hook
  that would otherwise trigger itself.
- **Set a field by its modifier**, as the API does: `post.set("views+", 1)` adds one, `post.set("tags+", "new")`
  appends, `post.set("tags-", "old")` removes.
- **Files:** set a file field to a file made with `$filesystem.fileFromPath`, `fileFromBytes` or `fileFromURL`
  (Go `filesystem.NewFileFrom...`); saving uploads it to the app's storage
  ([`$filesystem`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/javascript/pocketbase#filesystem)).

## Relations

A relation field holds ids. To get the related records, expand it:

```ts
const post = $app.findRecordById("posts", id)
$app.expandRecord(post, ["author"], null)
const author = post.expandedOne("author") // the users record, or null
const authorName = author?.getString("name")

// or follow the relation by hand
const sameAuthor = $app.findRecordById("users", post.getString("author"))
```

```go
post, err := app.FindRecordById("posts", id)
if err != nil {
	return err
}
if errs := app.ExpandRecord(post, []string{"author"}, nil); len(errs) > 0 {
	return fmt.Errorf("expand: %v", errs)
}
author := post.ExpandedOne("author")
```

`expandedAll(field)` returns the list for a multi-relation. To find the records that point *to* a record (a user's
posts), filter on the relation: `findRecordsByFilter("posts", "author = {:id}", ...)`. In the REST API, the same is
`?expand=author` and, backwards, `?expand=posts_via_author`.

## Transactions

Several saves that must all happen or none:

```ts
$app.runInTransaction((txApp) => {
  const order = new Record(txApp.findCollectionByNameOrId("orders"))
  order.set("total", 42)
  txApp.save(order)

  const stock = txApp.findRecordById("products", productId)
  stock.set("stock-", 1)
  txApp.save(stock) // throw (or fail) here and the order isn't saved either
})
```

```go
err := app.RunInTransaction(func(txApp core.App) error {
	orders, err := txApp.FindCollectionByNameOrId("orders")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	order := core.NewRecord(orders)
	order.Set("total", 42)
	if err := txApp.Save(order); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	stock, err := txApp.FindRecordById("products", productID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	stock.Set("stock-", 1)
	return txApp.Save(stock)
})
```

Inside the function, use `txApp` for everything; `$app` would wait for the transaction's own lock. Keep it short:
SQLite allows one writer at a time, so a long transaction holds up every other save.

## Queries and raw SQL

For what a filter can't say (joins, aggregates, `GROUP BY`), write the query. The query builder:

```ts
const rows = arrayOf(new DynamicModel({ author: "", posts: 0 }))
$app.db()
  .select("author", "COUNT(*) AS posts")
  .from("posts")
  .where($dbx.exp("published = {:p}", { p: true }))
  .groupBy("author")
  .orderBy("posts DESC")
  .limit(10)
  .all(rows)
```

```go
rows := []struct {
	Author string `db:"author" json:"author"`
	Posts  int    `db:"posts" json:"posts"`
}{}
err := app.DB().
	Select("author", "COUNT(*) AS posts").
	From("posts").
	Where(dbx.NewExp("published = {:p}", dbx.Params{"p": true})).
	GroupBy("author").
	OrderBy("posts DESC").
	Limit(10).
	All(&rows)
```

Or plain SQL, with bound parameters:

```ts
const result = new DynamicModel({ total: 0 })
$app.db()
  .newQuery("SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM posts WHERE author = {:author}")
  .bind({ author: userId })
  .one(result)
```

```go
var result struct {
	Total int `db:"total"`
}
err := app.DB().
	NewQuery("SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM posts WHERE author = {:author}").
	Bind(dbx.Params{"author": userID}).
	One(&result)
```

To get records (not plain rows) from a query, start from `$app.recordQuery("posts")` and finish with `.all(records)`
on `arrayOf(new Record())`. `$dbx` has the expression helpers: `hashExp`, `exp`, `and`, `or`, `not`, `in`, `like`,
`between` and the rest.

  [`core.Record`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/go/pocketbase/core/records#record) and
  [`core.App`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/go/pocketbase/core#app).

# API rules and filters

Every [collection](https://pocketone.dev/docs/collections) has five API rules, one per action: **list**, **view**, **create**, **update**
and **delete**. A rule decides who may do that action through the [REST API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest), and it's written in
the same filter language clients use to search. Superusers skip the rules; your own code (`$app.save`, `findRecords...`)
isn't checked against them either.

## The three kinds of rule

| Rule | Means |
|---|---|
| unset (`null`, the default; a lock in the dashboard) | only superusers |
| empty string `""` | anyone, signed in or not |
| a filter, like `author = @request.auth.id` | whoever the filter matches |

![The posts collection's API rules in the dashboard: list, view, create and update rules, and delete for superusers only](https://pocketone.dev/docs/screenshots/dashboard-api-rules.jpg)

Set them in the dashboard (the collection's **API rules** tab) or in a migration:

```ts
migrate((app) => {
  const posts = app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts")
  posts.listRule = "published = true || author = @request.auth.id"
  posts.viewRule = "published = true || author = @request.auth.id"
  posts.createRule = "@request.auth.id != '' && @request.body.author = @request.auth.id"
  posts.updateRule = "author = @request.auth.id"
  posts.deleteRule = null // superusers only
  app.save(posts)
})
```

```go
m.Register(func(app core.App) error {
	posts, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	posts.ListRule = types.Pointer("published = true || author = @request.auth.id")
	posts.ViewRule = types.Pointer("published = true || author = @request.auth.id")
	posts.CreateRule = types.Pointer("@request.auth.id != '' && @request.body.author = @request.auth.id")
	posts.UpdateRule = types.Pointer("author = @request.auth.id")
	posts.DeleteRule = nil
	return app.Save(posts)
}, nil)
```

## How a rule is applied

- **List** works as a filter: a client gets only the records the rule matches, never an error. A guest listing
  `posts` with the rule above sees only published posts.
- **View, update and delete** check the one record: if the rule doesn't match, the API answers 404, as if the record
  weren't there (so it doesn't leak which ids exist).
- **Create** checks the record that would be created, built from the request's body.
- Auth collections have a sixth rule, **manage**, for records allowed to change another record's email and password
  (a team admin, say).

## The filter language

```
title ~ 'hello' && (published = true || created > '2026-01-01 00:00:00')
```

| Operator | Means |
|---|---|
| `=` `!=` | equal, not equal |
| `>` `>=` `<` `<=` | greater, less |
| `~` `!~` | contains, doesn't contain (a `like`; `%` wildcards allowed) |
| `?=` `?!=` `?>` `?~` ... | the same, for any item of a multi-value field ("any tag is ...") |
| `&&` `\|\|` `( )` | and, or, grouping |

Values are quoted strings (`'text'`), numbers, `true`, `false` or `null`. Dates compare as `'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'`
strings, in UTC. Fields of related records are reached with dots: `author.verified = true`.

## What a rule can see

| Identifier | Is |
|---|---|
| `@request.auth.*` | the signed-in record: `@request.auth.id` (empty for a guest), `@request.auth.collectionName`, any of its fields (`@request.auth.role = 'admin'`) |
| `@request.body.*` | the submitted values (create and update): `@request.body.status`, `@request.body.title:isset = true` |
| `@request.query.*` | the URL's query parameters |
| `@request.headers.*` | the request's headers, lowercase with `_` for `-` (`@request.headers.x_token`) |
| `@request.method`, `@request.context` | the HTTP method; where the request came from (`default`, `oauth2`, `otp`, `password`, `realtime`, `protectedFile`) |
| `@collection.<name>.*` | another collection's records, matched like a join: `@collection.members.user = @request.auth.id && @collection.members.team = team` |
| `@now`, `@today...`, `@yesterday`, `@tomorrow` ... | the current time and date parts (`@todayStart`, `@monthEnd`, `@year`) |

Modifiers on a field:

| Modifier | Gives |
|---|---|
| `:isset` | whether the client sent the field (`@request.body.role:isset = false`: may not set `role`) |
| `:changed` | whether an update changes it (`@request.body.owner:changed = false`) |
| `:length` | the number of items in a multi-value field (`tags:length <= 5`) |
| `:each` | applies to every item (`tags:each ~ 'blog-'`) |
| `:lower` | compares lowercase (`email:lower = 'ada@example.com'`) |

## Recipes

| Who | Rule |
|---|---|
| anyone | `""` |
| any signed-in user | `@request.auth.id != ''` |
| signed-in users of one collection | `@request.auth.collectionName = 'customers'` |
| only verified users | `@request.auth.verified = true` |
| the record's owner | `author = @request.auth.id` |
| published, or mine | `published = true \|\| author = @request.auth.id` |
| create only as yourself | `@request.auth.id != '' && @request.body.author = @request.auth.id` |
| update, but not the owner field | `author = @request.auth.id && @request.body.author:isset = false` |
| members of the record's team | `@collection.members.team = team && @collection.members.user = @request.auth.id` |
| users with a role | `@request.auth.role = 'editor'` |

## Filters in the API and in code

The same language filters lists through the REST API:

```bash
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/posts/records?filter=(title~'hello')&sort=-created"
```

and in your code, where values go in as `{:params}` so they can't change the filter's meaning:

```ts
const mine = $app.findRecordsByFilter("posts", "author = {:me} && title ~ {:q}", "-created", 20, 0, {
  me: userId,
  q: search,
})
```

```go
mine, err := app.FindRecordsByFilter("posts", "author = {:me} && title ~ {:q}", "-created", 20, 0,
	dbx.Params{"me": userID, "q": search})
```

A rule is combined with the client's own `filter` (both must match), so clients can narrow what they may see, never
widen it.

## When a rule isn't enough

A rule answers "may this request do this to this record?" from data. When the answer needs code (a call to another
service, a limit per day, a check that spans many records), write a [hook](https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks) on the request
(`onRecordCreateRequest` and the rest) and throw a `ForbiddenError` there. Request hooks run after the rule: they see
only the requests it allows, so the two add up (the rule first, then your code).

## Next

- [Authentication](https://pocketone.dev/docs/authentication): how a request gets `@request.auth`.
- [Records](https://pocketone.dev/docs/records): filters in your own code.
- [Collections and fields](https://pocketone.dev/docs/collections): where rules live.

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/migrations

# Migrations

Your app's schema (its collections, fields, rules and indexes) lives in its database, but it belongs with your code: the
copy on your laptop and the one on your server need the same collections. Migrations are how: small files in
`pb_migrations/`, each with an **up** (make the change) and a **down** (undo it), that every copy of the app runs once,
in order.

## Automigrate: change the dashboard, get a file

With automigrate on (the default for `pocketone serve`), every collection change you save in the dashboard writes a
migration file:

```
pb_migrations/
  1732300000_created_posts.js
  1732300512_updated_posts.js
```

Commit those files with your code. When the app starts somewhere else, or when you run
[`pocketone deploy`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/deploy), it applies the ones it hasn't run yet. So the usual flow is: change
collections in your local dashboard, then deploy.

Turn it off with `--automigrate=false` or `automigrate: false` in [pocketone.yaml](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml)'s `server`
section, for example on a production server where nobody should change collections by hand.

## Write one yourself

For seed data, data fixes, or changes you'd rather write than click:

```bash
pocketone migrate create seed_categories
# pb_migrations/1732400000_seed_categories.js
```

Rename it `.ts` if you like; PocketOne runs TypeScript migrations directly.

```ts
// pb_migrations/1732400000_seed_categories.ts
migrate((app) => {
  const categories = app.findCollectionByNameOrId("categories")
  for (const name of ["News", "Guides", "Releases"]) {
    const record = new Record(categories)
    record.set("name", name)
    app.save(record)
  }
}, (app) => {
  for (const name of ["News", "Guides", "Releases"]) {
    const record = app.findFirstRecordByData("categories", "name", name)
    app.delete(record)
  }
})
```

```go
// migrations/1732400000_seed_categories.go
package migrations

import (
	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core"
	m "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/migrations"
)

func init() {
	m.Register(func(app core.App) error {
		categories, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("categories")
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		for _, name := range []string{"News", "Guides", "Releases"} {
			record := core.NewRecord(categories)
			record.Set("name", name)
			if err := app.Save(record); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}
		return nil
	}, func(app core.App) error {
		for _, name := range []string{"News", "Guides", "Releases"} {
			record, err := app.FindFirstRecordByData("categories", "name", name)
			if err != nil {
				return err
			}
			if err := app.Delete(record); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}
		return nil
	})
}
```

- The `app` a migration gets runs inside a transaction: if the up throws, nothing it did is kept.
- Files run in the order of their names, which start with a Unix time, so new files run after old ones.
- A Go build imports its migrations package (`_ "yourapp/migrations"`) so its files register; they run with the JS
  ones, in one order.
- [Collections and fields](https://pocketone.dev/docs/collections) shows creating and changing collections in a migration.

## Run, undo and inspect

```bash
pocketone migrate up          # apply every migration not yet applied (serve does this at start)
pocketone migrate down 1      # undo the last one
pocketone migrate collections # write one file with every collection as it is now (a snapshot)
pocketone migrate history-sync # forget applied migrations whose files are gone
```

The app records applied migrations in its `_migrations` table, so each runs once per database.

A snapshot (`migrate collections`) is a good way to start over: one file that creates every collection as it is, in
place of a long history. Delete the old files, keep the snapshot, and run `history-sync` on each existing copy.

## Extensions bring their own

PocketOne's extensions keep their own tables (the LLM ledger, API tokens, bulk mail) with their own migrations, tracked
apart from yours. They never appear in `pb_migrations`, and you don't need to copy their schema.

- [Collections and fields](https://pocketone.dev/docs/collections): what migrations change.
- [Deploy and live sync](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/deploy): how migrations reach your server.
- [CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli): every `migrate` option.

# Key-Value Store

**Keep a setting without making a collection.** Your app's title, a feature switch, the prompts your page sends a
model, the last time a job ran: each is one value, not a table of records. `$kv` stores it under a name and gives it
back:

```ts
const settings = $kv.get("storytime/settings") ?? { title: "Story Time", minutes: 10 }
```

```go
var settings Settings
found, err := kvv1.Get(app, "storytime/settings", &settings)
```

There's no collection to create and no migration to write. Values live in PocketBase's own `_params` table, beside its
settings, so they ride along in every backup. It's built into `pocketone` and on by default.

The examples show each thing in TypeScript, as [Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/overview) page code or `pb_hooks`, and in
Go. The Go examples use the contract's helpers (`kvv1` is `pocketone.dev/ext/contracts/kv/v1`).

## Read and write values

A value is anything JSON can hold: an object, a list, a string, a number, `true` or `false`.

```ts
$kv.set("storytime/settings", { title: "Story Time", minutes: 10, voices: ["alloy"] })

const s = $kv.get("storytime/settings") // { title: "Story Time", minutes: 10, voices: ["alloy"] }
const none = $kv.get("storytime/nothing") // null: no value under that name

$kv.delete("storytime/settings") // no error when there was nothing to delete
```

```go
err := kvv1.Set(app, "storytime/settings", Settings{Title: "Story Time", Minutes: 10})

var s Settings
found, err := kvv1.Get(app, "storytime/settings", &s) // found is false, and s untouched, when there's no value

err = kvv1.Delete(app, "storytime/settings")
```

Every call is quick and local (one read or write of your app's database), so `$kv` has no `Async` forms. `set`
replaces the whole value: to change one field, read the value, change it and set it again.

## Defaults until someone changes them

A common shape: ship defaults with your app, and store a value only once someone changes something.

```ts
const defaults = { title: "Story Time", minutes: 10 }

// read: the stored settings over the defaults
const settings = { ...defaults, ...($kv.get("storytime/settings") ?? {}) }

// save: only what the form sent
$kv.set("storytime/settings", { ...settings, minutes: Number(body.minutes) })
```

Merging over the defaults means a field you add in a later version gets its default on apps that saved settings
before it existed.

## List values

Names can share a prefix, and `list` returns every value whose name starts with it, sorted by name:

```ts
$kv.list("storytime/")
// [{ name: "storytime/settings", value: {...}, created: "2026-11-22T10:00:00Z", updated: "..." }, ...]
```

```go
entries, err := kvv1.List(app, "storytime/") // each has Name, Value (JSON), Created, Updated
```

`$kv.list()` with no prefix returns every value in the store.

## Names

A name is 1 to 128 characters: letters, digits and `_ - . : /`, starting with a letter or digit. Start yours with a
prefix of your own, such as your app's or extension's name (`storytime/settings`), so they never meet another
extension's. A name that breaks these rules throws (in Go, returns `kvv1.ErrInvalidName`).

Names starting with `_` are private to Go code on the app. Extensions keep their secrets there (LLM's provider keys
are `_llm/settings`): `$kv`, the API and agents can't read, change or list them.

A value is at most 1 MiB of JSON. For more than that, or for many similar things you want to filter, sort or let users
own, use a collection.

## From outside the app

Superusers can read and change values from the API, the `pocketone` command and agents, for example to fix a setting
on a live app:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" "https://app.example.com/api/_c/kv/v1?prefix=storytime/"           # list
curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" "https://app.example.com/api/_c/kv/v1/get?name=storytime/settings" # one value
curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -d '{"name":"storytime/settings","value":{"minutes":15}}' \
  https://app.example.com/api/_c/kv/v1/set
curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -d '{"name":"storytime/settings"}' https://app.example.com/api/_c/kv/v1/delete
```

`$TOKEN` is a superuser's token, or an [API token](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) with the `kv:read` scope (list, get) or
`kv` (all four). From your project folder, `pocketone remote kv` does the same on the project's remote:

```bash
pocketone remote kv list --prefix storytime/
pocketone remote kv get --name storytime/settings
pocketone remote kv set --name storytime/settings --value '{"minutes":15}'   # --value @settings.json reads a file
pocketone remote kv delete --name storytime/settings
```

Agents get them as MCP tools (`kv_list`, `kv_get`, `kv_set`, `kv_delete`). Users and guests can't reach the store:
your page code decides what, if anything, they see.

## Good to know

- **Where values live:** the value named `storytime/settings` is the `_params` row with id `kv:storytime/settings`.
  The `kv:` prefix keeps your names apart from PocketBase's own rows (its `settings`) and from rows other extensions
  keep there. Read and write through `$kv` or the helpers, never the table.
- **Transactions:** the Go helpers take any `core.App`, so inside `app.RunInTransaction` pass the transaction's app and
  the write is part of it. `$kv`, like `$app`, writes through the main app.
- **Turning it off:** `kv: {enabled: false}` in `pocketone.yaml` removes `$kv` and the API. The Go helpers keep
  working, since they need nothing but the database.

- [Key-Value Store reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/kv/extension): the extension's page.
- [kv/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/kv/v1): the contract, for extension authors.

# Authentication

Users sign in to an **auth collection**: a [collection](https://pocketone.dev/docs/collections) whose records have an email, a password and
the sign-in methods you turn on. Every app has one, `users`, and `_superusers` for the dashboard; add more for
different kinds of account (`customers`, `staff`). Signing in returns a **token**; the client sends it with each
request, and the request then knows who it's from: `@request.auth` in [API rules](https://pocketone.dev/docs/api-rules), `e.auth` in
[hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks) and [routes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/routes).

## Sign-in methods

Turn them on per collection, in the dashboard (the collection's **Options**) or in code:

![The users collection's Options: password, OAuth2 and one-time password on, multi-factor off, and its mail templates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/screenshots/dashboard-auth-options.jpg)

| Method | The user | Turn on |
|---|---|---|
| **Password** | enters an email (or another identity field) and a password | `passwordAuth` (on for `users`) |
| **One-time code** | asks for a code by email and enters it | `otp` |
| **OAuth2** | signs in with Google, GitHub, Apple, Microsoft and many more providers | `oauth2`, with each provider's client id and secret |
| **Multi-factor** | signs in with two methods (a password, then a code) | `mfa`, together with two of the above |

```ts
// pb_migrations/1732500000_users_signin.ts
migrate((app) => {
  const users = app.findCollectionByNameOrId("users")
  users.passwordAuth.enabled = true
  users.passwordAuth.identityFields = ["email"]
  users.otp.enabled = true
  users.otp.duration = 300 // a code lasts 5 minutes
  users.oauth2.enabled = true
  users.oauth2.providers = [{
    name: "google",
    clientId: $os.getenv("GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID"),
    clientSecret: $os.getenv("GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  }]
  app.save(users)
})
```

```go
m.Register(func(app core.App) error {
	users, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("users")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	users.PasswordAuth.Enabled = true
	users.PasswordAuth.IdentityFields = []string{"email"}
	users.OTP.Enabled = true
	users.OTP.Duration = 300
	users.OAuth2.Enabled = true
	users.OAuth2.Providers = []core.OAuth2ProviderConfig{{
		Name:         "google",
		ClientId:     os.Getenv("GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID"),
		ClientSecret: os.Getenv("GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET"),
	}}
	return app.Save(users)
}, nil)
```

## Sign in from a client

With the JavaScript SDK (`npm install pocketbase`, it works with PocketOne unchanged):

```js
import PocketBase from "pocketbase"

const pb = new PocketBase("https://myapp.example.com")

// password
await pb.collection("users").authWithPassword("ada@example.com", "a long password")

// one-time code: ask, then enter the code from the email
const { otpId } = await pb.collection("users").requestOTP("ada@example.com")
await pb.collection("users").authWithOTP(otpId, "123456")

// OAuth2: opens the provider's sign-in in a popup
await pb.collection("users").authWithOAuth2({ provider: "google" })

pb.authStore.isValid // true
pb.authStore.record  // the signed-in user
pb.authStore.token   // sent with every request from now on
```

The same over HTTP:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/users/auth-with-password \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"identity": "ada@example.com", "password": "a long password"}'
# {"token": "eyJhbGciOi...", "record": {"id": "...", "email": "ada@example.com", ...}}

curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/posts/records \
  -H "Authorization: eyJhbGciOi..."
```

Tokens expire (after 7 days for `users`, set per collection); `authRefresh` swaps a valid token for a fresh one. In
[Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages), sign-in works through a cookie instead: see [Sign users in on your
pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/authentication).

## Sign up, verify, reset

- **Sign up** is a create on the auth collection (`pb.collection("users").create({ email, password, passwordConfirm })`),
  allowed by its create rule (empty for `users`: anyone may sign up).
- **Verify an email:** `requestVerification(email)` sends a link; the user's `verified` field turns true when they open
  it. Require it in rules with `@request.auth.verified = true`.
- **Reset a password:** `requestPasswordReset(email)` sends a link to a page where the user picks a new one.
- **Change an email:** `requestEmailChange(newEmail)` sends a confirmation to the new address.

The emails' wording and links are set per collection (**Options** → mail templates), and they're sent through the
app's SMTP settings.

## Multi-factor auth

With `mfa` on, signing in with one method answers `401` with an `mfaId`; the client then signs in with a second method,
passing it:

```js
try {
  await pb.collection("users").authWithPassword(email, password)
} catch (err) {
  const mfaId = err.response?.mfaId
  if (!mfaId) throw err
  const { otpId } = await pb.collection("users").requestOTP(email)
  await pb.collection("users").authWithOTP(otpId, codeFromUser, { mfaId })
}
```

## The signed-in user in your code

In a hook or route, `e.auth` is the record that signed in, or `null`:

```ts
// pb_hooks/me.pb.ts
routerAdd("GET", "/api/me", (e) => {
  if (!e.auth) throw new UnauthorizedError("Sign in first.")
  return e.json(200, {
    id: e.auth.id,
    email: e.auth.email(),
    collection: e.auth.collection().name,
    superuser: e.hasSuperuserAuth(),
  })
})
```

```go
se.Router.GET("/api/me", func(e *core.RequestEvent) error {
	if e.Auth == nil {
		return e.UnauthorizedError("Sign in first.", nil)
	}
	return e.JSON(200, map[string]any{
		"id":         e.Auth.Id,
		"email":      e.Auth.Email(),
		"collection": e.Auth.Collection().Name,
		"superuser":  e.HasSuperuserAuth(),
	})
})
```

`$apis.requireAuth()` on a route does the check for you ([Custom routes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/routes#require-sign-in)). To sign a user
in from your own route (a magic link, a code from another system), find the record and answer with a token:

```ts
// pb_hooks/magic.pb.ts
routerAdd("POST", "/api/magic/{code}", (e) => {
  const link = e.app.findFirstRecordByData("magic_links", "code", e.request.pathValue("code"))
  const user = e.app.findRecordById("users", link.getString("user"))
  e.app.delete(link) // one use
  return $apis.recordAuthResponse(e, user, "magic")
})
```

```go
se.Router.POST("/api/magic/{code}", func(e *core.RequestEvent) error {
	link, err := e.App.FindFirstRecordByData("magic_links", "code", e.Request.PathValue("code"))
	if err != nil {
		return e.NotFoundError("", err)
	}
	user, err := e.App.FindRecordById("users", link.GetString("user"))
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if err := e.App.Delete(link); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return apis.RecordAuthResponse(e, user, "magic", nil)
})
```

The answer is the same `{token, record}` as a password sign-in, so the SDK's auth store takes it as is.

## Impersonation

A superuser can get a token for any user, to see the app as they do (support cases). In the dashboard, open the
record and choose **Impersonate**; over the API, `POST /api/collections/users/impersonate/{id}` with a superuser's
token. The token can't be refreshed and lasts as long as you ask (`duration`, in seconds).

## Tokens for scripts and other apps

A user's sign-in token is for that user's session. For a script, a server or another app that calls yours, give it
an [API token](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/tokens): named, scoped to what it may do, and revoked one by one.

- [API tokens and OAuth](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/tokens): access for scripts, apps and agents.

- [Let users sign in with Google](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/speedruns/google-oauth2): the provider setup, step by step.

# API tokens and OAuth

A script, a CI job or another service can't type a password. Give it an API token instead: a long secret that starts
with `pbt_`, acts as the account that owns it, and can be limited to a few scopes and given an expiry. Revoke it, and
it stops working at once.

This is on for every PocketOne app. You don't need to set anything up. Ordinary PocketBase sign-ins keep working as
before.

## Create a token in the dashboard

1. Sign in to the dashboard as a superuser and open **Settings → API tokens** (under **Access**).
2. Fill in a **Name**, so you can recognize the token later.
3. Optionally set **Expires in (days)**. Leave it empty and the token never expires.
4. Tick the **Scopes** the token needs. Tick none and it gets its owner's full rights.
5. The token is yours by default. To make one for another account, fill in **Owner collection** and
   **Owner (id or email)**.
6. Click **Create token**, then copy it. It's shown only once and never stored.

Send it with each request:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_…" https://myapp.example.com/api/collections/notes/records
```

## See and revoke tokens

The same screen lists every token: its name, its first characters, owner, scopes, expiry and when it was last used
(time and IP). Click **Revoke** and confirm to delete one. Anything using it stops working at once.

## Let apps and tools sign in

Some clients sign in for you instead of asking for a pasted token: `pocketone login`, Claude and other
[AI agents](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/mcp), or an app of your own. They send you to your app's own sign-in pages:

1. Sign in with whatever the collection allows: a password, an emailed code, or (for app users) Google and
   other providers, plus a second step if the account has MFA. Click **Sign in as a superuser** to sign in as one.
2. The consent page names the client and the account it will act as. Choose **Full access**, or **Only these** and
   tick the scopes it may use.
3. Click **Allow**.

On a machine with no browser (over SSH, say), the client shows a code instead. Open
`https://<your app>/api/_c/oauth/v1/device/verify`, enter it under **Connect a device**, sign in and allow. Codes last
10 minutes.

Each sign-in becomes an API token named `<client> (OAuth)`, bound to exactly what you approved. It shows up under
**Settings → API tokens** with an `oauth: <client id>` label. Click **Revoke** to disconnect the client.
`pocketone logout` revokes a browser login from your terminal.

## From your terminal

On the machine that runs the app, the `token` command works on the app's data folder, even before the first serve:

```bash
pocketone token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci --scope deploy --ttl 720h   # prints the secret
pocketone token create --collection users --record user@example.com --name script
pocketone token list
pocketone token revoke <id>
pocketone token revoke --all --superuser admin@example.com
```

`--scope` can be repeated. Without `--ttl` the token never expires.

For CI that runs `pocketone` against your app, put the token in `P1_TOKEN` instead of signing in
([Remote CLI](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/remote)).

To let an app of your own sign people in, register it once:

```bash
pocketone oauth clients add --name "My app" --redirect https://myapp.example.com/callback
```

It prints the client id, and a secret once. Add `--public` for a desktop or mobile app with no secret. Claude, the
`pocketone` CLI and other MCP clients don't need this.

## From pb_hooks

Add your own scopes, and they show up in the dashboard and on the consent page:

```js
// pb_hooks/scopes.pb.js
$apiTokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes:read', description: 'Read notes',
  paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'], methods: ['GET'] })

routerAdd('GET', '/api/notes/summary', (e) => { /* ... */ },
  $apis.requireAuth(), $apiTokens.requireScope('notes:read'))
```

A collection rule can check a scope too: `@request.headers.x_token_scope_notes_read = "1"`.

A scope can also limit a token to some records. Register it with `values: { description: 'a note id' }`, and a token can
hold `notes=abc123` instead of all of `notes`. Your route checks the record with
`$apiTokens.hasScope(e, 'notes', id)`. In the dashboard, a ticked scope that takes values has a box for them; leave it
empty for every value.

## What a token can do

- **No scopes:** everything its owner can do.
- **With scopes:** only the requests its scopes cover. Anything else gets `403`.
- **Which scopes:** the ones features add (`deploy`, and one for each admin feature, often with a `:read`
  version, such as `restore` and `restore:read`), plus your own. Some, like `deploy`, only superusers can hold. The
  [CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli) and [MCP reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/mcp) name the scope each operation needs.
- **Expiry:** never, unless you set one. Tokens from a sign-in last 30 days, and the client renews them; AI agents'
  tokens never expire. Expired tokens are deleted once a day.
- **Gone with the account:** deleting an account deletes its tokens.
- **No way around a revoke:** a token can't be traded for a PocketBase auth token, so revoking it really ends its
  access.

Only superusers see **Settings → API tokens**. Other signed-in users manage their own tokens through the
[token API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/api-tokens/v1). A token with scopes can only create tokens within those scopes.

## Change it or turn it off

There's no `pocketone.yaml` key for API tokens: they're always on, and a token does nothing until someone creates one.
To limit what a token can do, give it scopes and an expiry, or revoke it. Every key is in the
[pocketone.yaml reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference).

To restyle the sign-in pages, copy them into your app with `pocketone template eject oauth`.

## How it works

- [API Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) stores the tokens (only a hash of each secret), checks them on every request and
  adds the dashboard screen.
- [OAuth server](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens/oauth) runs the sign-in and consent pages and issues tokens for what you
  approved.
- They answer the [api-tokens/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/api-tokens/v1) and [oauth/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/oauth/v1) contracts.
- [Templates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/templates) lets you restyle the sign-in pages.
