Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks

# Hooks

A hook is a function your app calls when something happens: a record is about to be created, a request asks for a
list, an email is about to go out, the app starts. Your function sees the event, can change it or stop it, and then
lets it go on. Hooks are how you add rules, side effects and integrations without changing PocketOne itself.

In JavaScript, hooks live in `pb_hooks/*.pb.ts` files, which PocketOne loads at start and reloads when they change. In
Go, you bind them on your `app` in your own build. The examples on this page show both.

## Your first hook

Make `pb_hooks/posts.pb.ts` in your app folder:

```ts
// pb_hooks/posts.pb.ts
onRecordCreate((e) => {
  e.record.set("slug", slugify(e.record.getString("title")))
  e.next()
}, "posts")

function slugify(s: string): string {
  return s.toLowerCase().trim().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-").replace(/^-|-$/g, "")
}
```

```go
app.OnRecordCreate("posts").BindFunc(func(e *core.RecordEvent) error {
	e.Record.Set("slug", slugify(e.Record.GetString("title")))
	return e.Next()
})
```

Create a post (in the dashboard, or with `POST /api/collections/posts/records`) and it's saved with a slug. Three
things in that example hold for every hook:

- **The handler gets the event** (`e`): here the record being created, the app (`e.app`), and for request hooks the
  request and who made it.
- **`e.next()` lets the event go on**: to the next handler, then to the action itself. Code before `e.next()` runs
  before the action (the record isn't saved yet); code after it runs once the action is done.
- **Tags narrow a hook**: `"posts"` makes it run only for that collection. Pass several (`"posts", "pages"`), or none
  for every collection.

PocketOne runs `.pb.ts` files directly, with no build step, and writes the whole JS API's types to `types.d.ts` next to
`pb_hooks`, so your editor completes `e.record.` and flags mistakes. See [QuickJS hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs) for imports,
async handlers, shared state and limits.

## Stop or change an action

Throw an error before `e.next()` and the action doesn't happen. In a hook triggered by an API request, the client gets
the error:

```ts
// pb_hooks/posts.pb.ts
onRecordCreateRequest((e) => {
  if (e.record.getString("title").length < 3) {
    throw new BadRequestError("A title needs at least 3 characters.")
  }
  e.next()
}, "posts")
```

```go
app.OnRecordCreateRequest("posts").BindFunc(func(e *core.RecordRequestEvent) error {
	if len(e.Record.GetString("title")) < 3 {
		return e.BadRequestError("A title needs at least 3 characters.", nil)
	}
	return e.Next()
})
```

The client gets `400` with `{"message": "A title needs at least 3 characters."}`. Change the event instead, and the
action goes on with your change: set a field on `e.record`, or filter what a list request returns.

## Before and after: which hook to use

Record hooks come in layers. Pick the one that matches when your code should run:

| You want to | Hook | Runs for |
|---|---|---|
| Fill in or check fields on every save, from anywhere (API, dashboard, your own code) | `onRecordCreate`, `onRecordUpdate`, `onRecordDelete`, `onRecordValidate` | every save |
| Do something once a save has really happened (send a mail, call a webhook) | `onRecordAfterCreateSuccess`, `onRecordAfterUpdateSuccess`, `onRecordAfterDeleteSuccess` | every save, after the transaction commits |
| Clean up when a save failed | `onRecordAfterCreateError` (and Update, Delete) | every failed save |
| Act on what a client asked for (check who's asking, change the input, change the answer) | `onRecordCreateRequest`, `onRecordUpdateRequest`, `onRecordDeleteRequest`, `onRecordViewRequest`, `onRecordsListRequest` | API requests only |
| Change how a record looks in every API answer (hide or add a field per user) | `onRecordEnrich` | every record the API returns, realtime included |

The model hooks (`onModelCreate` and the rest) are the same layers for anything saved, collections and logs included.
Collections have their own (`onCollectionCreate`...).

A side effect like sending mail belongs in an `AfterSuccess` hook: a plain `onRecordCreate` runs inside the save's
transaction, so if something later fails, the record is rolled back but your mail already went out.

```ts
// pb_hooks/welcome.pb.ts
onRecordAfterCreateSuccess((e) => {
  const message = new MailerMessage({
    from: { address: e.app.settings().meta.senderAddress, name: e.app.settings().meta.senderName },
    to: [{ address: e.record.email() }],
    subject: "Welcome!",
    html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
  })
  e.app.newMailClient().send(message)
  e.next()
}, "users")
```

```go
app.OnRecordAfterCreateSuccess("users").BindFunc(func(e *core.RecordEvent) error {
	message := &mailer.Message{
		From:    mail.Address{Address: e.App.Settings().Meta.SenderAddress, Name: e.App.Settings().Meta.SenderName},
		To:      []mail.Address{{Address: e.Record.Email()}},
		Subject: "Welcome!",
		HTML:    "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
	}
	if err := e.App.NewMailClient().Send(message); err != nil {
		e.App.Logger().Error("welcome mail", "error", err)
	}
	return e.Next()
})
```

## Who's asking

Request hooks know who made the request. `e.auth` is the signed-in record, or `null` for a guest; superusers are
records of the `_superusers` collection. Request hooks run after the collection's [API rule](https://pocketone.dev/docs/api-rules) has let
the request through, so this hook decides only with a rule that lets guests in (an empty create rule); with a rule like
`@request.auth.id != ''`, the rule turns guests away first:

```ts
// pb_hooks/posts.pb.ts
onRecordCreateRequest((e) => {
  if (!e.auth) {
    throw new UnauthorizedError("Sign in to post.")
  }
  if (!e.hasSuperuserAuth()) {
    e.record.set("author", e.auth.id) // members can't post as someone else
  }
  e.next()
}, "posts")
```

```go
app.OnRecordCreateRequest("posts").BindFunc(func(e *core.RecordRequestEvent) error {
	if e.Auth == nil {
		return e.UnauthorizedError("Sign in to post.", nil)
	}
	if !e.HasSuperuserAuth() {
		e.Record.Set("author", e.Auth.Id)
	}
	return e.Next()
})
```

Most "who may do what" rules don't need a hook at all: [API rules](https://pocketone.dev/docs/api-rules) express them as filters on the
collection. Use a hook when the rule needs code.

## The app's own events

Hooks with no record cover the app's life and its other parts:

| Hook | When |
|---|---|
| `onBootstrap` | the app starts and opens its database (after `e.next()` it's open) |
| `onServe` | the HTTP server starts (Go builds add routes here) |
| `onTerminate` | the app stops |
| `onMailerSend` | any email is about to go out (change it, or stop it) |
| `onRealtimeConnectRequest`, `onRealtimeSubscribeRequest`, `onRealtimeMessageSend` | realtime clients connect, subscribe and get messages |
| `onBackupCreate`, `onBackupRestore` | a backup is made or restored |
| `onSettingsReload` | the app's settings change |

Every hook, with its event's type, is in the [hooks table](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/javascript/pocketbase#hooks) of the
JavaScript API, and on [`core.App`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/go/pocketbase/core#app) in Go.

## Order and errors

- Handlers run in the order they were bound: within a file from top to bottom, files in alphabetical order. In Go,
  `Bind(&hook.Handler{Id: "...", Priority: -10, Func: ...})` runs a handler earlier (lower first) and gives it an id
  you can `Unbind`.
- A handler that doesn't call `e.next()` stops the chain: later handlers and the action don't run. That's how you
  skip an action without an error. Most hooks should call it.
- An error thrown in a request hook becomes the response (`BadRequestError` is 400, `ForbiddenError` 403,
  `NotFoundError` 404, `UnauthorizedError` 401, `TooManyRequestsError` 429). Any other error is a 400 with a generic
  message, and its own text goes to the logs, so clients never see internals.
  An error in a model hook fails the save, and the request that caused it.

## When hooks reload

PocketOne watches `pb_hooks`. Change a file and the app's JavaScript restarts with the new code, in a moment, without
dropping the database or other requests. In development (`pocketone serve --dev`), a file with an error is skipped and
logged, so the rest keep working; in production the app stops on it, so a broken deploy shows up at once. A Go build
picks up hook changes when you rebuild and restart it.

## Next

- [Custom routes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/routes): add your own API endpoints.
- [QuickJS hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs): imports, `async` handlers, shared state, memory and time limits.
- [Records](https://pocketone.dev/docs/records): read and write records from a hook.
- [JavaScript API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/javascript/pocketbase): every global, hook and type.

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/routes

# Custom routes

Your app already serves the [REST API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest) for its collections. A custom route adds an endpoint of
your own: a webhook receiver, a report, a search that joins three collections, anything that isn't plain record CRUD.

In JavaScript, add routes with `routerAdd` in a `pb_hooks/*.pb.ts` file. In Go, add them in an `onServe` hook.

## A first route

```ts
// pb_hooks/hello.pb.ts
routerAdd("GET", "/api/hello/{name}", (e) => {
  const name = e.request.pathValue("name")
  return e.json(200, { message: `Hello, ${name}!` })
})
```

```go
app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se *core.ServeEvent) error {
	se.Router.GET("/api/hello/{name}", func(e *core.RequestEvent) error {
		name := e.Request.PathValue("name")
		return e.JSON(200, map[string]string{"message": "Hello, " + name + "!"})
	})
	return se.Next()
})
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/hello/Ada
# {"message":"Hello, Ada!"}
```

- **Methods:** `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, or `*` for any.
- **Paths:** `{name}` matches one segment, `{path...}` the rest of the path. API routes usually go under `/api/` (but
  not `/api/collections/`, which is the built-in API's), with a prefix of your own so they never meet a future one.
- A route's answer is whatever the handler returns: `e.json`, `e.string`, `e.html`, `e.redirect`, `e.noContent`,
  `e.blob`, or `e.stream`.

To serve HTML pages for people, rather than an API, [Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages) is usually the better fit: a file
per route, with templates.

## Read the request

```ts
// pb_hooks/feedback.pb.ts
routerAdd("POST", "/api/feedback", (e) => {
  const data = new DynamicModel({ message: "", rating: 0 })
  e.bindBody(data) // JSON, form or multipart

  const info = e.requestInfo()
  const page = info.query["page"] // ?page=...

  if (data.message.trim() === "") {
    throw new BadRequestError("Write a message first.")
  }
  const record = new Record(e.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("feedback"))
  record.set("message", data.message)
  record.set("rating", data.rating)
  record.set("page", page)
  e.app.save(record)
  return e.json(201, { id: record.id })
})
```

```go
se.Router.POST("/api/feedback", func(e *core.RequestEvent) error {
	data := struct {
		Message string `json:"message" form:"message"`
		Rating  int    `json:"rating" form:"rating"`
	}{}
	if err := e.BindBody(&data); err != nil {
		return e.BadRequestError("Couldn't read the body.", err)
	}
	page := e.Request.URL.Query().Get("page")

	if strings.TrimSpace(data.Message) == "" {
		return e.BadRequestError("Write a message first.", nil)
	}
	collection, err := e.App.FindCollectionByNameOrId("feedback")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	record := core.NewRecord(collection)
	record.Set("message", data.Message)
	record.Set("rating", data.Rating)
	record.Set("page", page)
	if err := e.App.Save(record); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return e.JSON(201, map[string]string{"id": record.Id})
})
```

- `e.requestInfo()` has the request's `query`, `headers`, `body` (already parsed) and `auth` in one object.
- `e.request` is the underlying HTTP request: `e.request.pathValue(...)`, `e.request.header.get(...)`,
  `e.request.method`.
- Saving through `e.app.save` runs your [hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks) and validation, as any other save does.

## Require sign-in

Routes are open to anyone unless you say otherwise. Add a middleware after the handler:

```ts
// pb_hooks/me.pb.ts
routerAdd("GET", "/api/me/summary", (e) => {
  const posts = e.app.countRecords("posts", $dbx.hashExp({ author: e.auth.id }))
  return e.json(200, { email: e.auth.email(), posts })
}, $apis.requireAuth())
```

```go
se.Router.GET("/api/me/summary", func(e *core.RequestEvent) error {
	posts, err := e.App.CountRecords("posts", dbx.HashExp{"author": e.Auth.Id})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return e.JSON(200, map[string]any{"email": e.Auth.Email(), "posts": posts})
}).Bind(apis.RequireAuth())
```

| Middleware | Lets through |
|---|---|
| `$apis.requireAuth()` | any signed-in record; `requireAuth("users")` only records of those collections |
| `$apis.requireSuperuserAuth()` | superusers |
| `$apis.requireSuperuserOrOwnerAuth("id")` | superusers, or the record whose id is the `{id}` path parameter |
| `$apis.requireGuestOnly()` | requests with no auth (a sign-up form) |
| `$apis.bodyLimit(bytes)` | bodies up to that size |
| `$apis.gzip()` | (compresses the answer) |

A client signs in through the [Authentication](https://pocketone.dev/docs/authentication) API and sends its token in the `Authorization`
header; `e.auth` is then that record.

## Middleware of your own

A middleware is a function that takes the event and calls `e.next()` to go on. Pass it to one route, or to all of them
with `routerUse`:

```ts
// pb_hooks/timing.pb.ts
routerUse((e) => {
  const start = Date.now()
  e.next()
  e.app.logger().info("request", "path", e.request.url.path, "ms", Date.now() - start)
})
```

```go
se.Router.BindFunc(func(e *core.RequestEvent) error {
	start := time.Now()
	err := e.Next()
	e.App.Logger().Info("request", "path", e.Request.URL.Path, "ms", time.Since(start).Milliseconds())
	return err
})
```

In Go, `se.Router.Group("/api/shop")` makes a group whose routes share middleware.

## Errors

Throw one of the API errors and the client gets its status and message as JSON:

| Throw (JS) | Return (Go) | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `new BadRequestError(message, data?)` | `e.BadRequestError(message, err)` | 400 |
| `new UnauthorizedError(message)` | `e.UnauthorizedError(message, err)` | 401 |
| `new ForbiddenError(message)` | `e.ForbiddenError(message, err)` | 403 |
| `new NotFoundError(message)` | `e.NotFoundError(message, err)` | 404 |
| `new TooManyRequestsError(message)` | `e.TooManyRequestsError(message, err)` | 429 |
| `new ApiError(status, message, data?)` | `router.NewApiError(status, message, data)` | any |

```json
{ "status": 400, "message": "Write a message first.", "data": {} }
```

Any other error becomes a 400 with a generic message; its real text goes to the app's logs, so internals never reach
clients. A record that isn't found (`findRecordById` on a missing id) becomes a 404.

## Next

- [Hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks): run code on the built-in API's events instead.
- [Records](https://pocketone.dev/docs/records): find and save records from a route.
- [Calling other services](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/javascript/pocketbase#http): `$http.send` for webhooks out.
- [JavaScript API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/javascript/pocketbase): `routerAdd`, `$apis` and the request event's every method.

# QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript

PocketOne runs your `pb_hooks` and `pb_migrations` on [QuickJS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm) instead of goja, the engine
stock PocketBase uses. It's the same JS API (`$app`, `routerAdd`, `onRecordCreate`, `cronAdd`, `$http`, …), so your
existing hooks run unchanged. On top of that you get:

- **Shared globals.** Top-level helpers and state are visible to every handler.
- **Imports.** ES modules with `import`/`export`, and `node_modules` packages.
- **TypeScript.** `.ts` hooks run directly.
- **Async.** Handlers can `await`, and the app keeps serving other requests while they wait.
- **Limits.** A runaway script stops with an error instead of taking the app down.

Each app gets one QuickJS VM. The engine is pure Go, so builds need no cgo, as with stock PocketBase.

This tutorial builds a small app that tries each of these. Every example below was run on `pocketone`, and the outputs
are real.

## Set up

Make a folder for the app, create a superuser, and start it:

```bash
mkdir -p qjs/pb_hooks/lib && cd qjs
pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com password --dir=pb_data
pocketone serve --dir=pb_data
```

Leave it running. PocketOne watches `pb_hooks`, so each file you add below is picked up without a restart.

## 1. Your PocketBase hooks run unchanged

Here's a hook written for stock PocketBase, with `require()` inside the handler and the global `$app`:

```js
// pb_hooks/legacy.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/legacy", (e) => {
  const util = require(`${__hooks}/lib/util.cjs`)
  return e.json(200, { shout: util.shout("hello"), users: $app.countRecords("users") })
})
```

```js
// pb_hooks/lib/util.cjs
module.exports = { shout: (s) => s.toUpperCase() + "!" }
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/legacy
# {"shout":"HELLO!","users":0}
```

A plain `.pb.js` file is still a CommonJS script, as in PocketBase. Nothing in it needs to change.

## 2. Top-level code is shared by every handler

On goja, each handler runs in a separate runtime from a pool, so it can't see the variables at the top of its own file.
That's why PocketBase hooks call `require()` inside every handler. On QuickJS, every hook file runs in the app's one
global scope:

```js
// pb_hooks/counter.pb.js
let hits = 0
function greet(name) {
  return `hi ${name}`
}

routerAdd("GET", "/hits", (e) => {
  hits++
  return e.json(200, { hits, msg: greet("there") })
})
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hits   # {"hits":1,"msg":"hi there"}
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hits   # {"hits":2,"msg":"hi there"}
```

The same file on goja (`pocketone serve --jsvm goja`) answers every request with a 400, because the handler can't see
`hits` or `greet`.

Globals live as long as the app's VM. A restart or a change to `pb_hooks` starts a fresh one (`hits` goes back to 0),
so keep anything that must last in the database. Use globals for caches, helpers and constants.

Hook files run before the app opens its database, as in PocketBase. A `$app` query at a file's top level fails, so to
fill a global from the database, do it in `onBootstrap`:

```js
let users = null
onBootstrap((e) => {
  e.next() // the database is open after this
  users = e.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("users")
})
```

## 3. Split your code into modules

Name a hook file `.pb.mjs` and it's an ES module, with `import` and `export`:

```js
// pb_hooks/lib/slug.mjs
export const slugify = (s) =>
  s.toLowerCase().trim().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-").replace(/^-|-$/g, "")
```

```js
// pb_hooks/modules.pb.mjs
import { slugify } from "./lib/slug.mjs"

routerAdd("GET", "/slug/{text}", (e) => {
  return e.json(200, { slug: slugify(e.request.pathValue("text")) })
})
```

```bash
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8090/slug/Hello%20World%21"
# {"slug":"hello-world"}
```

- `.mjs` files are ES modules; `.js` and `.cjs` files are CommonJS. Both kinds can load each other.
- `import` and `require()` find files the same way: relative paths first, then packages in `node_modules`.
- A module loads once per app, so every file that imports it shares the same instance and its state.

## 4. Write hooks in TypeScript

Name the file `.pb.ts` and write TypeScript:

```ts
// pb_hooks/typed.pb.ts
interface Total {
  count: number
  label: string
}

function total(count: number): Total {
  return { count, label: `${count} users` }
}

routerAdd("GET", "/typed", (e) => {
  return e.json(200, total(e.app.countRecords("users")))
})
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/typed
# {"count":0,"label":"0 users"}
```

PocketOne removes the types when it loads the file, with no build step. An error names the line in your `.ts` file.
Types aren't checked at run time: run `tsc --noEmit` or rely on your editor. The app writes the whole JS API's types to
`types.d.ts` in your project folder, next to `pb_hooks`, and a `tsconfig.json` that uses it if you don't have one
([JSVM page](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm#types)).

## 5. Async handlers

A handler can be `async`. Every Go function has an `.async` twin that does its work outside the VM and returns a
promise:

```js
// pb_hooks/async.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/slow", async (e) => {
  await sleep.async(2000) // waits outside the VM
  const n = await e.app.countRecords.async("users")
  return e.json(200, { waited: "2s", users: n })
})
```

Call `/slow`, and call `/hits` while it waits:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/slow &
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hits
```

`/hits` answered after 0.35 s, and `/slow` after 2.06 s. The app went on serving requests while `/slow` waited.

Without `.async`, a call that waits (`$http.send`, `sleep`) still lets other requests run, but those requests nest on
one stack and wait on each other: under load, a plain `sleep(100)` served 19 requests a second where
`await sleep.async(100)` served 481 ([How it performs](#how-it-performs)). Use `.async` for anything slow.

Two things to watch:
- After an `await`, other requests may have run in between. Use `e.app`, not the global `$app`.
- A transaction holds SQLite's write lock, so keep it short across `await`s.

### Timers

`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearTimeout`, `clearInterval` and `queueMicrotask` work as in browsers and Node.js, so
code and npm packages that use them run unchanged:

```js
// pb_hooks/timers.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/later", async (e) => {
  const word = await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 500, "later"))
  return e.string(200, word)
})
```

Each run of a timer's callback is a separate task with its own time limits. A thrown error is logged and the app carries
on.

A timer set while a request is being served belongs to that request: it's cleared once the request has its answer, or
when the client goes away. So a callback never writes to a response that's already finished. A handler that streams
from a timer stays open by waiting (`await new Promise(() => {})`) until the client leaves. Timers set at the top of a
hook file or in a cron job run until cleared. An app can have 1024 timers pending at once.

### Why there's no VM pool

goja runs JS synchronously: while a handler waits on the database or an HTTP call, its runtime can't do anything else.
To serve requests at the same time, PocketBase keeps a pool of runtimes (15 by default, `--hooksPool`) and makes more
when they're all busy. Each runtime loads every hook file separately. That's why a handler can't see the top of its own
file, why state can't be shared between requests, and why memory grows with load.

QuickJS here works like a Node.js process. Each app has one VM with an event loop. While a handler waits, the loop runs
other requests, and the handler picks up again when its result arrives. There's one copy of your code and your
globals, so nothing needs a pool (`--hooksPool` is accepted and ignored).

As in Node.js, the JS itself runs one piece at a time. A handler that computes for a long time holds the loop until it
finishes or hits its time budget. Keep heavy work out of the request path, or move it into Go.

## 6. Memory and time limits

Each app has a memory cap, and each task has a time budget:

```js
// pb_hooks/limits.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/hog", (e) => {
  const junk = []
  while (true) junk.push("x".repeat(1024 * 1024))
})

routerAdd("GET", "/spin", (e) => {
  while (true) {}
})
```

Both requests fail and the app keeps running:

| Request | Stopped after | Error in the request log |
|---|---|---|
| `/hog` | 0.08 s | `InternalError: out of memory at pb_hooks/limits.pb.js:3:36` |
| `/spin` | 5.0 s | `InternalError: interrupted at pb_hooks/limits.pb.js:5:27` |

Calls to `/hits` right after each one answered normally.

These are the limits in the `pocketone` binary:

| Limit | What it counts | Default | `js_limits` key |
|---|---|---|---|
| Memory | The JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds, for the whole app | 64 MiB | `memory` |
| JS time | Time spent running JS in one stretch of a task | 5 s | `task_time` |
| Wall time | Clock time of one stretch, sync Go calls (`sleep`, `$http.send`, queries) included | 30 s | `task_wall` |
| Await time | Clock time of a whole async handler, from its start until it returns, awaits included | 15 min | `await_time` |

A stretch is the JS between two `await`s: the start of a handler up to its first `await`, then each part that runs
when an awaited result comes back. A handler without `await` is one stretch. JS time and wall time start over with each
stretch. While a handler is awaiting an `.async` call (`sleep.async`, `e.app.save.async`, an `$llm` provider call,
`$http.send.async`), no JS runs and the VM serves other requests, so the wait counts toward none of the first three
limits, only toward await time.

So a handler can await a slow provider call for a minute or two, and a loop of awaits can run for several minutes,
while a loop that computes without awaiting is still stopped after 5 s:

```js
// pb_hooks/long.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/long", async (e) => {
  for (let i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
    await sleep.async(10000) // 60 s in all, none of it JS time
  }
  return e.json(200, { waited: "60s" })
})
```

When a handler passes its await time, or the client goes away (the browser closed the tab, a proxy gave up), the
request fails and the handler stops at its next `await`: the result of the call it's waiting for is dropped, the code
after the `await` never runs, and a new `.async` call from it throws. Work it handed off with no `await` (a detached
promise) keeps running after the handler returns.

Change the limits in `pocketone.yaml` ([pocketone.yaml](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml)):

```yaml
app:
  js_limits:
    memory: 128MiB # the JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds
    task_time: 10s # JS time per stretch
    task_wall: 60s # wall time per stretch, sync Go calls included
    await_time: 30m # a whole async handler, awaits included
```

With `task_time: 1s`, `/spin` stopped after 1.0 s instead of 5. A custom Go build sets the same limits in
`jsvm.Config.VM` ([JSVM](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm#configure)). On a multisite host each app has its own VM and its own
limits, so one app's runaway script doesn't stop the others.

### Jobs that take minutes

Await time allows a long request, but the network in front of your app usually doesn't. Cloudflare closes a proxied
request after about 100 seconds with no answer, and other proxies and browsers have their own limits. A request that
waits through minutes of work gets cut off on the way, and its handler stops with it.

For work that takes longer than a few seconds (generating images or audio, a chain of provider calls, a big import),
answer at once and do the work in the background:

1. The request saves a record for the job, starts the work without awaiting it, and answers with the record's id.
2. The work saves its progress and results on that record as it goes.
3. The page polls the record (or subscribes to it with realtime) and shows the progress.

```js
// pb_hooks/jobs.pb.js
routerAdd("POST", "/jobs", (e) => {
  const job = new Record(e.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("jobs"))
  job.set("status", "running")
  e.app.save(job)
  runJob(e.app, job.id) // no await: it keeps running after this answer
  return e.json(202, { id: job.id })
})

async function runJob(app, id) {
  const save = async (fields) => {
    const job = await app.findRecordById.async("jobs", id)
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(fields)) job.set(k, v)
    await app.save.async(job)
  }
  try {
    for (let step = 1; step <= 5; step++) {
      await sleep.async(10000) // stands in for a slow provider call
      await save({ progress: step * 20 })
    }
    await save({ status: "done" })
  } catch (err) {
    await save({ status: "failed", error: String(err) })
  }
}
```

The page then reads `/api/collections/jobs/records/<id>` every few seconds until `status` is `done`. A detached job
isn't tied to any request, so await time and abandoned requests don't stop it, but it isn't saved anywhere either: a
restart (a deploy, a hooks change) ends it. Keep its state on the record, so a job left `running` after a restart can
be found and started again (by a `cronAdd` job, say).

## How it performs

The same hook file, on the `pocketone` binary with each engine (QuickJS, and `--jsvm goja` with its default pool of 15):

```js
// pb_hooks/bench.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/b/ping", (e) => e.json(200, { ok: true }))
routerAdd("GET", "/b/db", (e) => e.json(200, { n: e.app.findRecordsByFilter("_superusers", "id != ''", "", 10, 0).length }))
routerAdd("GET", "/b/cpu", (e) => {
  const items = []
  for (let i = 0; i < 2000; i++) items.push({ id: i, name: "item" + i, tags: ["a", "b", "c"] })
  return e.json(200, { n: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(items)).length })
})
routerAdd("GET", "/b/wait", (e) => { sleep(100); return e.json(200, { ok: true }) })
routerAdd("GET", "/b/waitasync", async (e) => { await sleep.async(100); return e.json(200, { ok: true }) })
```

Each route got 50 concurrent clients for 10 seconds (`hey -c 50 -z 10s`, after a 3-second warm-up), with
`--dev=false`, on an Apple M1 Max (10 cores):

| Route | QuickJS req/s | p50 | p99 | goja req/s | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A JSON reply | 19,471 | 2.2 ms | 9.4 ms | 55,901 | 0.8 ms | 3.3 ms |
| A database query (10 rows) | 18,116 | 1.9 ms | 12.8 ms | 40,447 | 0.8 ms | 7.9 ms |
| CPU-heavy JS (2,000-object JSON round trip) | 84 | 591 ms | 648 ms | 409 | 91 ms | 525 ms |
| Waits 100 ms with `sleep(100)` | 19 | 1.93 s | 12.0 s | 491 | 102 ms | 113 ms |
| Waits 100 ms with `await sleep.async(100)` | 481 | 103 ms | 110 ms | – | – | – |

| Memory (resident) | QuickJS | goja |
|---|---|---|
| Idle, after start | 46 MB | 49 MB |
| After all the routes above | 313 MB | 3.1 GB |

What it shows:

- **goja does more requests a second.** Its pool runs handlers on every core at once. QuickJS runs an app's JS on one
  thread, like Node.js: about 18,000 short requests a second for one app, on one core.
- **QuickJS uses a tenth of the memory.** goja's runtimes each hold a copy of every hook file, and it makes more of them
  as load grows. On a host running many apps, that's the difference that counts.
- **Waiting costs nothing with `.async`.** `await sleep.async(100)` kept pace with goja's pool. A plain `sleep(100)`
  didn't, so use `.async` for anything slow.
- **CPU-heavy JS is slower.** Move heavy work into Go, a cron job, or a background task.

## Going back to goja

To run an app on PocketBase's own engine, set it in `pocketone.yaml`:

```yaml
app:
  jsvm: goja
```

You can also pass `--jsvm goja`. The startup lines list what that turns off: pages, `$mcp`, `$tokens`, `$bulkmail`, JS
contracts, shared globals and async handlers.

## Next

- [JSVM](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm): every file type, module resolution rule and setting.
- [Hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/hooks) and [Custom routes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/routes): what to write in a hook file.
- [JavaScript API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/javascript/pocketbase): every global, hook and type.
- [LLM skills for coding agents](https://pocketone.dev/docs/agents): give your agent the PocketOne skill so it writes hooks the QuickJS way.

# WASM

**Bring your own WASM.** Your page code is TypeScript, and most of the time that's all you need. Sometimes it isn't: the library you need only exists in Rust or Go, or the work (parsing, image processing, crypto, number crunching) is too slow in JS. WASM lets your page code call code written in another language, compiled to WebAssembly, as if it were a JavaScript function:

```ts
const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ greeting: string }>("hello", { name: "pocket" })
// out is { greeting: "Hello, POCKET!" }
```

It's built into `pocketone`. There's nothing to install and nothing to configure: put a module in `pb_hooks/` and call it from your page code.

## How it works

A module is a small program compiled to WebAssembly: a `.pb.wasm` file in `pb_hooks/`. A call works like running a command-line tool:

1. Your code calls `$wasm.run.async(name, input)`.
2. The module starts fresh, reads the input, and writes its answer.
3. Your code gets the answer back, parsed from JSON, and carries on.

The module runs in a sealed box. It can't touch your database, your files, the network or other programs; it sees only the input your code gives it, and its answer goes only back to your code. Your code stays in charge: it decides what goes in and what to do with what comes out. A module that crashes, loops or runs out of memory fails its own call, and the app goes on.

## Try it in two minutes

You don't need a compiler to try it. The Markdown module from the [recipes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/markdown) is kept built in the repository. In your app's folder:

```bash
curl -L -o pb_hooks/markdown.pb.wasm \
  https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/raw/main/ext/wasm/example/markdown/markdown.pb.wasm
```

Add an API route that saves a note with its Markdown rendered to HTML:

```ts
// pb_pages/notes.ts
export async function post(ctx: any) {
  const { body } = ctx.req.body()
  const note = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("notes"))
  note.load({ body, html: await $wasm.run.async<string>("markdown", body) })
  ctx.app.save(note)
  return ctx.res.json(201, { id: note.id, html: note.getString("html") })
}
```

Make a `notes` collection with two text fields, `body` and `html`, then post a note with `# Hello` and some `**bold**` text in its body:

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:8090/notes -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"body":"# Hello\n\nSome **bold** text"}'
```

The saved note's `html` field is the rendered HTML. This module passes raw HTML through, so for text your users write, add [Sanitize HTML](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/sanitize-html) after it.

## Write your first module

A module is an ordinary program: it reads its input from stdin and prints its answer to stdout. Here's one in Go:

```go
// main.go
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"os"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	var in struct {
		Name string `json:"name"`
	}
	json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&in)
	if in.Name == "" {
		os.Stderr.WriteString(`{"code":"no_name","message":"say who to greet"}`)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(map[string]string{
		"greeting": "Hello, " + strings.ToUpper(in.Name) + "!",
	})
}
```

Build it into your `pb_hooks/`. Go can build WebAssembly with nothing extra; [TinyGo](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/tinygo) makes the same program 15 times smaller and much faster to call:

```bash
GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o pb_hooks/hello.pb.wasm .                    # Go: 4.3 MB
tinygo build -target=wasip1 -opt=z -no-debug -scheduler=none -o pb_hooks/hello.pb.wasm .   # TinyGo: 284 KB
```

Call it from an API route:

```ts
// pb_pages/hello/[name].ts
export async function get(ctx: any) {
  const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ greeting: string }>("hello", { name: ctx.params.name })
  return ctx.res.json(out)
}
```

```bash
curl localhost:8090/hello/pocket
# {"greeting":"Hello, POCKET!"}
```

That's the whole contract:

- **Input:** your code's value arrives on stdin, as JSON (a string or bytes arrive as they are).
- **Output:** what the module prints comes back to your code, parsed if it's JSON.
- **Errors:** to fail, the module exits non-zero. If it prints `{"code", "message"}` to stderr, your code's `catch` gets those as `err.code` and `err.message`.

## Good to know

- **Calls are async.** Use `await $wasm.run.async(...)` in an `async` handler. The module runs off the JS engine, so the rest of your app keeps serving requests while it works.
- **Every call starts fresh.** Nothing carries over from one call to the next, so a module can't remember anything. When it needs to, your code keeps the state and passes it in: see [Keeping state in JS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/guides/state).
- **The first call compiles, later calls don't.** A module's first call compiles it and keeps the result on disk; every later call, after a restart too, loads it from there. A C, Rust or Zig module takes 17 to 33 ms the first time and 1 to 2 ms after; a Go module about a second, then 38 ms. [Choosing a language](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages) compares them.
- **Modules deploy with your app.** They live in `pb_hooks/`, so git, `pocketone deploy` and anything else that ships `pb_hooks/` ships them too. Replacing a module's file takes effect on the next call.

## Next

- **[Choosing a language](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages):** C and C++, Go, TinyGo, Rust, Zig, AssemblyScript, and what else runs.
- **[Recipes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes):** modules built on real libraries, each with page code that calls it: Markdown, HTML sanitizing, thumbnails, QR codes, diffs, CSV.
- **[Keeping state in JS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/guides/state):** modules that work on a series, with the state held by your app.
- **[Extension reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/extension):** every call, error code, limit and setting, and how it works inside.

# Bulk mail

Got a newsletter, a launch or a change to announce? Write it once, pick which users get it, and your app sends it at a
steady pace through its own mail settings. Every message gets an unsubscribe link, and people who unsubscribe, bounce
or complain are never mailed again.

This is on for every PocketOne app. Nothing is sent until a superuser starts a campaign.

## Before your first campaign

1. Sign in to the dashboard as a superuser and open **Settings → Mail**. Set up your mail server and sender there, as
   you would for any PocketBase app. Campaigns send through them.
2. Below that form, in the **Bulk mail** section, fill in **Postal address**. It's shown in every campaign footer, and
   anti-spam laws require one. Click **Save bulk mail settings**.
3. Open **Settings → Application** and check that **Application URL** is the address people reach your app on.
   Unsubscribe links are built from it.

## Send a campaign from the dashboard

1. Open **Mail** in the dashboard menu and click **New campaign**. It starts as a draft for the verified users of
   `users`.
2. Fill in **Name**, **Subject** and **Body**. Use `{{record.name}}` (any field of the user's record), `{{email}}` and
   `{{campaign.name}}` to fill in each message.
3. Under **Audience**, pick who gets it. With **Filter**, choose the **Collection**, an optional **Filter** in the same
   syntax as API rules (such as `verified = true`), and the **Email field**. Click **Count recipients** to see how
   many match, how many are suppressed, and a few sample addresses.
4. Click **Save changes**. Click **Preview** to see the message for one recipient, or fill in **Test address** and
   click **Send test**.
5. Click **Send** and confirm.

The campaign page shows its progress and a **Recipients** table. While it runs, you can **Pause**, **Resume** or
**Cancel** it.

To send later, set **Schedule (UTC)** before you save. The button then says **Schedule**. To send slower than your
app's limit, set **Max per second**.

For audiences a filter can't express, choose **SQL** and write a read-only `SELECT` that returns an `email` column.
Every other column it returns can be used in the message as `{{record.column}}`. A view works too: pick it as the
**Collection**.

## Send it again to new users

Each address gets a campaign at most once. Click **Send** on a finished campaign and only users who match now but
weren't mailed before get it.

## From your terminal

Write the campaign in the dashboard first. Then sign in to your app once
([Remote CLI](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/remote)) and run it from your terminal:

```bash
pocketone remote bulkmail preview --campaign <id>                  # see the message
pocketone remote bulkmail test --campaign <id> --to you@example.com
pocketone remote bulkmail start --campaign <id>
pocketone remote bulkmail pause --campaign <id>                    # also resume, cancel
```

`--limit 100` on `start` queues at most 100 new recipients, to send a campaign in batches. To see who an audience
reaches before you send:

```bash
pocketone remote bulkmail count --audience '{"collection": "users", "filter": "verified = true", "email_field": "email"}'
```

## From pb_hooks

`$bulkmail` does the same from your JS hooks:

```js
const { count, suppressed } = $bulkmail.count({ collection: "users", filter: "verified = true", email_field: "email" })
$bulkmail.start("CAMPAIGN_ID")
$bulkmail.suppress("someone@example.com")
```

## From an agent

An agent connected to your app over [MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/mcp) has a tool for each step: `bulkmail_count`,
`bulkmail_preview`, `bulkmail_test`, `bulkmail_start`, `bulkmail_pause`, `bulkmail_resume` and `bulkmail_cancel`.
Count and preview need a token with the `bulkmail:read` scope, the rest the `bulkmail` scope. Only superusers can run
campaigns.

## Unsubscribes, bounces and complaints

- **Unsubscribe:** every message ends with a footer holding your postal address and an unsubscribe link. It also
  carries the one-click unsubscribe headers that Gmail and Yahoo require from bulk senders. Opening the link shows a
  confirm button, so link scanners can't unsubscribe anyone.
- **Suppressions:** **Mail → Suppressions** lists the addresses that never get campaign mail, whatever the audience
  says. Unsubscribes are added automatically. Click **Add address** to add one by hand, or **Export CSV** to download
  the list.
- **Bounces and complaints:** to add those to the list too, open **Bounces and complaints** in the **Bulk mail**
  section. For Amazon SES, subscribe your SNS topic to the **Amazon SES (SNS) endpoint** shown there. For other
  providers, set a **Webhook secret** and point the provider at the **Generic webhook** URL.

## Limits

- Your app sends at most **5 messages a second** and **5,000 a day** (UTC), across all campaigns. The **Bulk mail**
  section shows your app's limits and how many it sent today. A host may set other limits for your app.
- A message counts as sent only once the mail server accepts it, so a restart doesn't send twice or skip anyone.
- A permanent error from the mail server fails that recipient. Other errors are retried, up to three attempts.
- A campaign pauses itself when more than 5% of its sends fail after the first 100, or when spam complaints pass 0.3%
  of its sends (at least 3). The reason shows next to its status.

## Try it locally

In dev mode with SMTP off, `pocketone` catches every mail, campaigns included, in an inbox at http://127.0.0.1:8025:

```bash
pocketone serve --dev
```

## Change it

There's no `pocketone.yaml` section for bulk mail; the [pocketone.yaml reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference) lists none.
Sending uses your **Settings → Mail** server and sender, and you lower the pace per campaign with **Max per second**.

## How it works

- [Bulk Mail](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bulkmail) runs the campaigns, the pages in the dashboard and `$bulkmail`.
- [bulkmail/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/bulkmail/v1) is the contract behind the command, the REST API and the MCP tools.
- [mail.suppression/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/mail.suppression/v1) keeps the suppression list and the unsubscribe link.
- [mail.feedback/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/mail.feedback/v1) takes bounce and complaint reports from your mail provider.

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm

# AI in your app

**Your app can call cloud models.** `$llm` writes text, draws pictures, reads text aloud, writes down what's said in
audio, makes music and video, and turns text into vectors for search. You bring the provider accounts and keys;
PocketOne connects them to your pages' code and your Go code.

```ts
const r: LlmTextAnswer = await $llm.text.completeAsync({
  model: "vultr/glm-5.3",
  prompt: "Summarize in one sentence: " + record.getString("body"),
  reasoning: "off",
})
// r.text is the summary
```

```go
r, err := textv1.Contract.Must(app).Complete(ctx, extkit.Internal, textv1.CompleteInput{
	Model: "vultr/glm-5.3", Prompt: "Summarize in one sentence: " + record.GetString("body"), Reasoning: "off"})
// r.Text is the summary
```

The examples show each thing in TypeScript, as [Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/overview) page code (endpoints
and a page's `.ts`), and in Go. The Go examples call the contract packages (`textv1` is
`pocketone.dev/ext/contracts/llm/text/v1`) with a `context.Context` named `ctx`.

## Add a provider

Open your dashboard, go to **Settings → LLM** and add a provider:

- **Vultr** (Serverless Inference): every kind, music and video included. Paste your API key.
- **Cloudflare Workers AI**: text, pictures, speech, transcription and embeddings, with a free daily allowance. Enter
  your account ID and a token with Workers AI permission.
- **OpenRouter**: one key for hundreds of models. Pictures need credits on your OpenRouter account; small text models
  run on its free allowance.
- **OpenAI-compatible API**: OpenAI, Groq, Together, or a model on your own machine with Ollama or llama-server. Give the
  endpoint with its version path (`http://localhost:11434/v1` for Ollama).

Press **New provider** and pick its type. Give it a short name (it's how your code picks it) and its key, press its
**Test**, then **Save changes**.

## Name a model

Every call names its model as `provider/model`: the name you gave the provider, a slash, and the provider's own id for
the model. With providers named `vultr`, `cf` and `or`:

| Model | Means |
|---|---|
| `vultr/glm-5.3` | Vultr's `glm-5.3` |
| `cf/@cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast` | Workers AI's Llama 3.3 |
| `or/black-forest-labs/flux.2-klein-4b` | OpenRouter's FLUX.2 Klein |

To see what you can use, ask: `$llm.text.modelsAsync()`, `$llm.image.modelsAsync()` and so on list each provider's models of that
kind, with their prices where the provider lists them.

Keep model names in one place in your app (a `_private/models.ts` module, say), so changing provider is one edit.

## What you can do

- [Structured answers](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/structured): get JSON back that matches a schema.
- [Streaming answers](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/streaming): show an answer as it's written.
- [Pictures, speech and music](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/media): generate files and save them on records.
- [Conversations](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/conversations): chats that remember, with LLM Chat.
- [Search and RAG](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/search): retrieval-augmented generation over your own files, web pages, Git repositories
  and records: knowledge bases (buckets), hybrid search with `$llm.search`, and `enrich` to ground any call in them.
- [Limits](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/limits): cap what the app spends, per day or month, for the whole app, each user and each guest.
- [Custom limits](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/custom-limits): your own rules in code with `$llm.onCall` and `$llm.onCallDone`: plan tiers, credits, team buckets.
- [Users and guests](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/users-and-guests): `$llm.for(ctx)`, so per-user and per-guest limits apply.
- [Spend and the ledger](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/spend): `$llm.ledger`: what's left of each limit, what someone spent, where the money goes.

Every member of `$llm`, with its options and types, is in the [LLM JavaScript API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/javascript/llm) reference, generated from the declarations your editor sees in `types.d.ts`.

## Thinking models

Many models think before they answer, and their thinking counts toward `maxTokens`. For short jobs (a label, a title,
some JSON) say `reasoning: "off"`; otherwise a short `maxTokens` can be spent entirely on thinking and the answer comes
back empty. For hard questions, `"high"` lets the model think longer. A model that doesn't think ignores it.

## When something goes wrong

A failed call throws an `Error` whose `code` says what went wrong, with a message you can show:

```ts
try {
  const r = await $llm.for(ctx).text.completeAsync({ model: "vultr/glm-5.3", prompt })
} catch (err: any) {
  if (err.code === "limit") return ctx.res.json(429, { error: err.message })   // "limit reached: ..., it resets at 00:00 UTC"
  throw err
}
```

| Code | Means |
|---|---|
| `not_configured` | No provider in Settings → LLM yet. |
| `unknown_model` | No model named, or no provider by that name. |
| `not_supported` | That kind of provider doesn't do this (music on Cloudflare, say). |
| `provider` | The provider said no: a wrong key, no credits, a model it doesn't have. Its message is kept, with your provider's name in front. |
| `timeout` | The provider didn't answer in time, and the request was cancelled. The message names the model and what ran out. Worth a retry. |
| `limit` | A limit refused the call before it reached the provider: one in Settings → LLM or your own ([Limits](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/guides/limits)). |

### Time limits

A provider sometimes drops a request and never answers. Calls don't wait on one for long:

- **Text** is always streamed from the provider, even from `completeAsync`, so a stalled answer is spotted as soon as
  the provider goes quiet: after 10 seconds with nothing from Vultr or OpenRouter (both send something every second
  while a model works, thinking included), 30 from Cloudflare, 2 minutes from other OpenAI-compatible APIs (OpenAI
  sends nothing while its reasoning models think, and a local server may take a while to read a long prompt).
- **Every call** also has an overall limit: 10 minutes for text, 3 for a picture, 2 for speech or alignment, 5 for a
  transcription, 1 for embeddings or starting a music or video job (following one with `wait` has its own limit).

Either one cancels the request and throws with code `timeout`: `vultr/glm-5.3: the provider sent nothing for 10s, so
the call was cancelled`, or `...: no answer in 3m0s, so the call was cancelled`.

To give up sooner, pass a `signal` (an [`AbortSignal`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs#cancelling-go-calls)) in any call's options. When
it fires, the promise rejects with its reason and the provider's request is cancelled:

```js
// at most 30 seconds, even in background work after the response was sent
const a = await $llm.text.completeAsync({ model: "vultr/glm-5.3", prompt, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) })

// or stop it yourself: a "Stop" button, a newer question
const c = new AbortController()
const s = $llm.text.streamAsync({ model, prompt, signal: c.signal }, (t) => { /* ... */ })
c.abort() // s rejects with an AbortError
```

`AbortSignal.timeout` rejects with a `DOMException` named `TimeoutError`, `abort()` with one named `AbortError`. The
same `signal` works on `chat.sendAsync(text, { signal })`. Go code passes a context with an earlier deadline, or
cancels it.

## Costs

Every call is billed by your provider, on your account. Every answer's `usage` says what it used, and
`usage.costMicroUSD` what it cost, in millionths of a US dollar (`1000000` is $1, so `usage.costMicroUSD / 1e6` is
dollars). It's a whole number, so costs add up exactly, and it's on every answer of every kind: what the provider
charged when it says (OpenRouter always does; Vultr does for media), else worked out from the model's listed prices,
with `usage.costEstimated` true, else `0` (free, or no prices PocketOne can count).

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/mcp

# MCP for AI agents

Point Claude, or any other MCP client, at your app and sign in. The agent can then read and change your data, check on
the app and run admin tasks, as you and with your rights, nothing more.

Every PocketOne app serves MCP at `/mcp`. It's on by default. You don't need to set anything up.

## Connect Claude

1. In your MCP client, add `https://<your app>/mcp` as a remote MCP server. In Claude, that's a custom connector.
2. A browser opens on your app's sign-in page. Sign in as an app user, or click **Sign in as a superuser**.
3. The consent page names the client and the account it will act as. Choose **Full access**, or **Only these** and tick
   what the agent may do.
4. Click **Allow**.

The agent stays connected until you disconnect it.

In Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http my-app https://<your app>/mcp
claude mcp login my-app        # or /mcp in a session
```

Claude and Claude Code connect without any setup on your side. Other MCP clients register themselves with your app
first.

## What the agent can do

Every tool call is one request to your app's own API, made as whoever signed in. Your API rules, hooks and rate limits
apply as they would to any request.

- **PocketBase's whole API**, as `pb_*` tools: records (`pb_list_records`, `pb_create_record`, …), files and auth for
  everyone; collections, settings, logs, crons, SQL and backups for superusers. SQL (`pb_run_sql`) goes straight to
  the database, past API rules and hooks.
- **Admin tasks** each feature adds, such as `restore_points` and `restore_restore_to` to
  [undo a mistake](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/restore), or `remote_status` and `remote_logs` to check on the app. The
  [MCP reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/mcp) lists them all.
- **Your app's own tools**, from `pb_hooks` (below).

A superuser gets what the API gives superusers. An app user gets what your collection rules give them, and doesn't see
the superuser-only tools.

## Add your own tools

Write the endpoint as you would anyway, then declare its tool at the top level of a `pb_hooks` file:

```js
// pb_hooks/blog.pb.js
routerAdd('POST', '/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish', (e) => { /* … */ }, $apis.requireSuperuserAuth())

$mcp.addEndpoint({
  name: 'blog_publish_post',
  description: 'Publish a draft post and email subscribers.',
  method: 'POST',
  path: '/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish', // {id} comes from the tool's id argument
  inputSchema: { type: 'object', required: ['id'], properties: { id: { type: 'string' } } },
})
$mcp.instructions('blog_publish_post also emails subscribers.')
```

The tool runs the request as the caller, so the route's own auth check is what protects it. When your app has its own
tools, agents are told to prefer them over `pb_*`.

## What's covered

- **Limited to scopes:** with **Only these**, each call is checked like a request from an
  [API token](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/tokens) with those scopes. Calls they don't cover get `403`, and tools they can't reach
  are hidden.
- **Only for MCP:** the agent's token works on `/mcp` and nowhere else.
- **Not tools:** sign-in endpoints that hand out a new token, and realtime subscriptions. A file download through
  `pb_download_file` is capped at 10 MB.
- **Browsers:** a web page on another site can't call `/mcp`. Clients that send no `Origin` header, such as Claude's
  servers and Claude Code, can.

Anyone who can sign in to your app can connect an agent, with their own rights. To give an agent less, choose
**Only these**, or sign it in as an account with fewer rights.

## Disconnect an agent

Each connection is an [API token](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/tokens) named `<client> (OAuth)`. Open **Settings → API tokens**,
find the one with the `oauth: <client id>` label, and click **Revoke**.

## Paste a token instead

A client that can't sign in can send a PocketBase auth token, or an API token, as `Authorization: Bearer …`. An API
token with scopes works only if one of them covers `/mcp`, so to limit an agent, use the consent page instead.

## Change it or turn it off

There's no `pocketone.yaml` key for MCP: it always serves `/mcp`, and an agent can do nothing until someone signs it
in. The name agents see is your app's **Settings → Application → Application name**. Every key is in the
[pocketone.yaml reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference).

`$mcp` isn't available in `pb_hooks` when the app runs PocketBase's own JS engine (`jsvm: goja`).

## How it works

- [MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mcp) serves `/mcp` and turns each tool call into a request to your app's API.
- The [OAuth server](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens/oauth) in [Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) runs the sign-in and consent
  pages, and issues the agent's token.
- Admin tools come from the [contracts](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts) your app answers. Another MCP server can stand in through
  the [mcp/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/mcp/v1) contract and serve the same tools.

Looking to teach a coding agent how to build with PocketOne? That's a different thing: see
[LLM skills for coding agents](https://pocketone.dev/docs/agents).


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml

# Configuration

Every `pocketone` flag has a default. `pocketone.yaml` lets you change those defaults in one file, next to your app,
instead of typing them on every start. The same file holds each extension's options, and your secrets go in a `.env`
beside it.

Without the file, nothing changes: PocketOne behaves like stock PocketBase. Every step below was run on `pocketone`.

## 1. Write the file

In your app's folder, create `pocketone.yaml`:

```yaml
server:
  http: 127.0.0.1:8090
app:
  dir: ./pb_data
  dev: false
```

Check it, create a superuser, and start the app:

```bash
pocketone config check
# pocketone.yaml: ok (2 sections)
pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com password
pocketone serve
```

`pocketone serve` listens on the address under `server`, and the data folder is `pb_data` next to the file. Relative
paths are relative to the file's folder, so the app starts the same from any working directory.

PocketOne looks for `pocketone.yaml` in the working directory, then next to the executable. `--config <path>` picks
another file.

## 2. Flags still win

A flag always beats the file. The file only changes the defaults:

```bash
pocketone serve --http=127.0.0.1:8091   # listens on 8091, whatever the file says
```

## 3. Keep secrets in a .env

Put secrets in a `.env` beside the file, and refer to them as `$VAR` or `${VAR}` in any value:

```bash
# .env
LISTEN=127.0.0.1:8090
STRIPE_KEY=sk_test_123
OTHER_SECRET=hidden
```

```yaml
server:
  http: ${LISTEN}
```

Your JS hooks don't see the `.env` unless you allow each name:

```yaml
app:
  env_allow: [STRIPE_KEY]
```

```js
// pb_hooks/env.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/env", (e) => {
  return e.json(200, { stripe: process.env.STRIPE_KEY || null, other: process.env.OTHER_SECRET || null })
})
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/env
# {"stripe":"sk_test_123","other":null}
```

`pocketone config check` says when it read secrets from a `.env`. Keep the `.env` out of git.

## 4. Set an extension's options

Each top-level key is a section owned by one extension. For example, keep three days of point-in-time history, and
give the app's JS more room:

```yaml
pitr:
  retention: 72h
app:
  js_limits:
    memory: 128MiB
    task_time: 10s
```

`js_limits` sets the limits of the JS engine your hooks run on (`memory`, `task_time`, `task_wall`, `await_time`);
[QuickJS hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs#6-memory-and-time-limits) shows what each one counts and stops.

To see every section your binary knows, with each key, run:

```bash
pocketone config
```

The [pocketone.yaml reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference) lists the same, with each key's type, default and meaning.

## 5. Choose which extension does a job

Extensions offer their abilities through [contracts](https://pocketone.dev/docs/how-pocketone-fits-together). When more than one
extension can do the same job, `providers` picks one. Both PITR and Backups can restore your data. PITR is used when
it's on, but you can choose Backups:

```yaml
providers:
  restore/v1: backups
```

The startup lines show the choice:

```
INFO standard: restore/v1 ← backups (providers:)
```

## The whole file

```yaml
server:
  http: ${LISTEN}
app:
  dir: ./pb_data
  dev: false
  env_allow: [STRIPE_KEY]
  js_limits:
    memory: 128MiB
    task_time: 10s
pitr:
  retention: 72h
providers:
  restore/v1: backups
```

## Next

- [pocketone.yaml reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference): every section and key.
- [Config](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/config): how the file is found, `.env` rules, and loading it in your own Go build.

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/deploy

# Deploy and live sync

Write your hooks, migrations and pages on your own machine, then send them to your running app with one command. Only
the files that changed are uploaded, and the app swaps them in while it keeps serving.

This is on for every PocketOne app. Its superusers can deploy to it, and the `pocketone` command can deploy to any
PocketOne app. You don't need to set anything up.

## Deploy from your terminal

Run these from your project folder, the one that holds `pb_hooks`, `pb_pages` and the rest:

```bash
pocketone link https://myapp.example.com   # add the app as a remote and sign in, once
pocketone deploy                           # upload what changed
```

`link` signs you in through your browser when the app offers it, or asks for an API token. When the deploy is done you
see a line like `Deployed <id>: 3 changed, 0 deleted, 41 unchanged.` With nothing to send, it says
`Up to date: no changes.`

A few more ways to run it:

```bash
pocketone deploy prod                   # to the remote named prod
pocketone deploy --dry-run              # list what would be sent, send nothing
pocketone deploy --restart              # restart afterwards if migrations or packages changed
pocketone deploy --force                # overwrite files that changed on the server since your last deploy
pocketone restart                       # restart later instead
```

Every command takes a remote's name or a URL. Without one, it uses the project's default remote.
[Remote CLI](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/remote) covers adding more remotes and signing in.

## When changes take effect

- **Right away:** `pb_hooks`, `pb_pages` and `pb_public`. Hooks reload by themselves, and pages and public files are
  read fresh on the next request.
- **After a restart:** migrations and npm packages. The deploy tells you `Migrations or packages changed` and leaves
  the restart to you: pass `--restart`, or run `pocketone restart`. Your first deploy that creates `pb_hooks` needs a
  restart too.

A deploy never restarts the app on its own.

## When the server changed too

If a file changed on the server since your last deploy, pull or `dev` (someone edited it there, or the dashboard
wrote a migration) and your deploy would overwrite it, the deploy stops, lists those files and sends nothing. Bring
them down with `pocketone pull` or `pocketone dev`, then deploy again, or pass `--force` to overwrite them. The record
of what you last deployed lives in `.pocketone/` in your project, so a fresh checkout or a CI run deploys without the
check.

## Work live with `dev`

```bash
pocketone dev
```

`dev` keeps your folder and the app in step both ways, and streams the app's logs. Your edits go up half a second after
you save. Changes made on the app, such as the migrations the dashboard writes when you edit a collection, come down
within a few seconds. After you upload a migration or new packages, type `r` and Enter to restart the app. Stop with
Ctrl+C.

If a file changed on both sides, your copy wins and the app's copy is saved in `.pocketone/conflicts/`. `dev` keeps
its state in `.pocketone/`, so add that folder to `.gitignore`. To leave files out, list gitignore-style patterns in
`.pocketoneignore`.

## Start from a running app

With nothing local, `clone` gets you a project folder in one step:

```bash
pocketone clone https://myapp.example.com   # makes ./myapp, signs you in, downloads the app's code
cd myapp
bun install                                 # if there's a package.json: dev and deploy upload packages from here
pocketone dev
```

It downloads the same files as `pull`, never `pb_data`, and remembers the app as the folder's remote. From there, `dev`
keeps both sides in step: a save is live on the app's next request.

## Pull files and read logs

```bash
pocketone pull                         # download pb_hooks, pb_migrations, pb_pages, pb_public, pb_templates, package.json, the lockfile, patches/
pocketone pull pb_hooks pb_public/index.html
pocketone logs                         # the last 100 lines, then follow
```

## Deploy from CI

1. Sign in to the dashboard as a superuser and open **Settings → API tokens**.
2. Fill in a **Name**, such as `ci`.
3. Under **Scopes**, tick `deploy`. Add `remote` if CI will pass `--restart`.
4. Click **Create token** and copy it. It's shown only once.

In CI, set `P1_TOKEN` to that token, then run
`pocketone deploy --restart`.

## From an agent

An agent with a terminal runs the same `pocketone deploy`. Over [MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/mcp), it can restart the app
with `remote_restart` and read its log with `remote_logs`. There's no MCP tool that uploads files.

## What's sent

- **Sent:** every `pb_*` folder except `pb_data` (so `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations`, `pb_pages`, `pb_public`,
  `pb_templates`), plus `package.json`, `bun.lock` or `bun.lockb`, and `patches/`. Dotfiles are included, such as
  `pb_public/.well-known`.
- **Packages:** with a `package.json`, the production `node_modules` tree goes too, so your hooks can `require` npm
  packages. Dev dependencies stay behind. `--no-node-modules` leaves the app's `node_modules` alone.
- **Never sent:** `pb_data` (your live data), `.git*` files and symlinks. Add your own patterns with `-e`.

Only superusers, or an API token with the `deploy` scope, can deploy. A token with `deploy:read` can only pull files
and read logs.

## Change it

There's nothing to set in `pocketone.yaml`. Your project's remotes are kept in `.pocketbase/remotes.json`, which you
can commit. Your logins are saved in your home folder, never in the project. Every `pocketone.yaml` key is in the
[pocketone.yaml reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference).

## How it works

- [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) gives the app its deploy API and adds the `deploy`, `dev`, `pull`, `logs` and
  `restart` commands.
- [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes) keeps your remotes and logins, and gives the app its restart and logs.
- [Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) makes the API tokens CI uses.
- The commands talk to the [deploy/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/deploy/v1) and [remote/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1)
  contracts, so they work against any app or host that offers them.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/remote

# Remote CLI

Everything an extension lets you do to an app, you can do from afar, three ways:

- the `pocketone` command, against any app you've signed in to;
- the REST API, from a script or another service;
- MCP, from an agent such as Claude.

Nobody writes these by hand. Each extension API is a [contract](https://pocketone.dev/docs/how-pocketone-fits-together): a Go interface with one method per
operation. PocketOne generates the command, the endpoint and the tool from that interface. Install an extension, or
use a host that provides a contract, and its commands show up in the `pocketone` you already have. There's no other
tool to install.

## From your terminal

Sign in to an app once, then run its commands:

```bash
pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com --default
pocketone login prod
pocketone remote whoami        # who you are there, your token's scopes, and the contracts the app offers
pocketone remote restore points
pocketone remote restore to --at -2h
```

`remote restore to` calls [restore/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1) on the app. On an app with
[PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr), you get the data as it was two hours ago, to the second. On an app with
[Backups](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/backups) only, you get the latest backup before that. The command is the same either way.

How a command is named and read:

- **Name:** `remote`, the contract's name, then the operation. restore/v1's `restore_to` is `remote restore to`,
  mail.suppression/v1's `check` is `remote mail suppression check`, remote/v1's `status` is `remote status`.
- **Flags:** one per field of the operation's input: `--at`, `--email`, `--campaign`.
  - Times take RFC 3339 (`2026-11-10T15:00:00Z`), a local time (`2026-11-10 15:00`) or a duration from now (`-2h`).
  - Lists take `a,b` or a repeated flag.
  - Anything else takes JSON, or `@file` to read it from a file.
- **Whole input:** `--json` takes the whole input as JSON (`@file` reads a file, `-` reads stdin). Flags you also
  give override its fields.
- **Which app:** `--remote` (`-r`) takes a remote's name or a URL. Without it you get the project's default remote.
- **Output:** JSON, so you can pipe it to `jq`. A stream (`remote logs`) prints one JSON line per entry until Ctrl-C.
- **Errors:** if the app doesn't offer the contract, the command says so ("this remote doesn't offer restore/v1").

In CI, set `P1_TOKEN` to an [API token](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) instead of
signing in. [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes) covers remotes and saved logins.

## From a script: REST

Every operation is an endpoint under `/api/_c/<contract>/`:

```bash
curl -X POST https://myapp.example.com/api/_c/restore/v1/restore \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"at": "2026-11-10T15:00:00Z"}'
```

`GET /api/_c/remote/v1` is the one fixed path. It answers who you are and lists every contract the app offers.

## From an agent: MCP

An app serves MCP at `/mcp` ([MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mcp)). Each operation is a tool named after its contract and
operation (`restore_points`, `restore_restore_to`, `remote_status`). Add `https://myapp.example.com/mcp` to Claude and
sign in.

## The same checks every way

The command, the endpoint and the tool all call the contract, so each passes the same checks:

- **Token scope:** each operation needs a token scope (`restore`, `restore:read`). An API token carries only the
  scopes it was given. A superuser's own sign-in passes all of them.
- **Superuser:** only superusers may call an operation, unless it's public.
- **Hooks:** the same hooks run, in Go and in `pb_hooks` (`onRestoreRestoreTo`).

## Every command, endpoint and tool

- [CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli): every command of `pocketone`, PocketBase's own included.
- [Extension APIs](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/apis): every contract endpoint.
- [MCP reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/mcp): every contract tool.

Each [contract page](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts) lists its operations all three ways. Each extension page lists the commands
it adds and the contracts it answers.

## Your own commands

An extension can replace a generated command with its own, or add new ones under `remote`, by providing
[cli.commands/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/cli.commands/v1). [Writing an extension](https://pocketone.dev/docs/writing-an-extension) explains how.

# Run PocketOne on a Linux server

This guide sets PocketOne up on a Linux server as a systemd service that starts at boot, runs as its own `pocketone`
user and serves your app over HTTPS. It takes a few minutes on any distribution with apt, dnf, yum, zypper or apk.

## Install the package

```bash
curl -fsSL https://pocketone.dev/install.sh | sh
```

The [install script](https://pocketone.dev/docs/installation#linux) installs the newest release's `.deb`, `.rpm` or `.apk` package for
your system. The package makes the `pocketone` system user and a systemd service, and leaves the service stopped.

### Or install a package by hand

Every [release](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/releases) has `.deb` (Debian, Ubuntu), `.rpm` (Fedora, RHEL,
Rocky, Alma, openSUSE) and `.apk` (Alpine) packages, named `pocketone_<version>_linux_<arch>.<deb|rpm|apk>`, and a
`checksums.txt` with the SHA-256 of each. To install one:

```bash
# Debian, Ubuntu
sudo apt install ./pocketone_<version>_linux_amd64.deb

# Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, Alma
sudo dnf install ./pocketone_<version>_linux_amd64.rpm

# openSUSE
sudo zypper install --allow-unsigned-rpm ./pocketone_<version>_linux_amd64.rpm

# Alpine
sudo apk add --allow-untrusted ./pocketone_<version>_linux_amd64.apk
```

The packages aren't signed; check them against `checksums.txt` (`sha256sum -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing`).

### What the package installs

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `/usr/bin/pocketone` | The binary. |
| `/usr/lib/systemd/system/pocketone.service` | The service (`.deb` and `.rpm`; Alpine uses OpenRC, so its package has the binary and config only). |
| `/etc/pocketone/pocketone.yaml` | The service's [pocketone.yaml](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml): data in `/var/lib/pocketone`. Kept when you upgrade. |
| `/etc/pocketone/service.env` | What the service passes to `pocketone serve`: your domain. Kept when you upgrade. |
| `/var/lib/pocketone` | The `pocketone` user's home, holding `pb_data` and your app's `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations`, `pb_public` and `pb_pages`. |

Installing makes the `pocketone` system user and leaves the service stopped.

## Run it as a service

Create your first superuser, as the `pocketone` user so the files it makes are that user's:

```bash
sudo -u pocketone pocketone superuser upsert <email> <password> --config /etc/pocketone/pocketone.yaml
```

Run any other `pocketone` command for the service's app the same way, with `sudo -u pocketone` and
`--config /etc/pocketone/pocketone.yaml`.

Then choose how it's reached, in `/etc/pocketone/service.env`:

- **Its own HTTPS.** Put your domain in `SERVE_ARGS`, after pointing the domain's DNS at the server:

  ```bash
  SERVE_ARGS=example.com
  ```

  `serve` then listens on ports 80 and 443 and gets a Let's Encrypt certificate for the domain by itself, as in
  PocketBase. List more domains with spaces between them.

- **Behind a reverse proxy** (Caddy, nginx) that handles HTTPS: leave `SERVE_ARGS` empty. PocketOne listens on
  `127.0.0.1:8090`; point the proxy there.

Start it now and at every boot, and follow its log:

```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now pocketone
journalctl -u pocketone -f
```

After changing `service.env` or `pocketone.yaml`, restart it: `sudo systemctl restart pocketone`. Secrets for
`pocketone.yaml` go in `/etc/pocketone/.env`, written in the yaml as `$NAME`; make it readable by the `pocketone`
user only (`sudo chown root:pocketone /etc/pocketone/.env && sudo chmod 640 /etc/pocketone/.env`).

To deploy your app, put its folders in `/var/lib/pocketone`, owned by the `pocketone` user, and restart the service:

```bash
sudo cp -r pb_hooks pb_migrations pb_public /var/lib/pocketone/
sudo chown -R pocketone:pocketone /var/lib/pocketone
sudo systemctl restart pocketone
```

Or push it from your machine with `pocketone deploy` ([Deploy and live sync](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/deploy)).

## A service without a package

With the plain binary in `/usr/local/bin` (the install script with `POCKETONE_NO_PACKAGE=1`, or a release zip), set
the service up yourself. Make the user and data folder, and the first superuser:

```bash
sudo useradd --system --user-group --home-dir /var/lib/pocketone --create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin pocketone
sudo -u pocketone pocketone superuser upsert <email> <password> --dir /var/lib/pocketone/pb_data
```

Save this as `/etc/systemd/system/pocketone.service`, with your domain in place of `example.com` (or, behind a
reverse proxy, no domain and no `AmbientCapabilities` line):

```ini
[Unit]
Description=PocketOne
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=pocketone
Group=pocketone
WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/pocketone
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/pocketone serve example.com --dir /var/lib/pocketone/pb_data --publicDir /var/lib/pocketone/pb_public
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
LimitNOFILE=4096
# lets the pocketone user listen on ports 80 and 443
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Then:

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now pocketone
```

## Upgrade

Run the install script again. It installs the newest release's package over the old one; the package manager restarts
the service if it's running and keeps your `/etc/pocketone` files and your data. For the plain binary of
[A service without a package](#a-service-without-a-package), run `sudo pocketone upgrade` (it keeps the old one as
`pocketone-<version>`), then `sudo systemctl restart pocketone`.

## Uninstall

```bash
sudo apt remove pocketone     # or: sudo dnf remove pocketone, sudo zypper remove pocketone, sudo apk del pocketone
```

This stops the service and removes the binary and the service. Your data in `/var/lib/pocketone` and the `pocketone`
user stay; delete them yourself if you're sure (`sudo rm -rf /var/lib/pocketone && sudo userdel pocketone`).
