# How the app runs

A desktop app is your PocketOne app, with the standard extensions, its server on a private port, and a native window
in front.

## Each user's data

Every user has their own data, in their own app-data folder, named by your app's `id`:

| Platform | Data folder |
|---|---|
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/<id>/pb_data` |
| Windows | `%AppData%\<id>\pb_data` |
| Linux | `~/.config/<id>/pb_data` |

It's an ordinary `pb_data`, so everything that works on one, from backups to point-in-time restore, works here too.

## Upgrades

Your migrations run every time the app starts. Ship a new version with new migrations, and each user's data is
upgraded the first time they open it, the same way `pocketone serve` upgrades a server's.

## The server and the window

- The server listens on a free `127.0.0.1` port, chosen each time, so it never collides with anything else.
- The window opens once the server answers.
- Only one copy runs at a time.
- Your hooks, migrations and public files come from the executable, never from disk.
- There is no superuser, and the superuser installer page never opens: the people using a desktop app aren't its
  admins.

## What each platform needs

| Platform | Needs |
|---|---|
| macOS | macOS 11 or newer |
| Windows | The WebView2 runtime, which Windows 10 and 11 already have |
| Linux | The GTK 4 and WebKitGTK 6.0 libraries; without them the app says which package to install |

## Sharing your app

A build runs on the machine that built it. Before you give it to other people, sign it (and on macOS, notarize it), so
it opens without warnings: [Signing and sharing](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/desktop/signing) has the steps for each platform.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/desktop/build

# Building

Run `pocketone desktop build` in your app's folder, the one with `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations` or `pb_public`. It embeds
those folders in a desktop app for each platform you ask for.

```sh
pocketone desktop build                                        # this machine's platform
pocketone desktop build --all                                  # all six below
pocketone desktop build --target windows/amd64,linux/amd64     # some of them
pocketone desktop build --out builds                           # somewhere other than dist/
pocketone desktop build --no-sign                              # skip the sign section
```

| Platform | `--target` | You get |
|---|---|---|
| macOS, Apple Silicon | `darwin/arm64` | `dist/darwin-arm64/<name>.app` and `<name>.dmg` |
| macOS, Intel | `darwin/amd64` | `dist/darwin-amd64/<name>.app` and `<name>.dmg` |
| Windows, x64 | `windows/amd64` | `dist/windows-amd64/<name>.exe` |
| Windows, Arm | `windows/arm64` | `dist/windows-arm64/<name>.exe` |
| Linux, x64 | `linux/amd64` | `dist/linux-amd64/<name>` |
| Linux, Arm | `linux/arm64` | `dist/linux-arm64/<name>` |

Each is one file (or one `.app` bundle) of about 40 MB, with your app and PocketOne inside. Windows builds open no
console window.

On a Mac, each macOS build also comes as a `.dmg`: the app and a link to Applications to drag it onto. With a `sign`
section in `pocketone.yaml`, every build is signed for you; see [Signing and sharing](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/desktop/signing).

## Name and size

`pocketone.yaml`'s `desktop` section names the app and sizes its window:

```yaml
desktop:
  name: Notes              # window title and file name; default: the folder's name
  id: dev.example.notes    # where each user's data lives; default: app.pocketone.<name>
  width: 900               # starting window size; default 1024 × 768
  height: 640
```

Choose the `id` once and keep it. It names the folder each user's data lives in, so a new `id` is a new, empty app for
everyone who installed the old one.

## The build image

Builds run in Docker, in the build image for your `pocketone`'s version: `ghcr.io/pocketonehq/pocketone-build:v<version>`,
pulled the first time. It holds Go, PocketOne's source and every dependency, vendored, so once it's here builds work
offline, and the same `pocketone` version always builds the same app.

`pocketone desktop build` mounts your app folder and the output folder into it, builds every platform there, and
keeps Go's build cache in a Docker volume (`pocketone-build-cache`), so rebuilds take seconds. On a Mac it then signs
the macOS bundles ad hoc, so they run on that Mac.

A development `pocketone`, built from a PocketOne checkout, has no published image. It builds its own,
`pocketone-build:dev`, from that checkout the first time (a minute or two). `pocketone desktop image` rebuilds it after
you change the source.

## Without Docker

With Go 1.27 or newer and a PocketOne checkout, `--local` builds with your own Go instead:

```sh
pocketone desktop build --local --all                        # inside the checkout
pocketone desktop build --local --source ~/src/pocketone     # anywhere else (or set P1_SOURCE)
```

It needs no C compiler either: every platform cross-compiles with plain Go.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/desktop/signing

# Signing and sharing

`pocketone desktop build` gives you apps that run on the machine that built them. Before you send them to other people,
sign them, so each operating system knows the app comes from you and hasn't been changed since:

| Platform | Unsigned, your users see | To sign, you need |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | "can't be opened", until they approve it in System Settings | An Apple Developer account and a Mac |
| Windows | A SmartScreen "Windows protected your PC" warning | A code-signing certificate |
| Linux | Nothing; Linux doesn't check | Optional: a GPG key, to publish a signature |

## Let desktop build sign

Add a `sign` section to `pocketone.yaml`, and every `pocketone desktop build` signs what it built, on your machine,
with your certificates. Name only the platforms you sign for:

```yaml
desktop:
  name: Hello
  id: dev.pocketone.hello
  sign:
    macos:
      identity: "Developer ID Application: Your Name (ABCDE12345)"
      notary_profile: pocketone-notary     # omit to sign without notarizing
    windows:
      # any command that signs {file} in place
      command: signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td SHA256 /a {file}
    linux:
      gpg_key: you@example.com
```

- **macOS:** it signs each `.app` with your Developer ID and the hardened runtime, puts it in a `.dmg`, signs the DMG,
  sends it to Apple to notarize, and staples the result to both. You get the raw `.app` and the `.dmg`.
- **Windows:** it runs your command on each `.exe`, with `{file}` replaced by its path. Use `signtool`, `osslsigncode`
  or your signing service's tool, whichever fits your certificate.
- **Linux:** it writes `<name>.sha256` and a detached `<name>.asc` GPG signature beside each binary.

Before it builds anything, it checks that the tools are installed, that the identity is in your keychain and that the
GPG key exists, so a missing piece fails in a second, not after the build. `pocketone desktop build --no-sign` skips
the section, for a quick build to try out.

Signing happens on your machine, not in the build image, because that's where your keychain and certificates are. So
macOS builds are signed, notarized and put in a DMG only when you build on a Mac; built elsewhere, they're unsigned
`.app` bundles. Windows and Linux builds sign anywhere their tools run (`signtool` only runs on Windows;
`osslsigncode` runs everywhere).

The sections below are the one-time setup for each platform, and the commands `desktop build` runs, if you'd rather
sign by hand.

## macOS

macOS wants two things for an app downloaded from the internet: a **Developer ID signature**, and **notarization**,
where Apple scans the app and records that it did. You do both on a Mac, with the tools that come with Xcode.

### Once: get a Developer ID certificate

1. Join the [Apple Developer Program](https://developer.apple.com/programs/) (paid, yearly).
2. In Xcode, open **Settings → Accounts**, add your Apple ID, select your team and choose **Manage Certificates**.
   Click **+** and pick **Developer ID Application**. Xcode creates the certificate and puts it in your keychain.
3. Check that it's there and copy its name:

   ```sh
   security find-identity -v -p codesigning
   #  1) 3F2A…  "Developer ID Application: Your Name (ABCDE12345)"
   ```

   `ABCDE12345` is your team ID.

4. Create an [app-specific password](https://account.apple.com) for your Apple ID (**Sign-In and Security →
   App-Specific Passwords**), and save it for the notary tool under a profile name:

   ```sh
   xcrun notarytool store-credentials pocketone-notary \
     --apple-id you@example.com --team-id ABCDE12345 --password <app-specific password>
   ```

### By hand: sign, notarize, staple

`desktop build` does this for you with a `sign.macos` section. By hand, for each macOS build (`dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app`, `dist/darwin-amd64/Hello.app`):

1. **Sign** with your Developer ID, the hardened runtime (`--options runtime`, which notarization requires) and a
   secure timestamp. `--force` replaces the ad hoc signature the build added:

   ```sh
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     --sign "Developer ID Application: Your Name (ABCDE12345)" dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app
   codesign --verify --strict --verbose=2 dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app
   ```

2. **Notarize:** zip the app and send it to Apple. It usually takes a few minutes:

   ```sh
   ditto -c -k --keepParent dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app Hello.zip
   xcrun notarytool submit Hello.zip --keychain-profile pocketone-notary --wait
   ```

   If it says `Invalid`, `xcrun notarytool log <submission id> --keychain-profile pocketone-notary` shows why.

3. **Staple** the result to the app, so it opens even when the user is offline, and check it:

   ```sh
   xcrun stapler staple dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app
   spctl --assess --type execute --verbose dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app
   # dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app: accepted
   # source=Notarized Developer ID
   ```

4. **Package** the stapled app to share it. A zip:

   ```sh
   ditto -c -k --keepParent dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app Hello-macos-arm64.zip
   ```

   or a disk image, which you sign too:

   ```sh
   hdiutil create -volname Hello -srcfolder dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app -ov -format UDZO Hello.dmg
   codesign --timestamp --sign "Developer ID Application: Your Name (ABCDE12345)" Hello.dmg
   ```

One download for both kinds of Mac: join the two executables with `lipo` before you sign, and ship one app.

```sh
cp -R dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app Hello.app
lipo -create dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app/Contents/MacOS/Hello dist/darwin-amd64/Hello.app/Contents/MacOS/Hello \
  -output Hello.app/Contents/MacOS/Hello
```

### Without an Apple Developer account

Without a Developer ID, macOS still runs your app, but anyone who downloads it is warned first. What they see depends on
how it's signed:

| Your app is | Someone who downloads it sees |
|---|---|
| Signed ad hoc (what `desktop build` does with no `sign.macos`) | "Apple could not verify it is free of malware", and the app doesn't open |
| Signed with a self-signed certificate | The same warning |
| Signed with a Developer ID, not notarized | A similar warning |
| Signed with a Developer ID and notarized | Only "downloaded from the internet, open it?" |

The warning only appears for downloaded apps, which macOS marks as quarantined. An app you build and run on your own
Mac opens without it.

**Opening it anyway.** For yourself, testers and people you know, that's fine. They:

1. Open the app and dismiss the warning.
2. Go to **System Settings → Privacy & Security**, scroll to **Security** and click **Open Anyway** next to the app.
3. Confirm, and the app opens from then on.

Or, if they're comfortable with Terminal, they remove the quarantine mark, and the app opens normally:

```sh
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Hello.app
```

**Self-signing.** You can make your own code-signing certificate: in Keychain Access, choose **Keychain Access →
Certificate Assistant → Create a Certificate**, set **Certificate Type** to **Code Signing**, and then mark it
**Always Trust** for code signing (double-click it, open **Trust**). Its name then goes in `sign.macos.identity`, without
`notary_profile`, since Apple only notarizes Developer ID apps.

It doesn't remove the warning: macOS can't trust a certificate it doesn't know, so a self-signed app gets the same
warning as an ad hoc one. What it gives you is the same identity from one version to the next, so macOS remembers what
your users allowed the app to do (files, camera, keychain items) when they update.

For an app you give to the public, only a Developer ID and notarization open it without warnings.

## Windows

Windows checks an **Authenticode** signature. You need a code-signing certificate from a certificate authority, such
as DigiCert, Sectigo or SSL.com. Certificates issued today keep their key on a hardware token or in the CA's cloud
signing service rather than in a file, so how you sign depends on which you get.

### Once: get a certificate

- **Organization validation (OV):** the CA checks that your business exists. For an individual, pick a certificate
  issued to you by name.
- **Extended validation (EV):** a stricter check, for businesses.
- **A cloud signing service**, such as Azure Trusted Signing, signs without a token, for organizations it can verify.

Either way, a new certificate starts with no reputation: SmartScreen may still warn for a while, until enough people
have installed your signed app.

### By hand: sign with signtool

On Windows, with the Windows SDK installed (it includes `signtool`) and your certificate on its token or in the
certificate store:

```bat
signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td SHA256 /a dist\windows-amd64\Hello.exe
signtool verify /pa /v dist\windows-amd64\Hello.exe
```

`/a` picks the best certificate it finds; `/sha1 <thumbprint>` picks one exactly. A cloud signing service gives you
its own `signtool` plugin or tool; follow its instructions for the same step. Sign `windows-arm64` the same way.

### From a Mac or Linux

[osslsigncode](https://github.com/mtrojnar/osslsigncode) signs Windows executables on macOS and Linux, if your
certificate's key is in a file or on a token it can reach:

```sh
osslsigncode sign -pkcs12 certificate.pfx -pass "$PFX_PASSWORD" -n "Hello" \
  -t http://timestamp.digicert.com -in dist/windows-amd64/Hello.exe -out Hello.exe
```

## Linux

Linux runs the binary you give it; there's no signature check to pass. What you can do is let people check the
download is yours and intact:

```sh
cd dist/linux-amd64
sha256sum Hello > Hello.sha256          # a checksum to publish next to the download
gpg --armor --detach-sign Hello         # Hello.asc: a signature anyone with your public key can check
```

Users check with `sha256sum -c Hello.sha256` and `gpg --verify Hello.asc Hello`. Packaging the app as a `.deb`,
Flatpak or AppImage, where the package or repository is signed, also works.

# All extensions

Each extension is a Go module in [`ext/`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext) with its own README; the pages here are those READMEs. Want to add one? Read [Writing an extension](https://pocketone.dev/docs/writing-an-extension).

## Standard extensions

These ship with `pocketone` and add no work to an app that doesn't use them.

| Extension | What it does |
|---|---|
| [API Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) | Long-lived API tokens with scopes. |
| [Auto TLS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/autotls) | Certificates on demand and wildcards through ACME. |
| [Backups](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/backups) | Restore an app to a moment from its own backups: the latest one before it. On by default. |
| [Bulk Mail](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bulkmail) | Campaigns to your app's own users, with audiences from a collection, a view or SQL. |
| [Cache](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/cache) | Cache buckets for every app in the process from one shared store: bytes or Go values, a budget per bucket, LRU/MRU/FIFO/LIFO eviction, TTLs, a cold disk tier that keeps identical values once. |
| [Config](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/config) | The pocketone.yaml config file, with secrets in a .env beside it. |
| [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) | pocketone deploy, dev, pull and logs, and the deploy API. |
| [Desktop](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/desktop/extension) | Build your PocketOne app into a native desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux, one executable each, from any machine. |
| [JSVM](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm) | PocketOne's JS engine: one QuickJS VM per app, real globals, async handlers, hard limits. |
| [Key-Value Store](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/kv/extension) | Named JSON values for an app's settings and state, with no collection or migration. On by default. |
| [LLM](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm/extension) | Cloud models for your app: text, pictures, speech, transcription, alignment, music, video and embeddings from Vultr, Cloudflare, OpenRouter or any OpenAI-compatible API. |
| [LLM Chat](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm-chat) | Stored conversations with a language model: $llm.chat.open(id).sendAsync(text), with history and summaries. |
| [LLM Search](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/llm-search) | RAG and hybrid search: knowledge bases (buckets) of files, folders, zips, web pages, Git repositories and collections; $llm.search, and enrich to ground $llm calls in them. |
| [MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mcp) | An MCP endpoint at /mcp so agents can manage your app and call its tools. |
| [Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/extension) | Server-rendered pages from a pb_pages folder. |
| [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr) | Point-in-time restore of your database with Litestream. On by default. |
| [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes) | Named remotes and saved logins for the pocketone command. |
| [S3 Fallback](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3-fallback) | A default bucket for uploads and backups when an instance has no S3 of its own. |
| [S3 Redirect](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3redirect) | File downloads as short-lived signed S3 redirects. |
| [Settings](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/settings) | One API for the settings an app's admins change for its extensions. On by default. |
| [Templates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/templates) | Theme an extension's own pages (the OAuth sign-in screens): eject its templates to pb_templates and edit them. |
| [UI Cache](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/uicache) | Dashboard cache headers that let updates through browsers and CDNs. On by default. |
| [Upgrade](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/upgrade) | pocketone upgrade to the latest release, keeping the old executable. |
| [Vacuum](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/vacuum) | Compact your app's SQLite databases on a schedule, so space freed by deleted records goes back to the disk. |
| [WASM](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/extension) | Bring your own WASM: Go, Rust or Zig modules called from page code, each a closed box. |

# Extension APIs

Every contract API a PocketOne app with its [standard extensions](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard) answers, under `/api/_c/<contract>/`. The core API (records, collections, auth, files, settings…) is the [REST API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest).

- **Auth:** an `Authorization` header with a superuser's auth token or an [API token](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens). Each operation needs its token scope; a superuser's own auth token passes every scope.
- **Discovery:** `GET /api/_c/remote/v1` says who you are and lists every contract the app offers ([remote/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1)).
- **Input:** a JSON body for `POST`, query parameters for `GET`. **Answers** are JSON; streams are server-sent events.
- **Same as the CLI and MCP:** every operation here is also a `pocketone` command and an MCP tool, behind the same checks ([how](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/remote)).

## api-tokens.verify/v1

[Contract page](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/api-tokens.verify/v1). Answered by [API Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) in the standard set.

| Endpoint | What it does | Token scope | Input |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/_c/api-tokens.verify/v1` | Checks an API token and says who it acts as and what it may do (its scopes, with their values). | `api_tokens_verify` | `token` (string), `ip` (string) |

## api-tokens/v1

Its own API under `/api/_c/api-tokens/v1/`: see [api-tokens/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/api-tokens/v1). Answered by [API Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) in the standard set.

|---|---|---|---|

| `POST /api/_c/bulkmail/v1/pause` | Stops sending a campaign; Resume carries on. | `bulkmail` | `campaign` (string) |

# API Tokens

Version 0.3.0 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

> Walkthrough for app owners: [API tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/tokens). This page is the technical reference.

Long-lived API tokens for your app: secrets that start with `pbt_`, for CI, deploys, scripts and agents. Each token
belongs to an account and acts as that account. It can be limited to scopes, given an expiry, and revoked on its own.
Send one as `Authorization: Bearer pbt_…`. Ordinary PocketBase auth tokens keep working unchanged.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Tokens is built into `pocketone` and always on. There's nothing to install or turn on.

In your own Go build, register it before the app starts:

```go
app := pocketbase.New()
tokens.MustRegister(app, apitokens.Config{})
app.Start()
```

To use `$apiTokens` in `pb_hooks`, bind it in jsvm's `OnInit` (the stock binary does):

```go
jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { tokens.BindJS(app, rt) }})
```

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/api-tokens`.

## Configure

There is no `pocketone.yaml` section, flag or environment variable for Tokens. In `pocketone`:
- any account (a superuser, or a record of any auth collection) can own tokens;
- a token never expires unless you give it an expiry.

A Go build can narrow both (see [Go config](#go-config)).

### Scopes

A token without scopes has its owner's full rights. A token with scopes works only on the requests its scopes cover,
plus remote/v1's whoami (`/api/_c/remote/v1`); anywhere else it gets `403`. Extensions, contracts and your own
`pb_hooks` register the scopes. In `pocketone` they are:

| Scope | From | Allows | Who can hold it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `deploy` | [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) | Deploy code (hooks, migrations, pages, public files, packages), read files and logs | superusers |
| `deploy:read` | [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) | Read deployed files and stream logs | superusers |
| `<name>`, `<name>:read` | each [contract](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts) the app provides | That contract's operations under `/api/_c/<id>/`: `remote` and `remote:read`, `restore` and `restore:read`, `settings` and `settings:read`, `bulkmail:read`, `cache`, ... | per contract |

Contract scopes are registered when the app serves, so **Settings → API tokens** on the running app lists every
scope. The `pocketone token` command works offline and doesn't see them: `token scopes` lists only `deploy` and
`deploy:read`, and `token create --scope restore` fails with `unknown scope "restore"`. Create a token with a
contract scope from the dashboard or the [REST API](#rest-api-api-tokensv1).

### Your own scopes

Declare a scope at the top level of a `pb_hooks` file. It then shows up in **Settings → API tokens** and on
[the OAuth server](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens/oauth)'s consent page:

```js
// pb_hooks/scopes.pb.js
$apiTokens.registerScope({
  name: 'notes:read',                        // lower-case letters, digits, ":" and "_"
  description: 'Read notes',                 // shown in the token screen and on the consent page
  paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'], // URL prefixes where a token holding it works
  methods: ['GET'],                          // optional: only these methods (GET covers HEAD)
})
$apiTokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes:write', description: 'Change notes', paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'] })
```

- `collections: ['users']` limits which accounts may hold the scope.
- Registering a name again merges its paths, methods and collections, so reloading hooks is safe.
- Two names whose headers would be the same (`notes:write` and `notes_write`) can't both be registered.

Check a scope on your own route:

```js
routerAdd('POST', '/api/notes/archive', (e) => { /* ... */ }, $apis.requireAuth(), $apiTokens.requireScope('notes:write'))
```

`$apiTokens.requireScope` refuses a signed-out request, and a token that doesn't hold the scope. Inside a handler,
`$apiTokens.hasScope(e, 'notes:write')` tells you the same.

Check a scope in a collection API rule. Every signed-in request carries `X-Token-Scope-<Name>: 1` for each scope it
holds, and rules read it as `@request.headers.x_token_scope_<name>` (`:` becomes `_`):

```
@request.auth.id = owner && @request.headers.x_token_scope_notes_write = "1"
```

- A PocketBase auth token or an unscoped API token holds every registered scope (except ones its collection can't
  hold).
- A scoped token holds only its own scopes. A signed-out request holds none.
- Headers a client sends with that prefix are always dropped, so they can't be forged.

`$apiTokens.ruleField('notes:write')` returns the rule field for a name, and `$apiTokens.scopes()` lists every registered
scope with its header and rule field.

### Scopes with values

A scope can let a token hold it for some values only, such as some record ids. The token's scope list then says
`name=value`, once per value (`notes=abc123`, `notes=def456`). The bare name still means every value. Declare the
values when you register the scope:

```js
$apiTokens.registerScope({
  name: 'notes',
  description: 'Your notes',
  paths: ['/api/notes/'],
  values: { description: 'a note id' }, // shown in the token screen
})
```

Paths and methods don't look at values: a token holding `notes=abc123` authenticates on every path `notes` covers. Your
route checks the value:

```js
routerAdd('GET', '/api/notes/{id}', (e) => {
  if (!$apiTokens.hasScope(e, 'notes', e.request.pathValue('id'))) throw new ForbiddenError('Not this note.')
  // ...
}, $apis.requireAuth())
```

- `$apiTokens.hasScope(e, name, value)` is true for the bare scope, for `name=value`, and for a PocketBase auth token or
  an unscoped token. Without a value it's true when the request holds the scope for any value.
- `$apiTokens.scopeValues(e, name)` returns `{ all: true }` for every value, or `{ all: false, values: [...] }`.
- The scope's header carries the values instead of `1` (`X-Token-Scope-Notes: abc123,def456`), so a rule's `= "1"` still
  means every value.
- A value is 1–200 letters, digits and `. _ : @ / + -`. A scope registered without `values` refuses `name=value`.
- In Go, `Values: &apitokens.ScopeValues{Description: "...", Check: func(owner, value) error}` adds a check when a token
  is created (for example, that the owner owns that record).

## Use

### From the dashboard

1. Open **Settings → API tokens** (under **Access**). Only superusers see this screen.
2. Fill in a **Name**. Optionally set **Expires in (days)**, and tick any **Scopes** (none means full rights). A
   scope that takes values shows a box when ticked: leave it empty for every value, or list some, comma-separated.
3. By default the token is yours. To make one for another account, fill in **Owner collection** (default
   `_superusers`) and **Owner (id or email)**.
4. Click **Create token**. Copy the token now: it's shown only once and never stored.

The list shows each token's name, its first characters, owner, scopes, expiry and when it was last used (time and IP).
Tokens issued by [the OAuth server](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens/oauth) carry an `oauth: <client id>` label. Click **Revoke** and
confirm to delete one; anything using it stops working at once.

App users who aren't superusers manage their own tokens through the [REST API](#rest-api-api-tokensv1).

### From the command line

The `token` command works on the local data dir, like `superuser`, so you can set up tokens before the first serve:

```bash
pocketone token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci --scope deploy --ttl 720h   # prints the secret
pocketone token create --collection users --record user@example.com --name script
pocketone token list                                    # every token, or one owner's with an owner flag
pocketone token revoke <id> [<id>...]
pocketone token revoke --all --superuser admin@example.com
pocketone token scopes
```

Pick the owner with `--superuser <email>`, or `--collection <name> --record <id or email>`. `--scope` can be repeated,
and takes `name=value` for a scope with values; without `--ttl` the token never expires.

### Using a token

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_…" https://myapp.example.com/api/collections/notes/records
```

- An invalid, revoked or expired token leaves the request signed out, like an invalid PocketBase token.
- A scoped token used outside its scopes gets `403` ("This API token's scopes (…) don't allow this request.").
- A token can't be exchanged for a PocketBase auth token (`auth-refresh` and `impersonate` refuse it), so revoking a
  token really ends its access.
- Expired tokens are deleted once a day. Deleting an account deletes its tokens.

### In the logs

- A rejected token is logged at debug level: `tokens: rejected API token`.
- The daily cleanup logs `tokens: deleted expired tokens` with a count when it deletes any, and
  `tokens: delete expired` as a warning if it fails.

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [OAuth](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens/oauth) (in Tokens) | Its access tokens are API tokens, issued with the client's id, the granted scopes and, when asked for, an audience. They show up under Settings → API tokens and can be revoked there. The OAuth server needs Tokens on the app. |
| [MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mcp) | An agent's OAuth sign-in to `/mcp` is an API token bound to `/mcp` that never expires; revoke it to disconnect the agent. Tool calls run as the token's owner. A full-access token's calls hold every registered scope; a token limited to scopes on the consent page has its calls checked like requests with those scopes (`WithScopes`). |
| [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) | Registers `deploy` and `deploy:read`; a `deploy` token is what CI uses. |
| [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes) | `pocketone login` takes a pasted API token when the remote has no OAuth server. In CI, put a token in `P1_TOKEN`. remote/v1's whoami (`/api/_c/remote/v1`) reports a token's id and scopes, whatever its scopes. |
| [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) | It's a standard member, so every instance gets its own tokens, routes and screen; reconfigure it on the host's set with `set.APITokens = apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{...})`. With Pocker, per instance, `extensions: {api-tokens: {enabled: false}}` turns it off and `collections: [...]` picks who may own tokens. |

### Building on Tokens

**Register a scope from Go.** Extensions register their scopes on the app, usually on bootstrap, and guard their routes:

```go
tk := tokens.For(app)
tk.MustRegisterScope(tokens.Scope{
    Name:        "notes:write",
    Description: "Change notes",
    Paths:       []string{"/api/collections/notes/records"},
    Methods:     []string{"POST", "PATCH", "DELETE"}, // optional
    Collections: []string{"users"},                   // optional: who may hold it
})
se.Router.POST("/api/notes/archive", h).Bind(apis.RequireAuth(), tokens.RequireScope("notes:write"))
```

- **Guards.** A Go scope can add `Match func(*core.RequestEvent) bool`: a token with the scope also works on any
  request it returns true for. It runs before the owner is loaded, so it may look only at the request.
- **Shared scopes.** Registering a name again merges its paths, methods, guards and collections, so several extensions
  can share one scope.
- **Scope values.** `Values: &tokens.ScopeValues{Description, Check}` lets a token hold a scope for some values only
  (`notes=abc123`). `Check(owner, value)` runs when a token is created; an error refuses it. Routes check the value
  with `tokens.HasScopeFor(e, "notes", id)`, or list them with `tokens.ValuesFor(e, "notes")` (`all` is true for every
  value). Through the contract: `grant.HasScopeFor`, `grant.ScopeValues`, and `apitokensv1.SplitScope` /
  `JoinScope` for the `name=value` form.
- **Read the token on a request.** `tokens.FromRequest(e)` returns the token a request used (nil for a PocketBase
  auth token), with its `Owner`, `Scopes` and `Audience`. `tokens.HasScope(e, "x")` is true for PocketBase auth
  tokens and unscoped API tokens.
- **Without importing this package.** Other extensions use the [api-tokens/v1](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/contracts/api-tokens/v1/tokens.go)
  contract instead: `tokensv1.Contract.Of(app)` registers scopes (`RegisterScope`), lists them and checks `Reaches`;
  `tokensv1.FromRequest(e)` is the request's token (its `Grant`: owner, scopes, audience, client id);
  `tokensv1.WithScopes` limits in-process requests. Deploy and MCP work this way. The `X-Token-Scope-*` headers work
  for rules and JS.
- **Audience.** A token created with `CreateOptions.Audience` (the OAuth server sets it from the RFC 8707 `resource`
  parameter) only works under that URL's path, plus remote/v1's whoami (`/api/_c/remote/v1`); elsewhere it gets `403`. When the audience has
  a path (like `https://host/mcp`), the token works there whatever its scopes: the scopes limit what that endpoint
  does on the token's behalf (MCP passes them on with `WithScopes`), not the endpoint itself.
- **Limit in-process requests.** `tokens.WithScopes(ctx, scopes)` returns a context whose requests are checked like a
  token limited to `scopes`, whatever credential they carry: `403` where the scopes don't reach, and only those
  scopes in the `X-Token-Scope-*` headers and `HasScope`. Requests made inside them with the same context inherit
  the limit, and a nested `WithScopes` only narrows it. No client value can set it. `tokens.ScopesFromContext(ctx)`
  reads it. `Reaches(scopes, method, pattern)` says whether scopes could cover a route pattern (`{name}` segments
  match anything), and `Scope.Infrastructure()` whether a scope only reaches contract APIs (`/api/_c/`).

**Go API.** `tokens.For(app)` returns the service: `Create(owner, CreateOptions{Name, Scopes, Expires, ClientId,
Audience})` returns the secret and record; also `Verify(secret)`, `List(owner)`, `Get(id)`, `Revoke(id)`,
`RevokeAll(owner)`, `DeleteExpired()`, `RegisterScope`, `MustRegisterScope`, `Scopes()`, `Collections()` and
`AllowedCollection(c)`. `tokens.BindJS(vm, app)` adds `$apiTokens`; the extkit extension (`tokens.New`) also binds it.

**JS.** `$apiTokens.registerScope({name, description, paths, methods, collections})`, `$apiTokens.requireScope(name)`,
`$apiTokens.hasScope(e, name)`, `$apiTokens.ruleField(name)` and `$apiTokens.scopes()`.

### REST API (api-tokens/v1)

The [api-tokens/v1](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/contracts/api-tokens/v1/tokens.go) contract, at `/api/_c/api-tokens/v1`. Any signed-in account; superusers
see and manage everyone's.

| Route | What |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/_c/api-tokens/v1` | Your tokens. Superusers see all, or one owner's with `?ownerCollection=&owner=`. |
| `POST /api/_c/api-tokens/v1` | `{name, scopes, ttl \| expires}` (`ttl` in seconds, `expires` RFC 3339); superusers may add `ownerCollection` and `owner`. Returns the secret once. A scoped token can only create tokens within its own scopes. |
| `DELETE /api/_c/api-tokens/v1/{id}` | Revoke one. |
| `POST /api/_c/api-tokens/v1/revoke-all` | Revoke all of yours (superusers: `{ownerCollection, owner}`). |
| `GET /api/_c/api-tokens/v1/scopes` | The registered scopes, who may own tokens, and whether you can. |

Owners can also list, view and delete their own tokens through the records API of `_api_tokens_tokens`.

### Checking a token from another server (api-tokens.verify/v1)

A server that a client hands one of this app's tokens to (a host in front of the app's accounts) asks the app what
the token allows with the [api-tokens.verify/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/api-tokens.verify/v1) contract:
`POST /api/_c/api-tokens.verify/v1` with `{"token": "pbt_...", "ip": "<client address>"}`, as a superuser (scope
`api_tokens_verify`). The answer is `{"valid": true, "grant": {...}}` with the owner and the scopes (values included),
or `{"valid": false, "reason": "invalid" | "expired"}`. In Go, `verifyv1.NewClient(appURL, superuserToken, nil)`.

## Example

[`example/main.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/api-tokens/example/main.go) runs one app with API tokens: Settings → API tokens, the token API (`/api/_c/api-tokens/v1`) and the `token` command.

```go
// Command example runs one PocketOne app with API tokens: Settings → API tokens in the dashboard, the token API (/api/_c/api-tokens/v1)
// and the `token` command.
//
//	go run ./example serve
//	go run ./example token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci
//	curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_..." http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"log"
	"net/http"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/apis"
	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/api-tokens"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/devusers"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"

	tk := apitokens.MustRegister(app, apitokens.Config{
		Collections: []string{"_superusers", "users"}, // who may own tokens
	})
	// an extension's scope: a token limited to "hello" only authenticates under /api/hello; a JWT or unscoped token
	// holds it too, and every request that holds it carries X-Token-Scope-Hello: 1 for rules and hooks
	tk.MustRegisterScope(apitokens.Scope{Name: "hello", Description: "Say hello", Paths: []string{"/api/hello"}, Methods: []string{"GET"}})

	app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se *core.ServeEvent) error {
		se.Router.GET("/api/hello", func(e *core.RequestEvent) error {
			return e.JSON(http.StatusOK, map[string]any{"hello": e.Auth.Email()})
		}).Bind(apis.RequireAuth(), apitokens.RequireScope("hello"))
		return se.Next()
	})

	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## Go config

```go
tokens.MustRegister(app, apitokens.Config{
    Collections: []string{"_superusers", "users"}, // who may own tokens (default: every auth collection)
    MaxTTL:      0,                                // cap on a token's lifetime (0: none)
})
```

With `MaxTTL` set, a token asked for with no expiry or a later one gets the cap instead. If you narrow `Collections`,
The OAuth server can only sign in accounts of those collections.

### Bringing tokens from another system

To keep tokens another system issued working (their owners already hold the secrets), register their prefix and
store each one with `Import`, which keeps only its hash, as `Create` does:

```go
tk.RegisterPrefix("ph_pat_") // pbt_ is always registered
rec, err := tk.Import(owner, "ph_pat_…", apitokens.CreateOptions{Name: "ci", Scopes: []string{"deploy"}})
```

Every registered prefix is checked the same way: a secret starts with one and has at least 32 characters after it.
`Import` takes a `pbt_` secret too (a token moving from another app). The one difference: tokens the app creates
always start with `pbt_`. A prefix is lower-case letters, digits and `_`, ends with `_`, and can't overlap one
already registered. The old system's hash is usually of something else, so import a secret when it's next used
(check it the old way, then `Import` it), not ahead of time.

## How it works

- Tokens live in the `_api_tokens_tokens` collection: owner (collection id and record id), name, `hash` (SHA-256 of the secret;
  the secret itself is never stored), display prefix, scopes, expiry, last use (time and IP), OAuth client id and
  audience.
- The bearer check is a middleware that runs just before PocketBase's own auth middleware; a second one, right after
  it, sets the scope headers. Last use is written at most once a minute per token.
- [`example/main.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/api-tokens/example/main.go) runs one app where superusers and users may own tokens, with a `hello` scope
  for `GET /api/hello`. Try it with `go run ./example serve` and
  `go run ./example token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci` (logins from
  [devusers](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/devusers/devusers.go): admin@example.com / password, user@example.com / password).

# OAuth

[Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) includes an OAuth 2.1 authorization server whose access tokens are API tokens: the
[oauth/v1](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/contracts/oauth/v1/oauth.go) contract. `pocketone login` signs in to it in the browser (or with a code on
another device), and MCP clients such as Claude or ChatGPT connectors register themselves and connect. Superusers and
app users sign in on your app's own pages, through PocketBase's own auth endpoints.

## Install

It comes with Tokens, which is in every app's [standard set](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard). There's nothing to install or turn
on. Its endpoints are under `/api/_c/oauth/v1/` (see [Endpoints](#endpoints)); its metadata is at
`/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`.

In your own Go build, configure it through Tokens:

```go
set := standard.New()
set.APITokens = apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{
	Branding: tokens.Branding{Accent: "#4f46e5"},
}})
```

`apitokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{Disabled: true}}` leaves it out.

## Configure

There is no `pocketone.yaml` section, flag or environment variable for OAuth Server. In `pocketone`:
- superusers and every auth collection may sign in;
- access tokens last 30 days, refresh tokens 180 days (renewed on each refresh);
- tokens for [MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mcp) never expire, since MCP turns that on for `/mcp`;
- client self-registration (`POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register`) is on, since MCP turns it on;
- Claude and Claude Code connect without registering (their client metadata documents from `claude.ai` and
  `claude.com` are trusted).

A Go build can change these (see [Go config](#go-config)).

### Sign-in methods

The pages offer exactly the methods each auth collection has on, so you set them where you always do: the
collection's options in the dashboard (**Collections →** the collection **→ Options**).
- **Password**, **One-time password** (an emailed code) and **OAuth2** providers each get their own form or button.
- **Multi-factor authentication** adds a second step.
- The collection's auth rule (for example `verified = true`) applies.

OAuth2 providers (Google, GitHub, …) are offered to app users only; PocketBase doesn't allow them for superusers.
**Register `<your app's URL>/api/_c/oauth/v1/provider/callback` as a redirect URI with each provider.**

The pages show **Settings → Application → Application name**.

### Behind a proxy

The server names itself (the issuer) after the scheme and host the browser used, with `https` when the request is TLS
or `X-Forwarded-Proto` says so. If a proxy rewrites the host, set `Config.Issuer` in a Go build so the issuer and the
provider callback URL stay stable.

### Scopes

A client may ask for any scope registered with [Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens#scopes), including your own from
`$apiTokens.registerScope`. `offline_access` is accepted (refresh tokens are always issued).

The consent page lets the user decide: **Full access** (no scopes: the account's full rights) or **Only these**, with a
box for each scope. The scopes the client asked for start ticked; the others the account may hold are there to tick,
except ones that only reach contract APIs under `/api/_c/` (like `deploy`), which appear only when asked for. With no scopes
asked, **Full access** starts selected. The token gets exactly what was ticked, and the token response's `scope` says
which.

### Your own sign-in pages

The built-in pages (sign-in, second step, one-time code, consent, device code, done, error) follow the system's light
or dark mode and work on phones. They're the `oauth` set of [Templates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/templates); to change them, eject
it:

```bash
pocketone template eject oauth      # asks before overwriting files you changed; --force doesn't ask
```

It copies the built-in Go templates to `pb_templates/oauth/`: `signin.tpl`, `mfa.tpl`, `otp.tpl`, `consent.tpl`,
`device.tpl`, `done.tpl`, `error.tpl`, and the shared `head.tpl` (with the CSS), `foot.tpl` and `hidden.tpl`. From then
on the server renders your copy of each file, read on every request; delete a file to go back to the built-in one. To
restyle every page, edit only `head.tpl`. See [Custom page templates](#custom-page-templates) for the data they get.

## Use

### Signing in

Whenever a client sends someone to your app (`pocketone login`, Claude, an app of yours), they see:

1. **Sign in to <app name>**: the form for app users (`users` first; with several user collections, a tab for
   each). At the bottom, **Sign in as a superuser** switches to the superuser form, which looks clearly different:
   a **Superuser** badge, **Superuser sign-in**, its own colors and a warning. **Sign in as a user instead** goes back.
2. **One more step** when the account has MFA, offering its other methods. After a password, when an emailed code is
   the only method left, it's sent right away.
3. **Check your email** for an emailed code.
4. The consent page: the client's name, the account, whether the client will act as a user (and which collection) or
   as a superuser, and the access: **Full access** or **Only these** scopes (see [Scopes](#scopes)). Click **Allow** or
   **Deny**, or **Not <email>? Use another account**.

With no user collection allowed, the superuser form is the only one. A browser stays signed in to these pages for 15
minutes. Failed attempts are limited to 10 per IP in 5 minutes.

On another device (over SSH, say), the client shows a code like `WDJB-MJHT`. Open
`https://<your app>/api/_c/oauth/v1/device/verify`, enter it under **Connect a device**, sign in and allow. Codes last 10 minutes.

### Log in from the command line

```bash
pocketone login prod
```

With OAuth Server on the remote, [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes) opens your browser on the pages above, or shows a
device code when there's no browser (`--device` asks for one). The CLI's commands (deploy, remote control) need a
superuser, so it asks for one (`account=_superusers`, below): you land on the superuser form, even if this browser
is signed in there as an app user. The client is the built-in `pocketone-cli`, named
**pocketone CLI** on the consent page (the name follows the command, so another build shows its own).

### See and revoke what's connected

Every sign-in creates an API token named "<client> (OAuth)". They're listed under **Settings → API tokens** with an
`oauth: <client id>` label; click **Revoke** to disconnect a client. Revoking the access token also ends its refresh
token. A client can revoke its own tokens at `POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/revoke`, which `pocketone logout` does.

### Register clients

Claude and the CLI need no registration, and MCP clients register themselves. For your own app:

```bash
pocketone oauth clients add --name "My app" --redirect https://myapp.example.com/callback
pocketone oauth clients add --name "Desktop" --redirect http://127.0.0.1/callback --public
pocketone oauth clients list
pocketone oauth clients rm <client_id>
```

`add` prints the client id, and the secret once for a confidential client. `--public` makes a client with no secret
(PKCE only), for desktop and mobile apps. `--redirect` can be repeated.

Redirect URIs must be `https`, `http` on a loopback address, or an app's custom scheme. Loopback URIs match any port
(RFC 8252); others must match exactly.

### In the logs

- `tokens: oauth: this collection may sign in but can't own API tokens; add it to apitokens.Config.Collections`, once per
  collection, when Tokens is narrowed in a Go build. The page then says signing in with that account type "isn't set
  up on this server yet".
- `tokens: oauth: auth methods` (error) when a collection's sign-in methods can't be read.
- `tokens: oauth: cleanup` (warning) when the half-hourly removal of expired codes fails.

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) | It's part of Tokens. Access tokens are API tokens owned by whoever signed in, with the client's id, the granted scopes and the audience. Every registered scope can be requested. |
| [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes) | remote/v1's whoami lists `oauth/v1` (and the `oauth` feature, its metadata); `pocketone login` then signs in in the browser (loopback redirect with PKCE) or with a device code, and renews through the refresh token. |
| [MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mcp) | MCP points clients here from its protected resource metadata, turns on self-registration, and makes tokens bound to `/mcp` never expire. Tool calls run as whoever signed in. |
| [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) | `pocketone login` gives the deploy commands a token for the account that signed in. |
| [Templates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/templates) | The pages are its `oauth` set: `pocketone template eject oauth` copies them to `pb_templates/oauth/` to edit. Without Templates, the built-in pages. |

On a [multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) host every instance that runs PocketOne has it, through the standard set.

### Account type

An `account` parameter on `/api/_c/oauth/v1/authorize` or `/api/_c/oauth/v1/device` names the auth collection the
client needs a token from (`_superusers`, or a user collection). The sign-in page then shows only that form, with no
links to the others. A browser signed in as another account type isn't taken to consent: it gets that form, with a
line saying who's signed in and what the client needs. No other account type is issued a token. An account type that
can't sign in here is an `invalid_request` error (sent back to the client, or the device request's 400). Without
`account`, the user chooses, as before.

### Audience (RFC 8707)

A `resource` parameter on `/api/_c/oauth/v1/authorize`, `/api/_c/oauth/v1/device` or `/api/_c/oauth/v1/token` (a URL on this server) binds the
access token to it: the token then only works under that URL's path. So a token issued for `/mcp` can't deploy, and a
deploy token can't drive MCP. Refreshed tokens keep it.

### Building on the OAuth server

- **Go API.** `tokens.OAuth(app)` returns the server. `Issuer(e)` is its public base URL;
  `EnableDynamicRegistration()` turns on `POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register`; `SetAccessTTL("/mcp", 0)` sets the lifetime of
  tokens bound to a resource (0: never expire). `FindClient`, `ListClients`, `AddClient` and `RemoveClient` manage
  clients.
- **Scopes.** Register a scope with Tokens (Go or `$apiTokens.registerScope`) and clients can ask for it; nothing else
  is needed.
- **Render the pages yourself.** `Config.Render(e, page, data)` renders any page (return `handled=false` to fall
  back), with `PageData`. It wins over ejected templates.

## Example

The OAuth server is on wherever Tokens is (its [example](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/api-tokens/example/main.go) runs it). To brand it and let MCP connectors
register themselves:

```go
set := standard.New()
set.APITokens = apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{
	DynamicRegistration: true, // MCP connectors register themselves (ext/mcp turns this on anyway)
	Branding:            tokens.Branding{Accent: "#4f46e5", Footer: "Example OAuth server"},
}})
app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{})
```

## Endpoints

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` | Metadata (RFC 8414). The issuer is `Config.Issuer`, else the request's own scheme and host. |
| `GET/POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/authorize` | Sign-in and consent pages. Authorization code with PKCE (S256 only; required). Optional `account` (see [Account type](#account-type)) and `resource`. |
| `POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/token` | `authorization_code`, `refresh_token` and `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`. Refresh rotates without logouts: the old access token lives out its time, and the old refresh token works again for 2 minutes, so two processes refreshing at once both succeed. |
| `POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/device`, `GET/POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/device/verify` | Device flow (RFC 8628): codes like `WDJB-MJHT`, valid 10 minutes. |
| `POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/revoke` | Revocation (RFC 7009): an access token or a refresh token (revokes both). |
| `GET/POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/provider/callback` | Where OAuth2 providers send the browser back after sign-in. |
| `POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register` | Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), when `DynamicRegistration` is on or an extension called `EnableDynamicRegistration()` (MCP does). Public clients by default. |

Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) belongs to the resource: MCP serves `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`.

## Clients

- **`pocketone-cli`** is built in: public, any `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/…` or `[::1]` redirect, device codes. It's
  what `pocketone login` uses.
- **Client ID metadata documents (CIMD):** an `https://` client id is fetched as a JSON document (`client_id` must
  equal the URL; its `client_name` and `redirect_uris` are used; public clients only; cached 10 minutes). Only
  `Config.CIMDHosts` are trusted (default `claude.ai`, `claude.com`); the metadata says
  `client_id_metadata_document_supported`.
- Registered clients live in `_api_tokens_oauth_clients`; codes, device codes and refresh tokens in `_api_tokens_oauth_codes`.

## How sign-in works

The pages never check passwords or codes themselves. Each step calls PocketBase's own auth endpoint in-process,
through the app's router, so the collection's auth rule, MFA, rate limits, superuser IP limits and every
`onRecordAuth*Request` hook apply as for the REST API, and the record the endpoint returns is the one signed in:

- password: `POST /api/collections/{c}/auth-with-password`;
- emailed code: `POST …/request-otp`, then `POST …/auth-with-otp`;
- OAuth2: the browser goes to the provider with the state and PKCE from `GET …/auth-methods`, comes back to
  `/api/_c/oauth/v1/provider/callback`, and `POST …/auth-with-oauth2` completes it (account linking and sign-up are
  PocketBase's);
- MFA: when an auth call answers 401 with an `mfaId`, the second page passes it along.

Only collections with a sign-in method on are offered. Access tokens are owned by the signed-in record, so every
collection that may sign in must also be allowed by Tokens (its default is every auth collection). The session is a
15-minute HttpOnly cookie on `/api/_c/oauth/v1`; forms carry a CSRF token; a provider round trip keeps its state in a signed
10-minute cookie.

## Go config

```go
apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{
    Collections:         nil,                  // who may sign in; default: _superusers + every auth collection
    AccessTTL:           30 * 24 * time.Hour,  // default; per resource with srv.SetAccessTTL("/mcp", 0)
    RefreshTTL:          180 * 24 * time.Hour, // default, renewed on each refresh
    DynamicRegistration: false,                // POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register (MCP turns it on)
    CIMDHosts:           nil,                  // default claude.ai, claude.com; an empty non-nil slice turns CIMD off
    Issuer:              "",                   // public base URL; default: the request's scheme and host
    Branding:            tokens.Branding{LogoURL: "/logo.svg", Accent: "#4f46e5", Footer: "Acme Inc."},
}})
```

`Branding` also takes a `Name` (default: Settings → Application name). `Accent` is the button color (default
`#16161a`).

## Custom page templates

The templates are Go `html/template` files, and their dot is `PageData` (`{{.AppName}}`, `{{.Action}}`, `{{.Hidden}}`,
`{{.CSRF}}`, `{{.ClientName}}`, `{{.Scopes}}`, `{{.ScopeChoices}}`, `{{.Superuser}}`, `{{.Providers}}`, `{{.Error}}`, …;
see `PageData` in [oauth_pages.go](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/api-tokens/oauth_pages.go)). Each page includes the others by name (`{{template "head" .}}`).
- Every POST form must include `{{template "hidden" .}}` and a `step` button.
- Steps: `password`, `request_otp`, `otp`, `oauth2:<provider>`, `use:<collection>` (switch forms; `use:` is the
  default user form), `allow`, `deny`, `switch`.
- Sign-in forms post `collection`; the MFA and code pages also post `mfa_id` / `otp_id`.
- Consent posts `access` = `full`, or `limited` with a `grant` field per ticked scope (from `data.scopeChoices`:
  `name`, `description`, `checked`). A consent form without `access` grants what the client asked for.

# Auto TLS

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

Automatic HTTPS certificates through ACME, with [CertMagic](https://github.com/caddyserver/certmagic) (Caddy's
certificate engine). PocketBase already gets Let's Encrypt certificates for `serve example.com`. Auto TLS takes over
that job and adds other certificate authorities, extra domains and wildcard certificates.

Status: stable on a multisite host, beta on a single app.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Auto TLS is built into `pocketone` and **off by default**. Turn it on with `--autotls` (or `auto: true` in
`pocketone.yaml`). It only does something when the app serves HTTPS, that is with `serve <domain>` or `--https`; on
plain HTTP it stays idle, and without it PocketBase's own certificates are used as before.

In your own Go build, register it before the app starts:

```go
import (
	"pocketone.dev/ext/autotls"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/extkit"
)

app := pocketbase.New()
extkit.MustRegister(app, autotls.NewApp(autotls.Config{Auto: true, Email: "ops@example.com"}))
app.Start()
```

## Configure

### Command-line flags

```sh
pocketone serve example.com --autotls --autotlsEmail ops@example.com
pocketone serve example.com --autotls --autotlsDomains "*.example.com" --autotlsDNS cloudflare   # token in $CF_API_TOKEN
```

| Flag | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--autotls` | `false` | Turn it on. |
| `--autotlsEmail` | | ACME account email, for expiry notices from the CA. |
| `--autotlsCA` | `letsencrypt` | `letsencrypt`, `letsencrypt-staging`, `zerossl`, or an ACME directory URL. |
| `--autotlsDomains` | | Extra domains, obtained at start (comma separated). Wildcards need `--autotlsDNS`. |
| `--autotlsDNS` | | DNS provider for DNS-01 challenges. Only `cloudflare` is supported. |
| `--autotlsDNSTokenEnv` | `CF_API_TOKEN` | Environment variable holding the DNS provider's API token. |

### pocketone.yaml

The `autotls` section sets the defaults for those flags. Flags win over the file.

```yaml
autotls:
  auto: true
  email: ops@example.com
  ca: letsencrypt
  domains: ["*.example.com"]   # wildcards need dns
  dns:
    provider: cloudflare
    api_token: $CF_API_TOKEN   # read from the .env beside pocketone.yaml
```

`storage` is only in the file: where certificates are kept (default `pb_data/.autotls`). The DNS token can be given
as `api_token` (write `$VAR` to read it from the `.env` beside the file) or through `api_token_env`, the name of an
environment variable. `api_token` is only used when `--autotlsDNS` names the same provider as the file.

The Cloudflare token needs permission to edit the zone's DNS.

There are no dashboard settings.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `autotls:`

Automatic HTTPS certificates (ACME): auto, email, CA, domains, DNS-01, certificate storage. The --autotls* flags win.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `auto` | bool |  | Get certificates through ACME (CertMagic). Flag: --autotls. |
| `email` | string |  | ACME account email, for expiry notices from the CA. Flag: --autotlsEmail. |
| `ca` | string |  | letsencrypt (default), letsencrypt-staging, zerossl, or an ACME directory URL. Flag: --autotlsCA. |
| `storage` | string |  | Where certificates are kept. Default pb_data/.autotls. |
| `domains` | list of string |  | Extra domains to get at start; wildcards (*.example.com) need dns. Flag: --autotlsDomains. |
| `dns.provider` | string |  | DNS provider for DNS-01 challenges (needed for wildcards): cloudflare. Flag: --autotlsDNS. |
| `dns.api_token` | string |  | The provider's API token. Write $VAR to read it from the .env beside the file. |
| `dns.api_token_env` | string |  | Or: the environment variable holding the token. Default CF_API_TOKEN. Flag: --autotlsDNSTokenEnv. |

## Use

Once on, there's nothing to click. Start the app as usual with `serve <domain>` (or `--https`):

- **Which hostnames get a certificate.** The domains given to `serve` and their `www.` variants, issued on the first
  request for each, plus `--autotlsDomains`, obtained at start. Any other hostname is refused at the TLS handshake, so
  a random `Host` can't trigger issuance.
- **How they're proved.** TLS-ALPN-01 on the HTTPS port, or DNS-01 when a DNS provider is set (needed for wildcards).
  HTTP-01 isn't used on a single app, because port 80 is PocketBase's redirect server.
- **Renewal** is automatic.
- **Where they're stored.** `pb_data/.autotls` by default, separate from PocketBase's own `.autocert_cache`.

Settings are checked at start, before anything touches the network. A wildcard domain without a DNS provider, a
Cloudflare provider without a token, or an unknown provider stops the app with an error such as:

```
tls.domains: wildcard "*.example.com" needs a DNS provider (tls.dns); per-hostname certificates work without one
```

With debug logging, the start shows `autotls: CertMagic serves HTTPS certificates` with the CA and extra domains.

Use `--autotlsCA letsencrypt-staging` while testing, so failed attempts don't count against Let's Encrypt's rate limits.

## Integrations

### Multisite hosts

On a [multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) host (any runtime: pocker or docker), the stock `pocketone` binary runs
`autotls.New()`, a host extension that gets certificates for every instance the host serves. It's configured by the same `autotls`
section:

```yaml
autotls:
  auto: true
  email: ops@example.com
  storage: ./pb_root/.pocker-certs   # default: .pocker-certs in the runtime's instance root
  domains: ["*.example.com", "example.com"]
  dns: { provider: cloudflare, api_token_env: CF_API_TOKEN }   # only needed for wildcards
```

- Without `dns`, every hostname the instance source maps gets its own certificate on its first TLS handshake, with any
  DNS host and no API token. Hostnames no instance serves never trigger issuance.
- Challenges include HTTP-01 on the host's port 80, as well as TLS-ALPN-01 and DNS-01.
- Certificate files (`server.tls.cert`/`key`) stay a core host feature. Setting both files and `auto` is an error.
- Certificates belong to the host, not to instances; the single-app extension (`NewApp`) is a separate type so
  it never runs per instance.

### Building on Auto TLS

- `autotls.New()` is a host extension (`multisite.Extension`) that provides the [tls/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/tls/v1)
  contract when `auto` is on. A host adds it to its host extensions (a `pocker.Server` built by hand takes it in
  `Extensions` too):

  ```go
  h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Extensions: []multisite.Extension{autotls.New()}})
  ```

- `AutoTLS.Config` can be set in Go before the server starts; the `autotls` section is read only when `Auto` is false
  there.
- `autotls.SupportedDNSProviders` lists the `dns.provider` values it understands.

## Example

Auto TLS is built into `pocketone`: [`examples/pocketone/binary/binary.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/examples/pocketone/binary/binary.go) registers it with the other default extensions.

## How it works

- Go module `pocketone.dev/ext/autotls`.
- On a single app, an `OnServe` hook swaps the TLS config of PocketBase's HTTPS server for CertMagic's. PocketBase's
  own host policy (the `serve` domains and `www.`) decides which on-demand hostnames are allowed. The certificate
  manager stops when the app terminates.
- TLS 1.2 is the minimum; `h2` and `http/1.1` are offered, and `acme-tls/1` stays on for TLS-ALPN challenges.
- A wildcard in `domains` covers one level (`*.example.com` covers `a.example.com`, not `a.b.example.com`).

# Backups

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

> Walkthrough for app owners: [Point-in-time restore](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/restore). This page is the technical reference.

Restore an app to a moment from its own backups. Ask for "Tuesday 15:00" and the app restores the latest backup made
at or before it, wherever its backups are kept (pb_data/backups or S3). Every app gets this; with
[PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr) on, PITR answers instead and restores any second in its window.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Backups is built into `pocketone` and **on by default**; there's nothing to install. In your own Go build:

```go
extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{backups.New()}, nil, nil)
```

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/backups`.

## Configure

There's nothing to configure: it reads the backups PocketBase already makes (Settings → Backups, including the
automatic schedule and S3). An app turns it off with `extensions: { backups: { enabled: false } }`.

## Use

It's the default provider of the [restore/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1) contract:

```bash
# what can be restored (superuser token)
curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" https://app.example.com/api/_c/restore/v1
# restore the latest backup at or before a moment
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"at":"2026-11-10T15:00:00Z"}' https://app.example.com/api/_c/restore/v1/restore
```

The answer names the backup it restores. The app restarts to apply it, as a restore from Settings → Backups does.
In the dashboard, Settings → Backups has a "Restore to a moment" section (restore/v1's own screen) that shows which
backup a moment uses.
Agents get the same through MCP (`restore_points`, `restore_restore_to`).

## Commands and APIs

Generated from the `pocketone` binary and the contracts this extension provides.

### [restore/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1)

| Operation | CLI | REST | MCP |
|---|---|---|---|
| [points](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1#points) | `pocketone remote restore points` | `GET /api/_c/restore/v1` | `restore_points` |
| [restore_to](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1#restore_to) | `pocketone remote restore to --at <time>` | `POST /api/_c/restore/v1/restore` | `restore_restore_to` |

## Integrations

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr) | Also provides restore/v1, at any second rather than at backup times; when it's on for an app, Backups steps aside. |
| [S3 Fallback](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3-fallback) | Backups kept on the host's storage are listed and restored the same way. |
| [Contracts](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts) | restore/v1 is the contract; any extension or host can provide it instead. |

## Example

```go
// Command example is a PocketBase app whose restore/v1 comes from its backups: create a backup in the dashboard
// (Settings → Backups), then `curl -H "Authorization: <superuser token>" http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/_c/restore/v1`
// lists it, and POST /api/_c/restore/v1/restore with {"at": "<RFC 3339 time>"} restores the latest backup before it.
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/backups"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/devusers"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/extkit"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"
	if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{backups.New()}, nil, nil); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## How it works

`Points` lists the backups filesystem (`app.NewBackupsFilesystem()`), newest first, by each file's time. `RestoreTo`
picks the newest backup at or before the moment and runs PocketBase's own `RestoreBackup`, which swaps pb_data and
restarts the app.

MIT


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bulkmail

# Bulk Mail

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

> Walkthrough for app owners: [Bulk mail](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/bulk-mail). This page is the technical reference.

Campaigns to your app's own users, from the dashboard. You pick who gets the mail with a collection, a view or SQL,
write the message, and Bulk Mail sends it at a steady pace through your app's mail settings. It adds one-click
unsubscribe, keeps a list of addresses that must never be mailed again, and handles bounces and spam complaints.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Bulk Mail is built into `pocketone` and **on** for every app. Nothing is sent until a superuser starts a campaign.

In your own Go build, register the extension before the app starts. Bind it into the JS runtime too if you want
`$bulkmail` in `pb_hooks`:

```go
mail := bulkmail.New(bulkmail.Config{Rate: 5, Daily: 5000})

app := pocketbase.New()
extkit.MustRegister(app, mail)
jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, mail) }})
app.Start()
```

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/bulkmail`.

## Configure

There is no `pocketone.yaml` section or command-line flag. The limits are fixed in the binary; `pocketone` uses the
defaults:

| Limit | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Per second | 5 | The most messages this app sends per second. A campaign can only lower it. |
| Per day | 5,000 | The most messages this app sends per UTC day, across all campaigns. |

In a custom build, set them with `bulkmail.Config{Rate, Daily}`. `Daily: bulkmail.NoBulkMail` forbids sending; the
screens then say so.

### Settings → Mail

Campaigns send through the app's own mail settings and from its sender, both set on **Settings → Mail**. Below that
form there's a **Bulk mail** section:

- **Postal address**: shown in every campaign footer. Anti-spam laws require one.
- **Unsubscribe mailbox**: optional. Adds a `mailto:` alternative to the `List-Unsubscribe` header.
- **Bounces and complaints** (click to open):
  - **Amazon SES (SNS) endpoint**: the URL to subscribe to the SNS topic your SES identity sends bounce and complaint
    notifications to.
  - **Allowed SNS topic ARNs**: comma separated. Empty accepts any topic with a valid AWS signature.
  - **Generic webhook** and **Webhook secret**: for other providers. The webhook is off until you set a secret.

The section also shows this app's limits and how many messages it sent today. Click **Save bulk mail settings**.

Unsubscribe links and the feedback URLs are built from **Settings → Application → Application URL**, so set it to
the address people reach your app on.

The settings are stored in the app's [key-value store](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/kv/extension) under the private name `_bulkmail/settings`
(only Go code reaches it), so they go along with its backups. Secrets are
never shown again after saving.

## Use

The dashboard gets a **Mail** link in its menu, with two pages: **Campaigns** and **Suppressions**. Only superusers see
them.

### Write a campaign

1. Open **Mail** and click **New campaign**. It starts as a draft for verified users of `users`.
2. Fill in **Name**, **Subject** and **Body**.
3. Under **Audience**, choose who gets it:
   - **Filter**: a **Collection** (or a view), an optional **Filter** in the same syntax as API rules, and the
     **Email field** that holds the address (an email or text field, or a view's computed column).
   - **SQL**: a read-only `SELECT` that returns an `email` column. Every other column is available to the message.

   Click **Count recipients** to see how many match, how many are suppressed, and a few sample addresses.
4. Optional: **Vars (JSON)** for values used in the message, a **Schedule (UTC)**, and **Max per second** to send
   slower than the app's limit.
5. Click **Save changes**. **Preview** shows the message for one recipient; **Send test** mails it to the
   **Test address**.

A view is the easy way to build a dynamic audience: it picks who gets mail and computes the columns the message
uses. The [example](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/bulkmail/example/demo.go) creates one called `newsletter_audience`.

### Placeholders

In the subject and body:

- `{{record.field}}`: a field or column of the recipient's row, for example `{{record.name}}`.
- `{{email}}`, `{{campaign.name}}` and `{{unsubscribe_url}}`.
- Campaign vars: `{"promo": "X"}` gives `{{promo}}`. A var can be computed once when sending starts:
  `{"count": {"sql": "SELECT COUNT(*) AS value FROM users"}}`.
- `{{if record.field}}…{{else}}…{{end}}` blocks, and `{{if !record.field}}` for the opposite.

Values are HTML-escaped in the body. An unsubscribe footer with your postal address is always added.

### Send

Click **Send** (or **Schedule** when a time is set) and confirm. The campaign page shows its status and progress
(sent, queued, skipped, failed), and a **Recipients** table you can filter by status. While it runs you can
**Pause**, **Resume** or **Cancel** it.

- Every address is queued once per campaign. Sending a finished campaign again mails only new matches.
- A message counts as sent only once the mail server accepts it, so a restart doesn't send twice or skip anyone.
- A permanent error (SMTP 5xx) fails that recipient. Other errors are retried, up to three attempts.
- A campaign pauses itself when more than 5% of its sends fail after the first 100, or when spam complaints pass
  0.3% of its sends (at least 3). The reason shows next to its status.

### Suppressions

**Mail → Suppressions** lists the addresses that never receive campaign mail, whatever the audience says.
Unsubscribes, permanent bounces and complaints are added automatically. Click **Add address** to add one by hand, a
row to edit or delete it, or **Export CSV** to download the list.

### Unsubscribing

Every message has a signed unsubscribe link and the `List-Unsubscribe` and `List-Unsubscribe-Post: One-Click`
headers that Gmail and Yahoo require for bulk senders. Opening the link shows a confirm button, so link scanners
can't unsubscribe anyone. The one-click request from a mail provider unsubscribes directly.

### Try it locally

In dev mode with SMTP off, `pocketone` catches every mail, bulk mail included, in an inbox at
http://127.0.0.1:8025:

```bash
pocketone serve --dev
```

## Commands and APIs
