# Pages specification

The contract for `ext/pages`, PocketOne's server-rendered multi-page app extension. The test fixtures
([`fixtures/`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/pages/fixtures)), the starter kits and pocketone.dev are written against this document. Where the
implementation and this document disagree, one of them is a bug.

v1 is a clean API. It keeps Pages' ideas (a folder of files that become routes, EJS, layouts, middleware,
private partials) and changes the shapes. Apps written for the npm package (0.x) don't run unchanged; "Changes from
0.x" (section 12) lists every difference.

Code files and templates come in TypeScript (`.ts`, `.ets`, `.tsx`) and plain JavaScript (`.js`, `.ejs`, `.jsx`),
which behave the same apart from types. Samples here use whichever is shortest; the user docs use `.ts` and `.ets`.

## 1. The `pb_pages` folder

Pages live in their own folder next to PocketBase's others:

```
myapp/
  pb_data/  pb_hooks/  pb_migrations/  pb_public/
  pb_pages/
```

- A single app finds it at `pb_pages` next to `pb_data`, or at `--pagesDir` (a relative path resolves against the
  working directory, like `--hooksDir`).
- Serving is automatic: the standard PocketOne binary includes pages, and an app serves its `pb_pages` whenever the folder
  exists (it starts serving if the folder appears later). There is no on/off switch; no folder, no pages.
- Under the multitenant host every instance has its own `pb_pages`.
- If the folder doesn't exist, the extension does nothing for that app.
- Page code can `require()` modules from `pb_pages` (`_private/` folders, then `node_modules`), then from the app's
  usual module paths. The same `require` works in modules, JSX/TSX components and EJS templates:
  - `./x` and `../x` are files in `pb_pages`, relative to the requiring file, never above `pb_pages`. Without an
    extension, `.js`, `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.jsx`, `.json` and `.cjs` are tried, then a folder's `package.json` or `index`.
  - A bare name (`pkg`, `pkg/sub`, `@scope/pkg`) is looked up first in `_private/` folders, from the requiring file's
    folder up to the top of `pb_pages`, the same lookup as `include` (4.2; the extensions above are tried). Then it's
    looked up in the nearest `node_modules` folder, the same way up. A package resolves through its `package.json`: `exports` (a string,
    or conditions, where `require`, then `node`, then `default` are used), else `main`, else `index.js`. With
    `exports`, only what it lists can be required, and no entry may point outside the package.
  - Then `pb_hooks/node_modules`, then the app folder's `node_modules` (the folder that holds `pb_pages`, where 0.x
    sites keep `package.json`).
  - Anything not found that way goes to the app's own module loader. If that fails too, the error lists the folders
    searched.
  - A require cycle (`a` requires `b`, which requires `a`) gets the exports as they are so far, as in Node.
  - `node_modules` is never routed or served, and isn't watched: after changing files in it, change any file in
    `pb_pages` (or restart) to reload.
- Page code runs in the app's JS VM, so PocketBase's JSVM globals (`$app`, `Record`, `$dbx`, `$security`, ...) are
  available, as far as the sandbox allows for untrusted apps.
- Deploying: `pb_pages` is part of an app's code, next to `pb_hooks` and `pb_migrations` (the `deploy` extension
  uploads it the same way).
- Pages' own file access (routes, static files, includes, assets) never leaves `pb_pages`.

### 1.1 Special names

A path segment (file or folder name) starting with one of these characters is never a URL:

| Prefix | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `+` | Framework file: `+config`, `+middleware` (`.js` or `.ts`); `+layout`, `+error`, `+404` (`.ets`, `.ejs`, `.jsx` or `.tsx`). `+middleware` and `+layout`: one of each per folder. `+config`, `+error` and `+404`: only at the top of `pb_pages` (in a subfolder they're an error at startup). Any other `+` name is an error at startup. |
| `_` | Private. `_private/` folders hold partials and modules for `include()` and `ctx.resolve()`. Other `_` names are ignored. |
| `-` | Ignored (drafts, notes). |
| `.` | Ignored (dotfiles), except a top-level `.well-known/`, which is served as static files (ACME challenges, `security.txt`, app links). |

`node_modules/` is never routed. Hook files (`*.pb.js`, `*.pb.ts`) belong in `pb_hooks`: in `pb_pages` they're a
startup error and never served.

### 1.2 Groups

A folder named `(name)` groups files without adding a URL segment: `(marketing)/about.ejs` serves `/about`. Groups can
carry their own `+layout.ejs`, `+middleware.js` and `_private/`.

## 2. Routes

### 2.1 Pages

A **page** is a template file: `.ets`, `.ejs`, `.md`, `.jsx` or `.tsx` (4.1, 4.5).

| File | URL |
|---|---|
| `index.ejs` | `/` |
| `about.ejs` | `/about` |
| `docs/index.md` | `/docs` (and `/docs/`) |
| `docs/routing.md` | `/docs/routing` |
| `products/[id].ejs` | `/products/123`, with `ctx.params.id = "123"` |
| `[org]/[repo]/index.ejs` | `/acme/web`, with `ctx.params = { org: "acme", repo: "web" }` |

- The extension is dropped. `index` maps to its folder.
- `[name]` matches exactly one non-empty segment. A segment may mix text and a parameter only as the whole segment;
  `post-[id].ejs` is an error at startup.
- A URL with a trailing slash matches the same route as without it. Pages never redirect to add or remove one.
- Matching is case-sensitive.

### 2.2 Route code: `.ts` files

A `.ts` file on a route path is that route's code; its extension says it runs, as in PHP.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `about.ts` beside `about.ets` | the page's code (3.2) |
| `feeds/rss.ts` (no template of that name) | an **endpoint** at `/feeds/rss`: its handlers send the whole response (3.3) |
| `index.ts`, `[id].ts` | the folder's URL, a `[param]` route, as for pages |

- Only `.ts` runs. `.js` and every other file is static (2.3), so browser scripts sit anywhere in `pb_pages`.
  `.d.ts` files are neither served nor run.
- An endpoint and a page or static file claiming the same URL is a startup error (`feed.ts` and `feed/index.ets`).
  A `.ts` beside a template of the same name is a pair, not a conflict.

### 2.3 Static files

Every other file is served as-is at its path (groups removed): `assets/app.css` serves `/assets/app.css`. Files that
mustn't be served (build inputs such as a Tailwind source) take a `-` prefix: `assets/-app.tailwind.css`.

- Content type from the extension.
- `ETag` from the content hash; `If-None-Match` answers `304`.
- Fingerprinted URLs (see `ctx.asset`, 6.5) are served with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`.

### 2.4 Precedence

1. `/api/...` and `/_/...` are PocketBase's. Pages never see them, and a `pb_pages/api/` folder is an error at
   startup.
2. Among matching routes the most specific wins: compare segment by segment from the left; a literal segment beats a
   `[param]`. So `products/new.ejs` beats `products/[id].ejs` for `/products/new`.
3. A static file and a page can't claim the same URL (startup error).
4. A URL nothing in `pb_pages` matches goes on to `pb_public`, then to PocketBase.
5. If `pb_pages/+404.ejs` exists, a `GET`/`HEAD` that nothing (pages, `pb_public`, PocketBase) answers renders it
   inside the root layout with status `404` (never for `/api/` or `/_/`). The root `+middleware.js` runs first;
   page code can still change the status.

The route table is built when the app starts and rebuilt when anything in `pb_pages` changes. A rebuild never
restarts the app or reloads `pb_hooks`. Startup errors (bad names, conflicts) are logged with the file path; the
previous table keeps serving if there was one.

## 3. Request flow

For a URL that matches a page or an endpoint, one JS call does all of this, in order:

1. **Plugins:** every plugin's `extendContext`, then every plugin's `onRequest` (built-in and custom plugins, in config
   order), so an `onRequest` can use what any plugin added to `ctx`.
2. **Middleware**, root first: every `+middleware.js` from `pb_pages/` down to the route's folder (groups included).
3. **Handlers**: the route's `.ts` (the page's code, or the endpoint): `load`, then the handler for the request method.
4. **Template** (pages only), then **layouts**, innermost first.
5. **Response.**

The call runs under the app's usual JS limits (execution time, memory), as one unit. If any step sends a response
(`ctx.res.redirect`, `json`, `html`, `text`, `file`, `sse`), the later steps are skipped.

**Async.** Middleware, `load`, method handlers, templates and components may be `async` (or return a promise). Each
step waits for the one before it to settle, while the app's event loop runs, so `await` works on the `.async` twin of
any Go function (`await ctx.app.countRecords.async('orders')`) and on any other promise. A rejected promise fails the
request like a thrown error. Sync code never makes a promise, so it runs exactly as it would without this.

### 3.1 Middleware

```js
// pb_pages/admin/+middleware.js
module.exports = (ctx, next) => {
  if (!ctx.auth) return ctx.res.redirect('/login')
  ctx.data.section = 'admin'
  return next()
}
```

- One signature: `(ctx, next)`. Call `next()` to continue; return its result.
- Returning without calling `next()` ends the request. If no response was sent, that's an error (500, and in dev
  the error page names the middleware file).
- Middleware may be async: `await next()` returns once the rest of the request (later middleware, handlers,
  template, layouts) has finished, and throws what it threw, so code after it can act on the outcome. A sync
  middleware that calls `next()` without returning it still has the rest of the request awaited after it.
- Share data through `ctx.data`.

### 3.2 Page code: `<page>.ts`

```js
// pb_pages/products/[id].ts, beside products/[id].ets
module.exports = {
  load(ctx) {
    ctx.data.product = ctx.app.findRecordById('products', ctx.params.id)
  },
  post(ctx) {
    const { qty } = ctx.req.body()
    // ...
    return ctx.res.redirect(`/products/${ctx.params.id}`, { flash: 'Added to cart' })
  },
}
```

- Exports any of `load`, `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`. All are optional: a page renders for any method.
- `load` runs for every method; then the method's handler, if there is one. `HEAD` runs `load` and `get` like
  `GET` (only the body is dropped), so keep side effects in `post`/`put`/`patch`/`delete`.
- A handler may set `ctx.data` fields, or return a plain object, which is shallow-assigned into `ctx.data`
  (`Object.assign`). There is no deep merge.
- Handlers may be async. A returned promise is awaited, and what it settles to is treated as a returned value.
- Each page has its own code file. Code several pages share goes in a `_private/` module or a `+middleware`.
- A method with no handler still renders the page, for every method (like PHP): a template can handle a form itself
  by checking `ctx.req.method`, with no `.ts`.

### 3.3 Endpoints: `<name>.ts`

Same exports as page code. There is no template, so a handler must send a response (`ctx.res.json`, `html`,
`redirect`, `sse`, ...); returning without one is a 500. A method with no handler answers `405`, with an `Allow`
header listing the methods that have handlers (`GET, HEAD` when there's a `get`), in the order
`GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE`. Folder middleware runs; layouts don't. Errors are JSON
(`{ "status": 404, "message": "..." }`) unless the request's `Accept` puts `text/html` first (a browser navigating to
it), when they're pages like any other (`+error.ejs` or the HTML error page).

```js
// pb_pages/feeds/latest.ts
module.exports = {
  get(ctx) {
    const posts = ctx.app.findRecordsByFilter('posts', 'published = true', '-created', 20)
    return ctx.res.json(posts.map((p) => ({ id: p.id, title: p.getString('title') })))
  },
}
```

## 4. Templates

### 4.1 EJS and ETS

`.ets` is EJS whose tags hold TypeScript; `.ejs` is the same with plain JavaScript. An `.ets` template is compiled
like an `.ejs` one, then esbuild (built into the binary) strips the types from the whole compiled function, since one
tag's code (`if (x) {`) is rarely valid on its own. Types are stripped, not checked. A TypeScript syntax error names
the template line (from the nearest line marker before it). Everything below applies to both.

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<% code %>` | Run code, no output |
| `<%= expr %>` | Output, HTML-escaped |
| `<%- expr %>` | Output, raw |
| `<%# comment %>` | Nothing |
| `<%%` | A literal `<%` |
| `-%>` | Also remove the newline right after the tag |
| `<%_` / `_%>` | Also remove whitespace before / after the tag on its line |
| `<script server> code </script>` | Same as `<% code %>` |

- Escaping replaces `&` `<` `>` `"` `'` with `&amp;` `&lt;` `&gt;` `&#34;` `&#39;`. `null` and `undefined` output as an empty string.
- A template is compiled once per content hash and reused.
- **`await`.** A template whose code uses `await` (in any tag) is compiled as an async function, so
  `<% const n = await ctx.app.countRecords.async('orders') %>` works. Including an async partial returns a promise:
  print it with `<%- await include('name') %>`, which makes the including template async too. Printing a promise
  without `await` is an error, not `[object Promise]`. `await slot('name', async () => { %>...<% })` defines a slot
  whose content awaits. Templates without `await` stay plain functions.

**In scope inside a template:** `ctx`, `data` (= `ctx.data`), `params` (= `ctx.params`), `include`, `slot`, `asset`
(= `ctx.asset`), `meta` (= `ctx.meta`), `require` (the same `require` as page code, 1).

A template returns its text. There is no `echo`; anything you want in the output goes through a tag.

### 4.2 Partials: `include`

```ejs
<%- include('nav') %>
<%- include('card', { product }) %>
```

- `include(name, locals?)` renders a template from a `_private/` folder and returns its text. Use `<%-` so its HTML
  isn't escaped.
- Lookup: `_private/` in the current template's folder, then each parent folder up to `pb_pages/`. For a template
  that is itself inside a `_private/` folder, the search starts at the folder containing that `_private/` (so its
  siblings are found first). A name starting with `/` looks only in `pb_pages/_private/`, unless it names a `_private/` folder itself
  (`/_private/card`, `/blog/_private/card`, as in 0.x), which is a path from the top of `pb_pages`. `..` is not allowed.
- `name` may include its extension. The exact name is tried first; then `.ets`, `.ejs`, `.md`, `.jsx` and `.tsx` are
  added, in that order, so a dotted name such as `nav.main` finds `nav.main.ets`.
- The partial sees the same `ctx`, plus `locals` as top-level variables. As in EJS, `locals` is also the whole object,
  so an optional one can be tested without a `ReferenceError`: `<% if (locals.subtitle) { %>`. A page or layout gets an
  empty `locals`.
- Including more than 32 levels deep is an error (recursion guard).

### 4.3 Slots and layouts

`+layout.ejs` files wrap pages. A page's layouts are every `+layout.ejs` from its own folder up to `pb_pages/`,
applied innermost first. A folder may have one layout.

```ejs
<!-- pb_pages/products/[id].ejs -->
<% slot('title', () => { %><%= data.product.getString('name') %><% }) %>
<h1><%= data.product.getString('name') %></h1>
```

```ejs
<!-- pb_pages/+layout.ejs -->
<html>
  <head><title><%- slot('title') || 'My shop' %></title></head>
  <body><%- slot() %></body>
</html>
```

- `slot(name, fn)` defines a named slot: `fn`'s output is captured and nothing is output in place.
- `slot(name)` returns a slot's content (`''` if not defined). `slot()` returns the content being wrapped: the page,
  or the inner layout. `<%- slot %>` (no call, as 0.x layouts wrote it) prints the same thing.
- Named slots defined by the page or by any inner layout are visible to every outer layout. Defining the same name
  again replaces it; inside the new definition's `fn`, `slot(name)` still returns the previous content, so a layout
  can wrap it (`slot('title', () => { %>Docs: <%- slot('title') %><% })`).
- Layouts are skipped when the response isn't HTML (a handler set another `Content-Type`) or after
  `ctx.res.layout(false)`.
- A page with an inner extension gets that type: `robots.txt.ejs` serves `/robots.txt` as `text/plain` and
  `feed.xml.ejs` serves `/feed.xml` as XML, so layouts are skipped. `.html` (or no inner extension) is HTML. Page
  code can still set another `Content-Type`.

### 4.4 Markdown pages

A `.md` page is EJS first, then Markdown (CommonMark + GFM tables, strikethrough, task lists, autolinks).

- Front matter between `---` lines at the top is YAML, removed before EJS runs. Each top-level key is passed to
  `ctx.meta(key, value)`, for pages and for included `.md` partials.
- Headings get `id`s: lowercased, characters other than `a-z 0-9 - _ space` removed, spaces to `-`; a repeated id
  gets `-1`, `-2`, ... appended.
- Fenced code blocks render as `<pre><code class="language-<lang>">`. Raw HTML passes through unchanged.
- Relative image paths go through `ctx.asset`.
- A `.md` partial is rendered (EJS, then Markdown) on its own and inserted as HTML; Markdown never runs twice on the
  same text. Leave blank lines around an `include` in Markdown so the HTML stays a block.

### 4.5 JSX and TSX

`.jsx` and `.tsx` files are templates too: pages, layouts (`+layout.tsx`), `+error`/`+404`, and partials in
`_private/`. They're compiled when first used by esbuild, which is built into the binary (no Node, no build step), and
cached by content like EJS. TypeScript types are stripped, not checked. TSX is the component style; the docs use
ETS (4.1) and treat TSX as the alternative, one style per app.

```tsx
// pb_pages/products/[id].tsx
import Price from './_private/Price'

export default function Product({ data, slot }: pages.Props) {
  slot('title', data.product.getString('name'))
  return (
    <article class="product">
      <h1>{data.product.getString('name')}</h1>
      <Price cents={data.product.getInt('price')} />
    </article>
  )
}
```

- The file's default export is a component: a function from props to markup. Props: `ctx`, `data`, `params`,
  `meta`, `asset`, `include`, `slot`, `children`, plus an `include`'s locals.
- JSX renders straight to HTML on the server. There's no virtual DOM, no hydration, no client-side React. Event
  handler props (functions) are dropped; use plain attributes (`onclick="..."`, `hx-get`, `data-on:click`).
- Text and attribute values are escaped. `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html }}` inserts raw HTML. `class` and
  `className` both work, as do `for` and `htmlFor`. `style` takes a string or an object (`{ marginTop: 4 }` →
  `margin-top:4`). `true` renders a bare attribute; `false`, `null` and `undefined` leave it out.
- `<html>` renders with `<!doctype html>` in front of it (JSX can't write a doctype).
- In a layout, `children` is the inner content. `slot(name)` reads a named slot, `slot(name, content)` sets one
  (content is JSX or a string), `slot()` is the same as `children`.
- `include(name, locals)` returns the partial's HTML, ready to put in JSX. An EJS/ETS template can `include` a
  `.jsx`/`.tsx` partial: its locals become props.
- Components are ordinary modules: `import Card from './_private/Card'` (resolved like `require`, 3.2). Partials
  are looked up with extensions in this order: `.ets`, `.ejs`, `.md`, `.jsx`, `.tsx`.
- **Async components.** Any component may be `async`, the file's default export included. The render waits for it
  wherever it sits in the tree; sibling async components run concurrently. `include()` of an async partial and
  `slot(name, content)` with async content work the same way, and a layout reads the slot once it has settled.

**TypeScript modules.** Route code (`.ts`), `+middleware.ts`, `+config.ts` and any `.ts` file reached by
`require`/`import` work like their `.js` versions. A module whose only export is `export default` behaves like
`module.exports = ...`.

**Types.** The extension adds its declarations to the app's `types.d.ts` (the JS engine's `TypeScript()` hook): a
`pages` namespace (`Context`, `Handlers`, `Middleware`, `Config`, `PluginFactory`, `Props`) and a permissive `JSX`
namespace. They add no globals. `pages.Data` and `pages.Context` are interfaces an app may extend.

## 5. Responses

| Situation | Response |
|---|---|
| A handler or middleware sent one | That one |
| Page rendered | `200 text/html; charset=utf-8` (or the status set with `ctx.res.status`) |
| `HEAD` | As `GET`, without a body |
| No handler for the method | Page: rendered as usual. Endpoint: `405` + `Allow` |
| Error thrown | `500` (see 8) |

JSON is only sent through `ctx.res.json` (and an endpoint's errors). Template output is never parsed as JSON.

## 6. The `ctx` object

One object per request, passed to middleware, handlers, templates and plugins.

### 6.1 `ctx.req`

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `method` | `"GET"`, `"POST"`, ... |
| `url` | `{ href, origin, pathname, search }` |
| `query(name)` | First value of a query parameter as a string, or `undefined` |
| `query(name, { all: true })` | Every value, as an array of strings |
| `query()` | `{ name: firstValue }` for every parameter |
| `header(name)` | Request header, `''` if absent |
| `cookie(name)` | Cookie value as a string, or `undefined` |
| `cookie(name, { json: true })` | Cookie parsed as JSON (`undefined` if absent or not JSON) |
| `cookies()` | `{ name: value }`, strings |
| `body()` | Parsed body: JSON object, or form fields (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`) as `{ name: value }` (repeated names as arrays) |
| `files(name)` | Uploaded files for a multipart field, as PocketBase `*filesystem.File` values ready for a record field |
| `ip` | Client IP as PocketBase resolves it (trusted proxy settings apply) |
| `event` | The underlying PocketBase `RequestEvent`, for anything not covered here |

Query values and cookies are strings unless you ask for JSON. Nothing is parsed for you.

### 6.2 `ctx.res`

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `status(code)` | Status for the rendered page. Returns `ctx.res`. |
| `header(name, value)` | Set a response header; returns `ctx.res`. `header(name)` reads it back. |
| `cookie(name, value, options?)` | Set a cookie. Non-string values are `JSON.stringify`'d; the value is then percent-encoded (`encodeURIComponent`), and `ctx.req.cookie` decodes it. Defaults: `path=/`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Secure` when the request is HTTPS. Options: `path`, `domain`, `maxAge` (seconds), `expires` (a `Date`, milliseconds since the epoch, or a date string; with `maxAge` too, browsers use `maxAge`), `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite`. |
| `clearCookie(name, options?)` | Expire a cookie (same `path`/`domain` as when set). |
| `redirect(location, { status = 302, flash }?)` or `redirect(location, status)` | Send a redirect. `status` must be a 3xx code. `flash` sets a one-time message (6.4). |
| `json(data)` / `json(status, data)` | Send JSON. |
| `html(html)` / `html(status, html)` | Send HTML as-is (no layouts). |
| `text(text)` / `text(status, text)` | Send plain text. |
| `file(path)` | Send a file from `pb_pages` (path relative to `pb_pages`). |
| `sse({ keepAlive }?)` | Start a `text/event-stream` response; returns `{ send(event, data, { id, retry }?), comment(text), close() }`. With `keepAlive` (seconds), a `: keep-alive` comment is written that often until the handler is done. |
| `layout(false)` | Render this page without layouts (e.g. an HTML fragment for htmx). |
| `sent` | `true` once a response has been sent. |

### 6.3 Data and routing

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `ctx.data` | Plain object shared by middleware, handlers and templates. Starts as `{}`. |
| `ctx.params` | Route parameters, strings. Never includes query parameters. |
| `ctx.route` | `{ path, name, file }`: the URL pattern without groups (`/products/[id]`, `/docs` for `docs/index.md`), the file name without extension (`[id]`, `index`) and the file relative to `pb_pages`, groups included. |

### 6.4 Flash messages

- `ctx.res.redirect(path, { flash: 'Saved' })` stores the message as JSON in a cookie (`pp_flash`, encoded like any
  cookie, `HttpOnly`, `Max-Age=300`).
- `ctx.flash()` on the next request returns it and clears it (`Max-Age=0`). It returns `undefined` when there is
  none. Calling it again in the same request returns the same value.
- A flash can be any JSON value.

### 6.5 Helpers

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `ctx.auth` | The authenticated record, or `null`. Set by PocketBase's own auth (an `Authorization` header) or by the `auth` plugin's cookie. |
| `ctx.app` | The app (`$app`): records, collections, settings. |
| `ctx.pb()` | A PocketBase JS SDK client (the bundled synchronous build) acting as the signed-in user (`ctx.auth`), or as a guest. Its requests go to the app's own API in-process (no network), so collection API rules, `expand` and field visibility apply exactly as for a browser. API errors throw the SDK's `ClientResponseError` (`e.status`, `e.response`). Only `/api/` routes; file uploads through the SDK aren't supported (use `ctx.app`). |
| `ctx.env(name)` | Environment variable, `''` if unset (the app's environment; under the sandbox, the instance's). |
| `ctx.log` | `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`: to the app's log. `debug` only shows in dev. |
| `ctx.meta(key, value?)` | Per-request key/value store for page metadata (title, description). Set with two arguments, read with one. |
| `ctx.asset(path)` | URL for a static file in `pb_pages`, with its content hash: `asset('app.css')` → `/assets/app.3f9a1c2b7d4e.css`. Relative paths resolve from the current file's folder; `/`-paths from `pb_pages`. A path that isn't a file in `pb_pages` is returned unchanged. |
| `ctx.include(name, locals?)` | Render a `_private/` partial from JS (handlers, middleware, plugins) and get its text; same lookup as the template `include`, from the route's folder. |
| `ctx.resolve(name, { mode }?)` | Load a module from `_private/`, looked up from the route's folder up (like `ctx.include`; wherever it's called from); without an extension, the name, then `.js`, `.ts` and `.json` are tried. Modes: `require` (default, the module's exports), `raw` (file text), `script` (text wrapped in `<script>`), `style` (wrapped in `<style>`). |
| `ctx.pagesDir` | The absolute path of this app's `pb_pages` folder, e.g. for listing files with `$os.readDir`. Read-only. |
| `ctx.store(name, value?)` | The app's in-memory store (`$app.store()`): set with two arguments, read with one. |
| `ctx.dev` | `true` in dev mode. |

Fingerprinted asset names carry the first 12 hex characters of the file's SHA-256: `name.<hash>.ext`.

## 7. Configuration: `+config.js`

```js
// pb_pages/+config.js
module.exports = {
  plugins: ['auth', 'realtime', 'datastar'],
  debug: false,
}
```

| Key | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `plugins` | `[]` | Module names, built-in names (`auth`, `realtime`), or custom plugin factories such as add-ons (9). Templates and Markdown are always on. |
| `debug` | `false` | Detailed error pages and `ctx.log.debug` output even outside dev mode. |

A string in `plugins` is a module name, required from `+config.js` (1): a `_private/` file (`'datastar'` finds
`_private/datastar.js`), a package in `node_modules` (`'my-plugin'`) or a path (`'./plugins/my-plugin.js'`). Its export, or its `default` export, must be a
plugin factory (9.2). Only when no module by that name is found is the string a built-in (9.1), so a
`_private/auth.js` or a package named `auth` would replace the built-in `auth`. To skip that order and load one exact
file, list `require('./path')` instead of the name: a `./` path is never looked up in `_private/` or `node_modules`. A module that is found but fails to load is an error; it never falls back to
the built-in.

`+config.js` runs on each page request, so these aren't caught at startup: unknown keys, names that are neither a
module nor a built-in, or a plugin listed twice make every page answer with an error (a 500; dev mode shows the
reason on the page), and the reason goes to the log.

## 8. Errors

- Anything thrown in middleware, a handler or a template becomes a `500`.
- **Dev mode or `debug: true`:** an HTML error page with the message, the file and line (template lines map to the
  `.ets`/`.ejs`/`.md` source), and the stack trimmed to `pb_pages`-relative paths.
- **Otherwise:** a plain "Something went wrong" page. The full error always goes to the app's log.
- `throw ctx.httpError(status, message)` sends that status (e.g. `404`, `403`) with a plain page showing `message`.
  From an endpoint it's JSON, unless the request asks for HTML first: `{ "status": 404, "message": "..." }`.
- A custom error page: `pb_pages/+error.ejs` renders for every `ctx.httpError` and every 500 outside dev mode, with
  `ctx.error = { status, message }`, inside the root layout.

## 9. Plugins

### 9.1 Built-in

Turned on by name in `+config.js` when no module by that name is found (7).

**`auth`:** cookie sessions on PocketBase auth, without calling the app over HTTP.
- Every request: reads the `pb_auth` cookie, validates the token, sets `ctx.auth` (or clears a bad cookie).
- The cookie holds `{ token, record }` as JSON (the JS SDK's cookie format), `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Secure` on
  HTTPS, lasting as long as the collection's auth token.
- `identity` arguments accept any of the collection's identity fields (email by default).
- **MFA:** pages has no second sign-in step yet, so every sign-in method (password, OTP, anonymous, OAuth2, and
  `register`'s sign-in) refuses an account that needs MFA, as PocketBase decides it: the collection has MFA on and its
  MFA rule matches the record (an empty rule matches everyone; a rule that can't be checked counts as a match). The
  error says so; nothing is signed in and an OTP isn't used up. A wrong password still says only that the credentials
  are invalid. `ctx.session.signIn(record)` is the exception: it signs in a record the app authenticated itself.
- `ctx.session.authMethods({ collection })` → `{ password: { enabled, identityFields }, otp: { enabled }, mfa:
  { enabled }, oauth2: { enabled, providers: [{ name, displayName }] } }`, as PocketBase's auth-methods API.
- `ctx.session.register(email, password, { collection = 'users', data, verify = true, signIn = true })`: creates the
  record; sends the verification email when `verify`; signs in when `signIn`.
- `ctx.session.signInWithPassword(identity, password, { collection })`
- `ctx.session.requestOTP(email, { collection, create = false })` → `otpId`. Always returns an id (unknown emails
  get one that never validates, as PocketBase does); with `create: true` a missing record is created first.
- `ctx.session.signInWithOTP(otpId, code, { collection })`
- `ctx.session.signInAnonymously({ collection })`
- `ctx.session.requestOAuth2(provider, { collection, redirectPath = '/auth/oauth/confirm', redirect = true })`:
  stores state in a cookie and returns the provider's URL; with `redirect` it also sends the redirect
  (`ctx.res.sent`). `redirectPath` must be a path on this site. PKCE is used when the provider supports it.
- `ctx.session.signInWithOAuth2(state, code, { createData }?)`: completes it on the redirect path (the state cookie
  carries the provider, collection and PKCE verifier; it lasts 10 minutes and works once). The sign-in runs through
  PocketBase's own `auth-with-oauth2` endpoint in-process, so sign-up, account linking (to the signed-in account,
  if any), the anti-hijacking checks and `onRecordAuthWithOAuth2Request` hooks behave as in PocketBase. `createData`
  is extra data for a new record. Returns `{ token, record, meta }` (`meta` is PocketBase's OAuth2 meta, with
  `isNew`). Accounts that need MFA throw an error: pages doesn't do MFA yet.
- Apple answers with a POST, so read `state` and `code` from `ctx.req.body()` there. On HTTPS the state cookie is
  `SameSite=None` so it survives that cross-site POST.
- `ctx.session.signIn(record)`: set the cookie for a record you authenticated yourself.
- `ctx.session.signOut()`
- Email flows, with PocketBase's own checks and mail templates: `requestVerification(email, { collection })`,
  `confirmVerification(token)`, `requestPasswordReset(email, { collection })`,
  `confirmPasswordReset(token, password, passwordConfirm)`, `requestEmailChange(newEmail)` (needs `ctx.auth`),
  `confirmEmailChange(token, password)`. Request methods never reveal whether an email exists.
- Every sign-in method sets `ctx.auth` for the rest of the request and returns `{ token, record }`.

**`realtime`:** PocketBase realtime from page code.
- `ctx.realtime.send(topic, data, { filter }?)` sends to every client subscribed to `topic` (the filter only narrows
  that set). `data` is always
  JSON-encoded (a string arrives as a JSON string, as PocketBase's own messages do).
- `filter(client)` returns `true` to include a client. `client` is PocketBase's realtime client: `id()`,
  `get(key)`, `set(key, value)`, `hasSubscription(topic)`.
- `ctx.realtime.client(id)` returns one client by id, or `null`.
- `ctx.realtime.subscribe(topic, { filter, expand, fields }?)` registers a realtime client for the request, with the
  visitor's auth, so PocketBase's realtime broadcast applies the collection's rules, filter, expand and fields as on
  `/api/realtime`. It returns an async iterator (and `close()`): record topics give `{ action, record }`, others the
  data sent. Each `next()` waits as an async Go call, off the VM's loop. The client is unregistered when the request
  ends (client gone, handler returned, await time passed) or on `close()`/`break`. Up to 64 unread messages queue;
  one more ends the subscription and the next `next()` throws.
- Sending never waits for slow clients: each message is handed to the client's queue in the background.

### 9.2 Custom plugins

A custom plugin is a factory that returns hooks:

```js
module.exports = (config) => ({
  name: 'my-plugin',
  onRequest(ctx) {},                       // before middleware
  extendContext(ctx) { ctx.hello = () => 'hi' },
  transform({ html, ctx, file }) { return html },     // after each page or layout renders (not partials)
})
```

- `config` is the plugin's entry in `+config.js` when it's an object (`{ factory, ...options }`), else `{}`.
- `name` is required and unique.
- 0.x hook names (`onExtendContextApi`, `onRender`, `onResponse`, `handles`) are an error that names the v1 hook to
  use.
- There's no hook for treating other kinds of files as pages: a page's inner extension already does that
  (`robots.txt.ejs` serves `/robots.txt` as `text/plain`, 4.5).
- Hooks run in config order. Every hook is optional.
- Custom plugins run with the same permissions as the rest of the app's code (sandboxed in a multitenant host).

### 9.3 Add-ons

Plugins for third-party libraries ship as JS files in `ext/pages/addons/`, not built into `ext/pages`. Copy one into
`pb_pages/_private/` and list it in `+config.js` by name (`'datastar'`).

**`datastar.js`** ([Datastar](https://data-star.dev)) adds `ctx.datastar`:
- `ctx.datastar.scripts({ spa: { scope, selector }, realtime }?)` returns the script tags (`spa` turns on
  client-side navigation for links under `scope`, swapping `selector`). With `realtime: true` the page subscribes to
  the `datastar` realtime topic and sets a `$clientId` signal to its realtime client id.
- `ctx.datastar.patchElements(html, { selector, mode }?)`, `ctx.datastar.patchSignals(signals, { onlyIfMissing }?)`
  (`signals` is an object), `ctx.datastar.executeScript(js)` send SSE events on the current response. The first one
  starts the stream (`ctx.res.sent` becomes `true`); later steps still run, but their output isn't sent and the
  automatic patch below doesn't happen. The stream closes when the request ends. It sends a keep-alive comment every
  30 seconds. `ctx.datastar.open({ keepAlive }?)` starts it before any patch (`keepAlive` in seconds, `0` for none).
- `ctx.datastar.signals()` returns the request's signals as an object (from the `datastar` query parameter on
  `GET`, the JSON body otherwise). `readSignals(target)` (or 0.x's `readSignals(request, target)`) merges them into
  `target` and returns it.
- Script helpers, each an `executeScript` (options `{ eventId, retryDuration, autoRemove = true, attributes }`;
  `autoRemove` adds `data-effect="el.remove()"` so the script tag removes itself, `attributes` is a list of extra
  attribute strings such as `'type="module"'`): `consoleLog(msg)`, `consoleError(err)`, `redirect(url)` (a full
  page load), `dispatchCustomEvent(name, detail, { selector, bubbles, cancelable, composed, eventId, retryDuration
  }?)` (on `document` by default), `replaceURL(url)` (`history.replaceState`) and `prefetch(urls)` (a
  `speculationrules` script that stays in the page).
- `mode` is one of `outer` (default), `inner`, `replace`, `prepend`, `append`, `before`, `after`, `remove`.
- When a request has `Datastar-Request: true`, the rendered page (without layouts) is sent as a `patchElements`
  event, into `Datastar-Selector` if given.
- `ctx.datastar.realtime.patchElements(html, options?, { filter }?)`, `.patchSignals(signals, options?, { filter }?)`
  and `.executeScript(js, { filter }?)` send the same events to `datastar` realtime subscribers (needs `realtime`).

## 10. Dev mode

On when the app runs in dev mode (`--dev`) or `+config.js` sets `debug: true`:
- detailed error pages (8);
- `ctx.log.debug` output;
- template cache keyed by content hash, so edits show on the next request (the route table is rebuilt on any file
  change in every mode).

## 11. Starter kits

`pocketone pages create <name> [--starter <kit>]` creates the folder `<name>` (it must not exist) and copies the
whole kit into it. Run it with `cd <name> && pocketone serve --dir ./pb_data` (`pocketone` keeps `pb_data` next to its
executable by default; `pb_pages` and `pb_migrations` are found next to `pb_data`). `pocketone pages starters` lists
the kits. Kits: `minimal` (default), `mvp`, `htmx`,
`daisyui`, `daisyui-docs`, `datastar`, `auth`. The command needs a build that includes `ext/pages`. It copies
`pb_pages/` plus anything beside it (`pb_migrations/`, `README.md`, a `package.json` for CSS tooling). Kits ship
inside `ext/pages` (`starters/`).

## 12. Changes from 0.x (npm PocketPages)

| 0.x | v1 |
|---|---|
| `pb_hooks/pages/`, booted by `require('pocketpages')` in a `.pb.js` | `pb_pages/`, no boot file, no npm install |
| `api` object, re-spread into each call | `ctx` with `req`, `res`, `data`, `params`, `route`, helpers |
| Query parameters mixed into `params`, JSON-parsed | `ctx.params` is route parameters only; `ctx.req.query()` returns strings |
| Cookies JSON-parsed on read | Strings; `{ json: true }` to parse |
| Middleware: return a value, or call `next(extra)`, chosen by arity | `(ctx, next)`, data on `ctx.data` |
| `+load.js`, `+get.js`, `+post.js`, ... per folder, results deep-merged | One `.ts` per page exporting `load`, `get`, `post`, ...; returned objects shallow-assigned |
| `+config.js` may export `(api) => ({...})` | It must export an object; a function is an error |
| Template output that parses as JSON is sent as JSON | Only `ctx.res.json` or an endpoint's errors |
| `<!-- slot:name -->` comments; layouts read `slot` / `slots` | `slot(name, fn)` to define, `slot(name)` / `slot()` to read |
| `echo()` writes during render | Templates return text; streaming only through `ctx.res.sse()` |
| `redirect(path, { message })` puts the flash in `?__flash=` | `ctx.res.redirect(path, { flash })`, one-time cookie, `ctx.flash()` |
| `asset()` fingerprint: full SHA-256 | First 12 hex characters |
| `+config.js` plugins: npm package names, EJS options | A name is required first (a `_private/` file or package), then a built-in; or a JS factory. EJS and Markdown always on |
| Plugin hooks `onRequest({ request, response })`, `onExtendContextApi`, `onRender`, `onResponse`, `handles` | `extendContext(ctx)`, `onRequest(ctx)`, `transform`; a 0.x hook name is an error |
| `*.pb.js` beside pages in `pb_hooks/pages/` | Hook files stay in `pb_hooks`; in `pb_pages` they're a startup error |
| `require('../lib/x')` could reach `pb_hooks` from the pages folder | `require` never leaves `pb_pages`; use `require(__hooks + '/lib/x')` |
| Cookies (and `pb_auth`) readable by browser JS | `HttpOnly` by default; pass `{ httpOnly: false }` for a cookie the page's JS reads. `pb_auth` stays `HttpOnly`, so `pb.authStore.loadFromCookie(document.cookie)` no longer works |
| Realtime `send(topic, message)` sent the message as is; `filter(clientId, client, topic, message)` replaced the subscription check | The data is JSON-encoded (a string arrives quoted: `JSON.parse` it); `filter(client)` narrows clients that are subscribed to the topic |
| `.md`, `.jsx`, `.tsx` were static files unless a plugin handled them | Always pages |
| EJS ran over the whole `.md` file, front matter included | Front matter is plain YAML, read before EJS runs |
| auth plugin through the JS SDK over HTTP (`api.pb()`) | `ctx.session.*`, direct app calls |
| `url()`, `stringify()`, micro-dash globals | Removed: use `ctx.req.url`, `JSON.stringify`, plain JS |
| `pb()` (js-sdk plugin over HTTP to `localhost:8090`) | `ctx.pb()`: same SDK, built in, in-process, as the signed-in user |
| Route with fewer segments could match a longer URL | Segment counts must match |
| `create-pocketpages` | `pocketone pages create <name> [--starter <kit>]` |

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr

# PITR

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

> Walkthrough for app owners: [Point-in-time restore](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/restore). This page is the technical reference.

Point-in-time restore: your database as it was at any moment in the last few days, restored from the dashboard.
History is recorded with [Litestream](https://litestream.io), next to your data or in an S3-compatible bucket.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

PITR is built into `pocketone` and **on by default**. Every app it serves starts recording history the first time it
serves; there's nothing to install.

To run without it:

```bash
pocketone serve --pitr=false
```

In your own Go build, register it before the app starts:

```go
app := pocketbase.New()
pitr.MustRegister(app, pitr.Config{})
app.Start()
```

## Configure

### On, off and how far back

Set it in `pocketone.yaml`:

```yaml
pitr:
  enabled: true          # false turns it off
  retention: 72h         # how far back a restore can go
  snapshot_interval: 24h # how often a full copy is taken
```

Or with flags, which win over the file:

| Flag | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--pitr` | `true` | Record history while serving. `--pitr=false` turns it off. |
| `--pitrRetention` | `72h` | How far back a restore can go. |

A shorter `snapshot_interval` makes restores faster and uses more storage.

### Where the history is stored

By default the history is kept next to your database, in `pb_data/litestream/`. That protects you from mistakes in
your data, but not from losing the disk. To keep it somewhere else, use your own S3-compatible bucket:

1. Open **Settings → Backups** in the dashboard and find **Point-in-time restore**.
2. Tick **Store the history in my own S3 bucket** and fill in the endpoint, bucket, region, access key and secret.
   Tick **Force path-style addressing** for MinIO and similar servers. The prefix defaults to `litestream`.
3. Click **Test connection** to check that the bucket accepts a write, then **Save**.

From then on the history is recorded in the bucket, starting with a fresh copy, so restores go back to the moment you
saved. The secret is never shown again after saving. If the app runs with an encryption key (`--encryptionEnv`), the secret
is stored encrypted.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `pitr:`

Point-in-time restore: on by default, retention, snapshot interval. The --pitr and --pitrRetention flags win.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | bool |  | On unless false. The --pitr flag wins. |
| `retention` | duration |  | How far back a restore can go. Default 72h. The --pitrRetention flag wins. |
| `snapshot_interval` | duration |  | How often a full copy is taken. Default 24h. Shorter: faster restores, more storage. |

## Use

### What's covered

Your database: records, collections, settings and superusers. **Not** uploaded files, `pb_hooks`, `pb_public` or the
logs database. Use PocketBase's backups for those.

History starts with the first change after PITR is turned on, and goes back as far as the retention allows (72 hours
by default).

### Restore from the dashboard

1. Open **Settings → Backups**. **Restore to a moment** (the [restore/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1)
   contract's section) shows how far back you can go; **Point-in-time restore** shows how big the history is and where
   it's stored.
2. Under **Restore to**, pick a date and time, then click **Restore**.
3. The app keeps serving while the old database is rebuilt, then restarts with it.

Only superusers see this section.

### Undo a restore

The database you replaced is kept in `pb_data/litestream/before-restore.db`, and history keeps recording, so a restore
can be undone. After a restore, the section shows when you restored and to what time, with an **Undo this restore**
button.

### From the command line

```bash
pocketone pitr status
pocketone pitr restore --at 2026-11-11T14:05:00Z --to /tmp/then.db   # a copy, any time
pocketone pitr restore --at 2026-11-11T14:05:00Z                     # in place
```

`--at` takes an RFC 3339 time. With `--to`, you get a copy of the database as it was, to inspect or pull records
from; the app keeps running. Without `--to`, run it while the server is stopped: the restore is swapped in when it
next starts.

### What it costs

About 176 KiB of memory per serving app, and the storage for your history. Replication runs only while the app is
serving, never during CLI commands.

## Commands and APIs

Generated from the `pocketone` binary and the contracts this extension provides.

### Commands

What it adds to the `pocketone` binary ([CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli)):

| Command | |
|---|---|
| [`pocketone pitr restore`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-pitr-restore) | Restore the database as it was at --at, into --to, or in place on the next start |
| [`pocketone pitr status`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-pitr-status) | Show the restorable window and history size |

### [restore/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1)

| Operation | CLI | REST | MCP |
|---|---|---|---|
| [points](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1#points) | `pocketone remote restore points` | `GET /api/_c/restore/v1` | `restore_points` |
| [restore_to](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1#restore_to) | `pocketone remote restore to --at <time>` | `POST /api/_c/restore/v1/restore` | `restore_restore_to` |

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) | PITR is in the standard set, so every instance that runs PocketOne has it, and a restore restarts only that instance. With an isolate runtime ([Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker)), the `pitr` section sets the defaults for all of them, each instance can override `enabled` and `retention` (below), and sleeping instances cost nothing. |
| [S3 Fallback](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3-fallback) | Mount `litestream` on a backend and every app without its own bucket keeps its history there, under its own prefix. An app's own bucket (Settings → Backups) still wins. |
| [Multitenant](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/tenants) (planned) | Sets each instance's `enabled` and `retention` from its plan, for example a plan without PITR. |
| PocketBase backups | `pb_data/litestream/` is left out of backup zips, and restoring a zip doesn't wipe it. |

### Per-instance settings (pocker)

Each instance can override `enabled` and `retention` in its `extensions.pitr` settings, from `instances.yaml` or a
provider:

```yaml
instances:
  - id: abc
    extensions: { pitr: { retention: 168h } }
  - id: free-plan-app
    extensions: { pitr: { enabled: false } }
```

Each instance's history goes to `instances/<id>/litestream/` in the shared bucket, or its own `pb_data/litestream/`.
A bucket in an instance's settings is refused, so credentials never sit in instance data.

### Building on PITR

- **Store history somewhere else.** PITR asks PocketBase for a filesystem of kind `litestream` (`pitr.Kind`) through
  `OnFilesystemCreate`. Answer it and the history goes to your filesystem; S3 Fallback works this way.
- **Set it per instance.** Write `extensions.pitr.enabled` and `extensions.pitr.retention` into an instance's settings;
  PITR reads them when the instance starts. Multitenant will work this way.
- **Go API.** `(*pitr.Extension).Status(ctx, app)` returns the restorable window, size, destination and last restore;
  `Restore(ctx, app, at)` restores an app to a time.
- **restore/v1.** PITR provides the [restore/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1) contract (superusers):
  `GET /api/_c/restore/v1` for the window, size, destination and last restore, `POST /api/_c/restore/v1/restore`
  with `{"at": "<RFC 3339 time>"}` to restore. Without PITR the same calls restore the latest backup before the
  moment ([Backups](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/backups)), so clients and agents don't care which is on.

## Example

[`example/main.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/pitr/example/main.go) runs one app with point-in-time restore on, keeping three days. Run it with `go run ./example serve` from this folder.

```go
// Command example runs one PocketOne app with point-in-time restore: Litestream copies data.db continuously into
// pb_data/litestream/, and Settings → Backups gets a "Point-in-time restore" section.
//
//	go run ./example serve
//	go run ./example pitr status
//	go run ./example pitr restore --at 2026-11-11T14:05:00Z --to /tmp/then.db
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"log"
	"time"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/devusers"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/pitr"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"

	pitr.MustRegister(app, pitr.Config{
		Retention: 72 * time.Hour, // on by default; Enabled: false turns it off
		// Bucket: &pitr.Bucket{Endpoint: "...", Bucket: "...", Region: "auto", AccessKey: "...", Secret: "...", Label: "EU"},
	})

	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## How it works

- Go module `pocketone.dev/ext/pitr`, Litestream v0.5.18 (pinned).
  [`example/main.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/pitr/example/main.go) runs one app with local history.
- Litestream continuously copies `data.db` to its destination: the app's own bucket (its PITR settings), else a
  filesystem of kind `litestream` (an `OnFilesystemCreate` handler, such as S3 Fallback), else `pb_data/litestream/`.
  Buckets go through PocketBase's own S3 client, not the AWS SDK. Each LTX file's timestamp is kept in object
  metadata, so restoring to a time doesn't depend on upload times.
- Replication runs only while the app serves (`OnServe`), never for CLI commands. On terminate it's flushed and
  detached, so under pocker a sleeping instance costs nothing.
- A restore is built into a side file while the app keeps serving, then swapped in by `app.Restart()`. The replaced
  database is kept as `pb_data/litestream/before-restore.db`.
- Apps with different retention get separate Litestream stores, since Litestream applies retention per store.
- Cost per serving app: about 176 KiB of memory, 4 goroutines, 5 file descriptors. Binary: about +4 MiB.

# Remotes

Version 0.1.0 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

> Walkthrough for app owners: [Remote CLI](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/remote). This page is the technical reference.

Named remotes for the `pocketone` command: the apps a project deploys to, each signed in to once. Give an app a name
like `prod`, log in, and commands such as `pocketone deploy prod` know where to go and who you are.

```bash
pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com
pocketone login prod
pocketone deploy prod          # Deploy
```

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Remotes is built into `pocketone` and **on**: the `remote`, `login`, `logout` and `link` commands are always there, and
every app provides [remote/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts): whoami at `GET /api/_c/remote/v1` (so other machines can sign
in to it), status, restart and logs. There's nothing to install: it's in the [standard set](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard).

In your own Go build, use the standard set, or register it through its contracts yourself:

```go
app := pocketbase.New()
extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{remotes.New(remotes.Config{})}, nil, nil) // remote/v1; on *pocketbase.PocketBase also the commands
app.Start()
```

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/remotes`. Add [Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) for API tokens and
[the OAuth server](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens/oauth) for browser login.

## Configure

There is no `pocketone.yaml` section, flag or settings screen. Remotes keeps two files and reads a few environment
variables.

### The project's remotes

`.pocketbase/remotes.json` in the project holds names and URLs only, so commit it:

```json
{"default": "prod", "remotes": {"prod": {"url": "https://myapp.example.com"}}}
```

Commands find it by walking up from the current folder. It isn't a `pb_*` name, since `pb_*` folders are deployed.

### Saved logins

Logins are saved per user, keyed by URL, in `~/.config/pocketone/credentials.json` (mode 0600). Set
`P1_CONFIG_DIR` to use another folder; with `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` set, it's `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pocketone/`.

### Environment variables

| Variable | What it does |
|---|---|
| `P1_TOKEN` | A token that overrides the saved login, for CI or for one command (`P1_TOKEN=... pocketone deploy staging`). |
| `P1_CONFIG_DIR` | Where saved logins are kept. |

A token in the environment wins over a saved login. Every PocketOne variable starts with `P1_`, in every build (the
`pockethost` binary reads `P1_TOKEN` too). The `pocketone` folder comes from the command's name, so a build shipped
under another name keeps its logins apart (`~/.config/pockethost`).

## Use

### Manage remotes

```bash
pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com --default
pocketone remote list            # names, URLs and who you're logged in as; * marks the default
pocketone remote default prod
pocketone remote rm staging      # the saved login stays; see logout
pocketone remote whoami prod     # who you are there, your token's scopes, and what the app offers
```

A URL without a scheme gets `https://`. The first remote you add becomes the default. A command that names no remote
uses the default, else the only remote, else the one called `default`. Any command also takes a URL in place of a
name: `pocketone deploy https://other.example.com`.

### Log in

```bash
pocketone login prod
```

`link` signs in the same way when it adds a remote. Either way you sign in as one of the app's superusers (or its
users, on the browser pages). `login` tries, in order:

1. **The browser**, when the remote runs [the OAuth server](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens/oauth). Your browser opens, you sign in
   and approve, and the command finishes. Over SSH or without a display it shows a code to enter on another device
   instead; `--device` asks for that, and `--no-browser` prints the URL without opening it.
2. **A superuser's email and password**, when the remote has no OAuth server (stock PocketBase, such as an app a
   multisite host runs in Docker). The password isn't shown as you type. The login lasts 30 days; changing that
   superuser's password ends it. A superuser with multi-factor authentication on signs in with a token instead.
3. **A pasted token** (`pbt_...`, a PocketHost token, or a PocketBase auth token): paste it at the email prompt, or
   pass `--token <token>` or `--token-stdin`.

A browser login keeps a refresh token and renews itself when it's within a day of expiring.

You'll see `Logged in to https://myapp.example.com as admin@example.com (oauth).`

### Link in one step

```bash
pocketone link https://myapp.example.com
pocketone link https://myapp.pockethost.io ph_pat_...
```

`link` adds the remote (named `default`, or `--name`), makes it the default if there's none yet, and logs in. It takes
the same login flags.

### Log out

```bash
pocketone logout prod
```

Forgets the saved login. A browser login is also revoked on the remote (its refresh token); a pasted token stays
valid until you revoke it in the dashboard. If the remote can't be reached, it tells you to revoke it in the dashboard.

## Commands and APIs

Generated from the `pocketone` binary and the contracts this extension provides.

### Commands

What it adds to the `pocketone` binary ([CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli)):

| Command | |
|---|---|
| [`pocketone link <url> [token]`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-link) | Adds a remote (default name "default") and signs in to it |
| [`pocketone login [remote]`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-login) | Signs in to a remote and saves the login |
| [`pocketone logout [remote]`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-logout) | Forgets the saved login (and revokes it, for a browser login) |
| [`pocketone remote add <name> <url>`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-remote-add) | Adds or replaces a remote |
| [`pocketone remote default <name>`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-remote-default) | Sets the default remote |
| [`pocketone remote list`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-remote-list) | Lists remotes and whether you're logged in |
| [`pocketone remote rm <name>`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-remote-rm) | Removes a remote (its saved login stays; see logout) |
| [`pocketone remote whoami [remote]`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-remote-whoami) | Shows who you are on a remote and what it offers |

### [remote/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1)

| Operation | CLI | REST | MCP |
|---|---|---|---|
| [whoami](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1#whoami) | `pocketone remote whoami` | `GET /api/_c/remote/v1` | `remote_whoami` |
| [status](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1#status) | `pocketone remote status` | `GET /api/_c/remote/v1/status` | `remote_status` |
| [restart](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1#restart) | `pocketone remote restart` | `POST /api/_c/remote/v1/restart` | `remote_restart` |
| [logs](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1#logs) | `pocketone remote logs --n <n>` | `GET /api/_c/remote/v1/logs` | `remote_logs` |

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) | `deploy`, `dev` and `pull` resolve their remote and login through Remotes and find deploy/v1 in whoami's contracts; `restart` and `logs` use remote/v1. |
| [OAuth](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens/oauth) (in Tokens) | Provides oauth/v1, so whoami lists it; `login` then signs in through the browser (loopback redirect on 127.0.0.1 with PKCE) or a device code. |
| [Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) | Provides the API tokens `login` takes when pasted. Whoami reports a token's id and scopes. |

### remote/v1

Remote control of an app, at `/api/_c/remote/v1`:

| Operation | Endpoint | Token scope |
|---|---|---|
| whoami | `GET /api/_c/remote/v1` | none needed (any token may ask who it is) |
| status | `GET /api/_c/remote/v1/status` | `remote:read` |
| restart | `POST /api/_c/remote/v1/restart` | `remote` |
| logs | `GET /api/_c/remote/v1/logs?n=100` (server-sent events) | `remote:read` |

Whoami says who the request's credential is and what the app offers, so clients can discover it:

```json
{"auth": {"collection": "_superusers", "id": "…", "email": "admin@example.com"}, "via": "token",
 "tokenId": "…", "scopes": ["deploy", "remote"], "contracts": ["deploy/v1", "oauth/v1", "remote/v1", "api-tokens/v1"],
 "extensions": ["tokens", "remotes", "deploy"],
 "app": {"name": "Acme", "url": "https://myapp.example.com"}}
```

`via` is `token` for an API token, `jwt` for a PocketBase auth token, and empty with no credential (`auth` is then
`null`, and `extensions` is left out). `contracts` are the contract APIs the app offers, each at `/api/_c/<id>/`:
everything a client can use (oauth/v1's metadata is at `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`). Restart answers at once and restarts just after (on a multisite host,
only that instance).

### Building on Remotes

- **remote/v1 client.** `remotev1.NewClient(url, token, httpClient)` (ext/contracts/remote/v1) calls whoami, status,
  restart and logs.
- **Go client.** The CLI client lives with the contract, in
  [`remoteclient`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/contracts/remote/v1/remoteclient) (ext/contracts/remote/v1/remoteclient), so other extensions'
  commands use it without importing this one. `remoteclient.Open(dir, name)` resolves a remote and its credential
  (environment first, then the saved login, renewing a browser login when due) and returns a `*remoteclient.Client`:
  base URL, bearer token, an HTTP client with short connect timeouts, and `JSON`, `NewRequest`, `Do` and `Whoami`.
  It also holds the linked project (`LoadProject`), saved logins (`LoadCredentials`) and the sign-ins
  (`LoginWithToken`, `OAuthLogin`, `PasswordLogin`). Deploy's commands build on it.
- **Commands.** `remotes.Commands()` returns the `remote`, `login`, `logout` and `link` commands, for a binary that
  isn't a `*pocketbase.PocketBase`. The rest of `remote` is generated: every operation of every contract the binary
  links is a `remote ...` command ([cli.commands/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/cli.commands/v1)), such as `remote status`,
  `remote restart`, `remote restore to --at -2h`.
- **Login.** `remotes.BrowserLogin` is the sign-in `login` tries first (`remoteclient.OAuthLogin`; tests replace it).

## Example

[`example/main.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/remotes/example/main.go) is an app with remotes and API tokens. Run two copies and add one as a remote of the other; its comment has the commands.

```go
// Command example is a PocketOne app with remotes and API tokens: run two copies, add one as a remote of the other's
// project and sign in.
//
//	go run ./example serve --http=127.0.0.1:8090                # the "remote"
//	go run ./example remote add local http://127.0.0.1:8090    # in a project folder
//	go run ./example login local                               # browser sign-in: admin@example.com / password
//	go run ./example remote whoami
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/api-tokens"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/devusers"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/extkit"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/remotes"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"

	// registered through their contracts (the standard set does this for you): remotes provides remote/v1 (whoami at
	// /api/_c/remote/v1, status, restart, logs) and the remote/login/logout/link commands; tokens adds API tokens
	// and the OAuth server login signs in through
	if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{}), remotes.New(remotes.Config{})}, nil, nil); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

# S3 Fallback

Version 0.0.2 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

A default bucket for instances that have no S3 of their own. You name your S3-compatible backends once, then mount
each kind of file on one: record uploads, backup zips, PITR history, or any extension's own kind. Every instance gets
its own folder in the bucket and can't reach anything outside it. The credentials never reach the instance.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

S3 Fallback is in the [standard set](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard), so it's built into `pocketone` and every isolate on a
[multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) host has it (Docker containers run stock images). It does nothing until the
`storage` section below mounts a backend. Its main use is a multisite host, where each instance gets its own folder in
one bucket; a single app with mounts keeps its files at the backend's root.

In your own Go build, reconfigure the member instead of adding it again:

```go
set := standard.New()
set.S3Fallback = s3fallback.New(s3fallback.Config{Backends: backends, Mounts: mounts})
```

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/s3-fallback`.

## Configure

The `storage` section of `pocketone.yaml` is read on first use. Fields set in Go win.

```yaml
storage:
  backends:                        # named S3-compatible destinations
    r2-eu:   { endpoint: https://<account>.eu.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, bucket: pocketbase-eu, region: auto, access_key: $R2_KEY, secret: $R2_SECRET }
    b2-cold: { endpoint: ..., bucket: ph-backups, region: ..., access_key: ..., secret: ... }
  mounts:                          # filesystem kind -> backend
    storage:    r2-eu              # record uploads
    backups:    b2-cold            # backup zips
    litestream: r2-eu              # PITR history (ext/pitr)
  # enabled: false                 # off for every instance
```

Each backend also takes `prefix` (prepended to every key, so several deployments can share a bucket) and
`force_path_style` (for MinIO and similar servers). With no mounts the extension does nothing and files stay on local
disk, as in PocketBase.

Each instance can turn it off in its own settings, from `instances.yaml` or a mothership. Only `enabled` is read per
instance; backends and mounts are the operator's:

```yaml
instances:
  - id: blog
    extensions: { storage: { enabled: false } }
```

The old shape (`bucket:` with `uploads:` / `backups:`) still works, with a warning: it becomes a backend named
`default`, mounted for uploads and backups.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `storage:`

A default S3 bucket for apps without their own (on a multisite host, one folder per instance): backends and mounts for uploads, backups, PITR history.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | bool |  | On for every instance unless false; an instance's extensions.storage.enabled overrides it. |
| `backends` | map of object |  | Named S3-compatible destinations: endpoint, bucket, region, access_key, secret, prefix, force_path_style. |
| `mounts` | map of string |  | Filesystem kind (storage, backups, litestream, ...) to backend name. |
| `bucket.endpoint` | string |  | S3 endpoint URL. |
| `bucket.bucket` | string |  | Bucket name. |
| `bucket.region` | string |  | Bucket region (auto for R2). |
| `bucket.access_key` | string |  | Access key id. |
| `bucket.secret` | string |  | Secret key; use a $VAR from the .env. |
| `bucket.prefix` | string |  | Prepended to every key, to share a bucket. |
| `bucket.force_path_style` | bool |  | Path-style addressing, for MinIO and similar servers. |
| `uploads` | bool |  | Deprecated: with bucket, false keeps uploads off it. |
| `backups` | bool |  | Deprecated: with bucket, false keeps backups off it. |

## Use

There's nothing to do day to day. To an instance nothing is configured: Settings show S3 off, and uploads, thumbs,
`$app.newFilesystem()` and the Backups screen work as before. Files land in the bucket under
`<prefix>instances/<id>/<kind>/`. Downloads stream through the server, or redirect to the bucket with
[S3 Redirect](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3redirect).

When an instance turns on its own S3 (Settings → Files storage, or Settings → Backups), PocketBase's normal code takes
over with the instance's credentials. Files already in the default bucket stay there, as PocketBase's own S3 switch
doesn't move files either.

It applies to instances created with the extension on. Files already on an instance's local disk are not read or moved.

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) | Every instance the set reaches gets the extension. An isolate (Pocker) gets the root `instances/<id>/`. |
| [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr) | Mount `litestream` and every instance without its own bucket keeps its history there. An instance's own PITR bucket still wins. |
| [S3 Redirect](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3redirect) | Downloads become signed redirects to the bucket. Nothing to wire: the fenced filesystem signs with its prefix, so S3 Redirect treats it like any S3 mount. |

### Building on S3 Fallback

- **Your own kind.** Any kind an extension asks for through PocketBase's `OnFilesystemCreate` is served when it's mounted.
  PITR's `litestream` works this way. Uploads and backups step aside when the app turned on its own S3; for other
  kinds, the extension asking checks its own app setting first.
- **Go API.** `Bind(app, root)` serves an app's filesystems from the mounts under `root` (`""` for an app that has
  the process to itself, `instances/<id>/` for an isolate, as under Pocker). `FS(root, kind)` returns the same
  fenced filesystem outside a hook; close it when done. `Config()` returns the effective configuration.

## Example

There's no `example/main.go` yet. [`modes_test.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/s3-fallback/modes_test.go) shows it on the `pocketone` binary, as a single app
and on a multisite host; [`storage_test.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/s3-fallback/storage_test.go) and [`mounts_test.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/s3-fallback/mounts_test.go) show it in Go.

## How it works

- PocketBase asks `OnFilesystemCreate` before it creates a filesystem. For a mounted kind, the extension answers with the
  backend, fenced to `<backend prefix><root><kind>/`. An instance can't list, read, write or delete anything outside
  it.
- The fence is a driver that adds the prefix to every key and strips it from listings. Signed download URLs are made
  with the backend's own credentials.

### Status

Works and is tested, in-process and on the `pocketone` binary as a single app and on a multisite host, against an in-memory bucket that checks signed downloads ([`modes_test.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/s3-fallback/modes_test.go)); not yet deployed.

MIT
