Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3redirect

# S3 Redirect

Version 0.0.2 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

File downloads as short-lived signed redirects to your bucket, after PocketBase's own access check.

When an app keeps its files in S3 (Settings → Files storage), PocketBase normally downloads each file from the bucket
and streams it to the browser. With S3 Redirect, `/api/files/...` answers **302** with a presigned GET URL instead,
and the browser fetches the file straight from the bucket. The app's bandwidth, memory and connections stay free.
With Cloudflare R2 the downloads cost no egress either.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

S3 Redirect is built into `pocketone` and **on by default**. It only acts when S3 file storage is on: turn on S3 in
Settings → Files storage and downloads redirect. With files on local disk, nothing changes.

To stream files through the app as before:

```bash
pocketone serve --s3Redirect=false
```

In your own Go build, register it before the app starts:

```go
import "pocketone.dev/ext/s3redirect"

app := pocketbase.New()
s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 * time.Minute})
app.Start()
```

Then turn on S3 in Settings → Files storage.

## Configure

Set it in `pocketone.yaml`:

```yaml
s3redirect:
  enabled: true   # false streams files through the app
  ttl: 5m         # how long each signed URL is valid
```

Or with flags, which win over the file:

| Flag | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--s3Redirect` | `true` | Redirect downloads when S3 file storage is on. `--s3Redirect=false` streams them. |
| `--s3RedirectTTL` | `5m` | How long each signed URL stays valid (at most 7 days). |

Keep the TTL short: anyone holding a URL can fetch the file until it expires, protected files included.

The bucket itself is PocketBase's own S3 setting, in **Settings → Files storage**. There are no other settings
screens.

**Bucket CORS.** A redirect followed by `fetch()` or `<img crossorigin>` from your site needs a CORS rule on the
bucket allowing `GET` from your origin. Plain `<img>`, `<video>` and links need nothing.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `s3redirect:`

Signed S3 redirects for file downloads: enabled, URL lifetime. The --s3Redirect and --s3RedirectTTL flags win.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | bool |  | On unless false (it only acts when S3 file storage is on). Flag: --s3Redirect. |
| `ttl` | duration |  | How long each signed URL stays valid. Default 5m, max 7 days. Flag: --s3RedirectTTL. |

## Use

Once S3 is on, there's nothing to click. File URLs stay the same; they answer with a redirect:

- **Access checks don't change.** PocketBase still finds the record, checks protected-file tokens and the view rule,
  and creates thumbnails on first request. The redirect happens only after all of that.
- **The file token stays private.** It never goes into the bucket URL, and the redirect sends
  `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`.
- **Same headers as PocketBase:** inline or attachment (`?download=1`), the filename, and forced content types (SVG,
  CSS, JS) are signed into the URL as S3 `response-*` overrides. Range requests work, because S3 serves them.
- **Caching:** the browser may reuse the redirect for 80% of the TTL (`Cache-Control: private`, never shared
  caches); the file itself gets PocketBase's usual 30-day `Cache-Control`.
- **Falls back to streaming** when S3 is off, the extension is turned off, or signing fails. A failed signature logs a
  warning, `s3redirect: signing failed, streaming instead`.
- Only `GET` and `HEAD` requests are redirected.

**Inline vs attachment:** PocketBase decides this from the stored content type; S3 Redirect goes by the file
extension (it doesn't ask the bucket, so a redirect costs no extra round trip). They agree for every file PocketBase
names.

### Try it

```
cd example && go run . serve
```

The example runs one app with its own in-process bucket, nothing to set up. It:

- starts an S3-compatible bucket on `127.0.0.1:9199` ([gofakes3](https://github.com/johannesboyne/gofakes3),
  objects kept in `pb_data/demo-s3.bolt`), and points the app's Files storage at it;
- seeds a `demo_files` record with an image (thumbs `100x100`) and a protected text file, uploaded through PocketBase;
- prints the URLs to open. Each answers `302` to the bucket.

The bucket only serves presigned GETs whose signature, re-computed with the **AWS SDK's own SigV4 signer**, matches
and hasn't expired, and logs each one (`demo bucket: presigned GET ..., signature valid`). Unsigned or edited URLs get
`403`. So a working download proves the signatures are AWS-compatible, not just accepted by a lenient fake.

`S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0` skips the demo bucket (use your own Files storage settings); `S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR` moves it.
The example is its own Go module, so its demo dependencies (gofakes3, the AWS SDK signer) never reach the extension's
`go.mod`.

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) | It's a standard member, so every instance that runs PocketOne has it. With Pocker, the `s3redirect` section sets the defaults and each instance can override `enabled` and `ttl` (below). |
| [S3 Fallback](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3-fallback) | Apps without their own S3 settings keep files in its bucket (for isolates, as under Pocker, fenced to `instances/<id>/storage/`). Its driver signs, so those downloads redirect too. |

### Per-instance settings (Pocker)

```go
set.S3Redirect = s3redirect.New(s3redirect.Config{}) // a standard member: reconfigure it on the host's set
```

```yaml
s3redirect:            # server defaults
  enabled: true        # on unless false
  ttl: 5m

instances:
  - id: abc
    extensions:
      s3redirect: { enabled: false }   # per instance: enabled, ttl
```

It's an [extkit](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/extkit/extkit.go) extension, so the same value works on a standalone app and on every instance
of a multisite host; it doesn't link a runtime.

### Building on S3 Redirect

- **Supply your own bucket.** S3 Redirect signs for whatever filesystem PocketBase serves the download from: the
  app's own S3 settings, or one an extension supplies through `OnFilesystemCreate`. Implement `s3redirect.Signer`
  (`SignedURL(key, ttl, now, overrides)`) on your filesystem driver and its downloads redirect. Nothing else needs
  wiring; a filesystem that can't sign (local disk) streams as usual.
- **Your own download handlers run first.** The extension binds `OnFileDownloadRequest` last (priority 1000, id
  `s3redirect.HookID`, `__ext_s3redirect__`), so your Go or JS handlers can still change the served file or answer
  themselves without calling `e.Next()`. Unbind the id to turn it off for one app.

## Example

[`example/main.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/s3redirect/example/main.go) starts its own in-process S3 bucket, points the app's file storage at it and seeds a record, so every download redirect works with nothing to set up. Run `go run . serve` in `example/` and open the URLs it prints.

```go
// Command example runs one PocketOne app whose file downloads redirect to an S3 bucket, with nothing to set up:
// it starts its own S3-compatible bucket in-process (gofakes3, stored in pb_data/demo-s3.bolt), points the app's
// Files storage at it, and seeds a "demo_files" record with an image and a protected document.
//
//	go run . serve
//
// Open the URLs it prints. Each answers 302 with a signed URL; the bucket logs every fetch and only serves it if the
// signature is valid and unexpired, checked independently with the AWS SDK's SigV4 signer.
//
// Set S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0 to skip the demo bucket and use whatever Files storage you configure in the dashboard.
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"log"
	"os"
	"time"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/devusers"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/s3redirect"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"

	s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 * time.Minute})

	if os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO") != "0" {
		addr := os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR")
		if addr == "" {
			addr = "127.0.0.1:9199"
		}
		registerDemo(app, addr)
	}

	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## How it works

- Go module `pocketone.dev/ext/s3redirect`, no dependencies beyond PocketOne.
- The redirect is an `OnFileDownloadRequest` handler; the hook already exists upstream, so there's no core change.
- Signing is SigV4 query-string auth in [`sigv4`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/s3redirect/sigv4/sigv4.go), checked against AWS's documented example. It needs
  no change to PocketBase's S3 client. The TTL is clamped to between 1 second and 7 days.

# Settings

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

One API for the settings an app's admins change for its extensions: PITR's S3 bucket, Bulk Mail's sending settings,
and any extension that registers a section. The dashboard screens, the CLI and agents all use it.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Settings is built into `pocketone` and **on by default**; there's nothing to install. In your own Go build:

```go
extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{settings.New(), pitr.New(pitr.Config{})}, nil, nil)
```

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/settings`.

## Configure

There's nothing to configure.

## Use

It provides the [settings/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/settings/v1) contract (superusers only):

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" https://app.example.com/api/_c/settings/v1                      # which extensions
curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" "https://app.example.com/api/_c/settings/v1/get?extension=pitr" # one extension's
```

Agents get the same through MCP (`settings_list`, `settings_get`, `settings_save`, `settings_test`).

## Commands and APIs

Generated from the `pocketone` binary and the contracts this extension provides.

### [settings/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/settings/v1)

| Operation | CLI | REST | MCP |
|---|---|---|---|
| [list](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/settings/v1#list) | `pocketone remote settings list` | `GET /api/_c/settings/v1` | `settings_list` |
| [get](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/settings/v1#get) | `pocketone remote settings get --extension <value>` | `GET /api/_c/settings/v1/get` | `settings_get` |
| [save](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/settings/v1#save) | `pocketone remote settings save --extension <value> --values <json>` | `POST /api/_c/settings/v1/save` | `settings_save` |
| [test](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/settings/v1#test) | `pocketone remote settings test --extension <value> --values <json>` | `POST /api/_c/settings/v1/test` | `settings_test` |

## Integrations

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr) | Its S3 destination is a section. |
| [Bulk Mail](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bulkmail) | Its sending settings are a section. |
| [Contracts](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts) | settings/v1 is the contract; a host could provide it instead. |

## Example

```go
// Command example is a PocketBase app with settings/v1: the standard extensions' admin settings (here pitr's) behind
// one API. `curl -H "Authorization: <superuser token>" http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/_c/settings/v1` lists them.
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/devusers"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/extkit"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/pitr"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/settings"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"
	if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{settings.New(), pitr.New(pitr.Config{})}, nil, nil); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

# Templates

Version 0.0.2 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

Some extensions serve pages of their own, such as the OAuth sign-in, consent and MFA screens the CLI and MCP agents
sign in through. Templates lets you restyle them: eject an extension's templates into your app's `pb_templates`
folder and edit them. Any file you keep there replaces the built-in one; delete it to go back.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Templates is built into `pocketone` and on by default; there's nothing to install. In your own Go build:

```go
extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{templates.New(templates.Config{})}, nil, nil)
```

## Configure

Nothing to configure. Your copies live in `pb_templates/` next to `pb_data` (in a Go build, `templates.Config.Dir`
moves it). `pocketone deploy` and `pocketone dev` sync it like `pb_hooks`.

## Use

See the template sets your app's extensions offer, and what you've changed:

```sh
pocketone template list
```

Eject one to edit it (leave out the name to eject every set):

```sh
pocketone template eject oauth
```

That copies every file of the set into `pb_templates/oauth/`. Edit any of them; the next request uses your copy, no
restart. Keep only the files you change if you like: the rest come from the built-in set.

Ejecting again is safe: files you haven't changed are left alone and missing ones are written back. Files you did
change are listed and only overwritten if you answer yes; without a terminal to ask in it refuses, and `--force`
overwrites them without asking.

The files are Go templates (`html/template`): `{{.AppName}}` prints a value (HTML-escaped), `{{if .Error}}…{{end}}`
and `{{range .Providers}}…{{end}}` branch and loop, and `{{template "head" .}}` includes another file of the set
(`head.tpl`). A broken file shows its error instead of the page, so you see what to fix.

## Commands and APIs

Generated from the `pocketone` binary and the contracts this extension provides.

### Commands

What it adds to the `pocketone` binary ([CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli)):

| Command | |
|---|---|
| [`pocketone template eject [set]`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-template-eject) | Copies a template set (every set without a name) into pb\_templates/&lt;set&gt;/ for you to edit |
| [`pocketone template list`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-template-list) | Lists the template sets extensions offer, and what you've changed in pb\_templates |

## Integrations

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens) | Its OAuth pages are the `oauth` set: sign-in, MFA, one-time code, consent, device code, done and error, with a shared `head` and `foot`. Without Templates it serves them built in. |

### Building on Templates

An extension adds its own set through the [templates/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/templates/v1) contract: embed a
folder of `.tpl` files, add it under a name in `Register` (`templatesv1.Add(app, "mine", files)`), and render a page
with `templatesv1.Contract.Of(app)`'s `Render`. Declare templates/v1 in `WorksWith` and render the embedded set
yourself (`templatesv1.Parse`, `templatesv1.Write`) when nothing provides it.

## Example

A PocketBase app with one inline set, `hello`, served at `/hello`. Run `go run . template eject hello`, edit
`pb_templates/hello/page.tpl`, and reload.

```go
// Command example is a PocketBase app with templates/v1 and one template set, "hello", served at /hello. Run
// `go run . template eject hello`, edit pb_templates/hello/page.tpl, and reload /hello.
package main

import (
	"log"
	"net/http"
	"testing/fstest"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core"

	templatesv1 "pocketone.dev/ext/contracts/templates/v1"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/extkit"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/templates"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{templates.New(templates.Config{})}, nil, nil); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	// an extension would go:embed its set; this one is inline
	templatesv1.Add(app, "hello", fstest.MapFS{"page.tpl": {Data: []byte(`<h1>Hello, {{.}}!</h1>`)}})
	app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se *core.ServeEvent) error {
		se.Router.GET("/hello", func(e *core.RequestEvent) error {
			return templatesv1.Contract.Must(app).Render(e, "hello", "page", http.StatusOK, "world")
		})
		return se.Next()
	})
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## License

MIT

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/uicache

# UI Cache

Version 0.0.2 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

PocketBase tells browsers and CDNs to keep every dashboard file for 14 days, including files whose name never changes.
Behind a CDN such as Cloudflare, that means a new or updated dashboard screen from an extension, or the dashboard's own
libraries after an upgrade, can take up to two weeks to show up. UI Cache sends headers that let those changes through
within minutes, and keeps the long cache for the files that can safely have it.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

UI Cache is built into `pocketone` and **on by default**; there's nothing to install. In your own Go build:

```go
extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{uicache.New()}, nil, nil)
```

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/uicache`.

## Configure

There's nothing to configure. An app turns it off with `uicache: {enabled: false}` in its pocketone.yaml, which brings
back PocketBase's own headers.

## Use

Nothing to do day to day. Check the headers with curl:

```bash
curl -sI https://app.example.com/_/extensions.js | grep -i cache-control
```

| Dashboard path | Cache-Control | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `/_/extensions.js`, `/_/index.html` | `no-cache` | Checked on every load: `extensions.js` is every extension's screen joined into one file, rebuilt when any of them changes. |
| `/_/assets/<name>-<hash>.js` (and `.css`) | PocketBase's own (14 days) | The name changes with the content, so a new build is a new URL. |
| Everything else (`libs/`, `fonts/`, `images/`, `/_/extensions/<name>/...`) | `public, max-age=300` | Five minutes: fresh soon after an update, still cached while you browse. |

`/_/` itself (the dashboard page) is sent without a cache lifetime by PocketBase and left alone. In dev mode
(`--dev`) UI Cache does nothing, as PocketBase sends no cache headers there.

After turning it on for an app that sits behind a CDN, purge `/_/*` there once: copies cached under the old 14-day
header stay until they expire.

## Integrations

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) | Every instance gets it with the standard set; turn it off for one with `extensions.uicache.enabled: false`. |
| Extensions with dashboard screens ([Tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/api-tokens), [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr), [Bulk Mail](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bulkmail), ...) | Their `main.js` reaches the browser through `/_/extensions.js`, so an updated screen shows on the next load. |

An extension that serves other files from `/_/extensions/<name>/` gets the five-minute policy. To cache one longer,
put a content hash in its name and set its own `Cache-Control` in a middleware that runs before UI Cache's
(`uicache.MiddlewareID`); a header that's already set is kept.

## Example

A PocketBase app with UI Cache, to see the headers locally.

```go
// Command example is a PocketBase app whose dashboard sends cache headers that let changes through: run
// `go run . serve`, then `curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8090/_/extensions.js | grep -i cache-control` shows `no-cache`.
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/devusers"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/extkit"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/uicache"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"
	if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{uicache.New()}, nil, nil); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## How it works

PocketBase's dashboard middleware (in `apis/serve.go` and `apis/extensions.go`) sets its 14-day `Cache-Control` only
when the response has none yet. UI Cache binds a router middleware in `OnServe`, which runs before route and group
middleware, and sets the header first. No PocketBase code changes.

# Upgrade

Version 0.0.4 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

`pocketone upgrade` replaces the `pocketone` executable with the latest PocketOne release and keeps the old one beside
it as `<name>-<version>` (for example `pocketone-0.0.3`), so a project can keep running the engine it was built with.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Upgrade is built into `pocketone`: the `upgrade` command is always there. There's nothing to turn on.

In your own Go build, register the command before the app starts:

```go
import "pocketone.dev/ext/upgrade"

app := pocketbase.New()
upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{})
app.Start()
```

## Configure

Nothing to configure: no `pocketone.yaml` section, no environment variables, no settings screens. The command has one
flag:

| Flag | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--backup` | `true` | Back up `pb_data` after upgrading, if the current folder has one. `--backup=false` skips it. |
| `--yes`, `-y` | `false` | Move from a stable release to a prerelease without asking. |

## Use

Run it from your project folder:

```bash
pocketone upgrade
```

It:

1. Picks the newest release on GitHub that fits what you're running, and stops if you already have it:
   - The newest release is offered, prereleases included: `0.1.0-alpha.2` goes to `0.1.0-alpha.3` or `0.1.0`,
     whichever is newest.
   - **From one prerelease to the next** (or to a stable release), it just upgrades.
   - **From a stable release to a prerelease** (`0.1.0` to `0.1.1-alpha.1`), it asks first. No means the newest stable
     release instead, if there's a newer one. `--yes` answers yes for you; with no answer (no terminal), it's no.
   - A local build upgrades to the newest release without asking.
2. Downloads the archive for your platform and checks it against the release's `checksums.txt` before touching
   anything.
3. Renames the current executable to `<name>-<version>` and puts the new one in its place. **Old copies are never
   deleted**, so `pocketone-0.0.3 serve` still runs a project on that version. A local build with no release version
   is kept as `<name>.old`, which the next such upgrade replaces.
4. Backs up `pb_data`, when the current folder has one, as `@upgrade_<tag>.zip` in PocketBase's backups.
5. Prints the new version, where the old one was kept, and the release notes.

Two cases where it does something else:

- **Installed with Homebrew:** it prints `brew update && brew upgrade pocketone` instead (`brew update` refreshes the tap, which Homebrew otherwise does only once a day). Homebrew keeps the previous version until
  `brew cleanup`.
- **In a Docker container:** it refuses; upgrade the image instead.

It needs write access to the folder the executable is in.

A kept executable doesn't undo migrations: once a newer version has served a `pb_data`, an older one may not open it.
The backup is the way back for that.

## Commands and APIs

Generated from the `pocketone` binary and the contracts this extension provides.

### Commands

What it adds to the `pocketone` binary ([CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli)):

| Command | |
|---|---|
| [`pocketone upgrade`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-upgrade) | Upgrades this executable to the latest release, keeping the old one as &lt;name&gt;-&lt;version&gt; |

## Integrations

Nothing integrates with it yet. Other tools can reuse its release code:

- **Custom builds** that publish their own releases set `Owner`, `Repo`, `ArchivePrefix` and `ArchiveExecutable` in
  `upgrade.Config`. Release archives are named `<prefix>_<version>_<os>_<arch>.zip`, with a goreleaser-style
  `checksums.txt` in the same release.
- **Go API.** `Config.FetchReleases(ctx)` lists the published releases, prereleases included, and
  `upgrade.UpgradeFor(current, releases, stableOnly)` picks the one to upgrade to and `upgrade.NeedsConfirm(current, release)`
  says whether to ask first. `Config.FetchRelease(ctx, tag)`
  fetches GitHub's latest stable release (tag `""`) or a given one;
  `Config.DownloadArchive(ctx, release, goos, goarch, dir)` downloads and checks a platform's archive.
  `upgrade.KeptName(exe, version)` is the name an old executable is kept under.

## Example

[`example/main.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/upgrade/example/main.go) is a PocketOne app with just the `upgrade` command. Try it with `go run ./example upgrade`.

```go
// Command example is a PocketOne app with just the upgrade command. A local build has no release version, so it is
// kept as "example.old"; release builds are kept as "<name>-<version>".
//
//	go run ./example upgrade
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/upgrade"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{})
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

# Vacuum

Version 0.0.2 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

SQLite doesn't give space back to the disk when records are deleted; the file stays as big as it ever was. Vacuum
compacts your app's databases on a schedule (SQLite's `VACUUM`), so the space comes back. It only compacts a database
when enough of it is free space (10%, or 64 MB), so a busy, tidy app is left alone.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Vacuum is built into `pocketone`. In your own Go build:

```go
extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{vacuum.New()}, nil, nil)
```

## Configure

The app's admins turn it on and set how often in the dashboard, in the **Vacuum** section at the bottom of
**Settings → Backups** (a settings/v1 section, so the CLI and agents can change it too). `pocketone.yaml` sets the
defaults until they do:

```yaml
vacuum:
  enabled: true
  every: 168h   # weekly; at least 1h
```

Without either, it's off.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `vacuum:`

Defaults for compacting the app's SQLite databases (VACUUM): on or off, and how often. The app's admins change them in Settings.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | bool |  | Compact the databases on a schedule, until the app's admins change it in Settings. |
| `every` | string | `168h` | How often, e.g. 24h or 168h (weekly). |

## Use

Once on, every `every` while the app serves, Vacuum checks `data.db` and `auxiliary.db` and compacts the ones with
enough free space (PocketBase's own online `VACUUM`; writes wait while it runs). `VACUUM` needs free disk space about the
size of the database it compacts.

The same section shows its status: whether it's on, how often, the next run, and the last run's bytes given back and
databases skipped. It's [vacuum/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/vacuum/v1), also on the command line:

```sh
pocketone remote vacuum status
```

## Commands and APIs

Generated from the `pocketone` binary and the contracts this extension provides.

### [vacuum/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/vacuum/v1)

| Operation | CLI | REST | MCP |
|---|---|---|---|
| [status](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/vacuum/v1#status) | `pocketone remote vacuum status` | `GET /api/_c/vacuum/v1` | `vacuum_status` |

## Integrations

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Settings](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/settings) | Its on/off and schedule are a settings/v1 section, in the dashboard, the CLI and for agents. |
| [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) | A host may compact its instances itself: when it provides [vacuum/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/vacuum/v1) for them, Vacuum steps aside in each instance: the Vacuum section shows the host's status, read-only, with no setting. |
| [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr) | A compacted database is a new file to Litestream, so the next replication starts a fresh generation. |

### Building on Vacuum

`vacuum.App(app)` compacts a running app now and returns what it did. `LoadSettings`/`SaveSettings` read and change the
app's settings.

## Example

A PocketBase app that compacts its databases once when it starts serving.

```go
// Command example is a PocketBase app that compacts its databases once when it starts serving (vacuum.App), the work
// the extension does on its admins' schedule. Run `go run . serve` and watch the log for "vacuum: once".
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core"

	"pocketone.dev/ext/extkit"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/vacuum"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{vacuum.New()}, nil, nil); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(e *core.ServeEvent) error {
		go func() {
			run := vacuum.App(app)
			app.Logger().Info("vacuum: once", "saved_bytes", run.Saved, "skipped", run.Skipped, "error", run.Error)
		}()
		return e.Next()
	})
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

# WASM

Version 0.0.3 · Owners: [@octavonu](https://github.com/octavonu)

**Bring your own WASM (BYOW).** Call code written in Go, Rust, Zig or anything else that builds for WASI from
your page code, when you need a library from another language or more speed than JS gives you. A module is a small program
compiled to WebAssembly that your code calls like a function. Input in, output out, or an error. It can't reach the database, files, network, environment or other
processes; your code gives it what it needs and decides what to do with the result.

One call does it:

```ts
const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string; words: number }>("summary", { title: "Hello", body: "one two three" })
// out is { text: "Hello", words: 3 }
```

`"summary"` names the module, `pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm`. The object is its input, sent to it as JSON, and `out` is
the JSON it writes back, parsed. If the module fails, the call rejects with a `WasmError`. Calls are only `async`: the
module runs off the JS engine, so the app keeps serving other requests while it works.

In an API route, the input comes from the request and the output goes into the record it saves:

```ts
// pb_pages/posts.ts
export async function post(ctx: any) {
  const { title, body } = ctx.req.body()
  const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string }>("summary", { title, body })
  const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts"))
  record.load({ title, body, summary: out.text })
  ctx.app.save(record)
  return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id, summary: out.text })
}
```

Use it for what JS does badly or slowly: parsing (EDIFACT, XML, binary formats), crypto, validation, number
crunching, or a library that only exists in Go, Rust or C.

WASM is an extension; the `.pb.wasm` files it runs are modules. Beyond this page: a page for [each language](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages) (C, Go, TinyGo, Rust, Zig, AssemblyScript), [keeping state in JS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/guides/state) between calls, and [recipes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes) built on real libraries (Markdown, HTML sanitizing, thumbnails, QR codes, diffs, CSV).

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

WASM is built into `pocketone`: it's a member of the [standard set](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard), which every app gets,
standalone or an instance on a multisite host, and the set binds `$wasm` into the JS engine ([`ext/jsvm`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm)). Put a
`.pb.wasm` file in `pb_hooks` and call it from your page code.

In your own build, the set already has it. To change its settings, replace the member:

```go
set := standard.New()
set.WASM = wasm.New(wasm.Config{MaxConcurrent: 4})
```

Without the set, register it and bind it yourself:

```go
w := wasm.New(wasm.Config{})

app := pocketbase.New()
extkit.MustRegister(app, w)
jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, w) }})
app.Start()
```

`$wasm` needs PocketOne's JS engine; with PocketBase's own (`--jsvm goja`) extensions bind nothing.

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/wasm`. Modules are `pb_hooks/<name>.pb.wasm`; nothing else
needs setting up.

## Configure

The defaults suit most apps. To change them, pass them to `wasm.New` (`set.WASM = wasm.New(...)` in a standard set):

| Field | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Dir` | `pb_hooks` beside the data dir | The module folder. |
| `MaxCallMemoryMB` | 32 | Memory each call may allocate (its heap, stack and input). Every call has its own, not shared: 8 calls at once may take 8 × 32 MB. A call that needs more crashes alone. |
| `Timeout` | 5s | Time limit for a call's run (compiling comes before it). |
| `MaxConcurrent` | 8 | Calls running at once in the app. More wait, up to `Timeout`, then fail as `busy`. |
| `MaxModulesMB` | 10 | MB of modules running at once: the `.wasm` sizes of the calls running, added up (file sizes, not memory). More wait, as above. It's also the largest module that runs. |
| `MaxPayload` | 4 MB | Largest input or output of a call. |
| `CacheDir` | the app's `pb_cache/wasm` | Where compiled modules are kept between calls and restarts (see How it works). `"off"` compiles every call. Keep it where only the server's process writes: it holds machine code the process runs. |

Its `pocketone.yaml` section has only `enabled`: `wasm: {enabled: false}` turns `$wasm` off on a single app. With Pocker, each instance can override all of these but `CacheDir`, which is the host's (see Integrations).

## Use

### Modules are files

A module is one file in `pb_hooks/`, `pb_hooks/<name>.pb.wasm`, called as `<name>`:

```
pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm
pb_pages/posts.ts
```

It ships with the rest of your code: git, `pocketone deploy`, or SFTP. Like `node script.js`, every call reads the
module's file as it is then. A change in `pb_hooks/` also restarts the app, as for a `.pb.js` (under pocker the new
app takes over once it has started). To turn a module off, remove or rename it. Hidden files and files that don't end
in `.pb.wasm` are ignored, so upload a new version under a hidden name (`.summary.pb.wasm.part`) and rename it over the
old one: no call reads it half written.

A module that can't run (a broken module, a module over `MaxModulesMB`) fails its calls with `not_loaded` and says
why, and `$wasm.modules()` says it too; the other modules run as usual.

### The manifest: `--describe`

A module says what it is itself: run as `<name> --describe` (the function asked for is `--describe`, with nothing on
stdin), it prints its manifest. Answering is optional, and so is each field; a module that exits non-zero or prints
nothing gets the defaults:

```json
{
  "description": "Summarizes a post: its title and first words, and a word count",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "functions": ["run"],
  "language": "Rust",
  "repository": "https://github.com/you/summary",
  "examples": [
    {
      "function": "run",
      "input": {"title": "Hello", "body": "one two three"},
      "output": {"text": "Hello: one two three", "words": 3}
    }
  ]
}
```

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `description` | what it does |
| `version` | the author's version, as you write it (`1.2.0`, `2026-11-15`): up to 32 letters, digits and `.+_-`; only shown |
| `functions` | the functions your code may call (default `["run"]`) |
| `language` | what it's written in, shown when the module doesn't say: a Go module always does, a Rust one unless it's stripped (`strip = true`), a Zig one never |
| `repository` | where its source is: an `http(s)` URL (no `javascript:`, no credentials), at most 256 characters |
| `examples` | up to 16 calls to try it with: `function` (default `run`), `input` (a JSON string is the module's stdin as it is, anything else goes as JSON, as with `$wasm.run.async`) and, optionally, the `output` it gives |

The manifest is only shown, by `$wasm.modules()`, for people and for tests (run each example and compare its
output): calls don't read it, nothing runs the examples, and nothing fetches the repository. A function that isn't
in `functions` still reaches the module, which answers it; by convention, with the code `no_such_function`. Function
names can't start with `-`, so `--describe` is never one of them. Try it locally:
`wazero run summary.pb.wasm --describe`, and an example:
`printf '%s' '{"title":"Hello","body":"one two three"}' | wazero run summary.pb.wasm run`.

The examples keep the manifest as `manifest.json` beside the source and build it in (Go's `//go:embed`, Rust's
`include_str!`, Zig's `@embedFile`), so the module is still one file. Any other field is refused: a module can't ask
for anything, so a manifest that expects more (dependencies, permissions) is shown as an error in
`$wasm.modules()`, and the module runs with the defaults. A manifest is at most 64 KB. `$wasm.modules()` checks it
with wazero's interpreter (below), within the module's limits.

### Calling from page code

```ts
await $wasm.run.async(name, input)            // the module's "run"
await $wasm.call.async(name, fn, input)       // one of its functions (its first argument)
await $wasm.inspect.async(name, fn, input)    // {output, stderr, error, compileMs, runMs}, for trying a module out
$wasm.modules()  // [{name, running, description, version, functions, language, repository, examples, size, error}]
$wasm.limits()   // {maxCallMemoryMB, timeoutMs, maxConcurrent, maxModulesMB, maxPayload}
```

Calls are async only, in an async handler. The JS engine runs one VM per app and can't interrupt a call into Go, so a
module called synchronously would hold the VM, and with it every other hook and request of the app, while it compiles
and runs (a Go module's first call compiles for over a second). A call runs off the VM instead, and the app serves other
requests meanwhile. `$wasm.run(...)` without `.async` throws, saying so.

The input is the module's stdin: a string or bytes (an `ArrayBuffer`, a `Uint8Array` or another typed array) as they are, nothing for
`undefined` or `null`, anything else as JSON. So `$wasm.run.async("edifact", raw)`, with `raw` a string, hands over the raw text,
byte for byte. The output is the module's stdout: parsed if it's JSON, a string if not, `null` if empty.

A failed call rejects with an `Error` named `WasmError`, with `code`, `message`, `retryable` and `module`:

```ts
try {
  record.set("summary", (await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string }>("summary", post)).text)
} catch (err) {
  const w = err as WasmError
  if (w.name !== "WasmError" || w.code !== "empty_body") throw err
}
```

| Code | |
|---|---|
| `not_found` | no `<name>.pb.wasm` in the folder |
| `not_loaded` | in the folder, but it can't run (the message says why: a broken module, too large), or the app isn't serving |
| `no_such_function` | the module has no such function (the code modules give, by convention) |
| `timeout` | over the time limit (retryable) |
| `crashed` | it trapped, panicked or ran out of memory |
| `too_large` | input or output over the limit |
| `busy` | the calls running left no room for this one (retryable); the message gives the numbers |
| `module_error` | it exited non-zero without a code of its own |
| anything else | the module's own code (below) |

`$wasm.inspect.async` makes the same call but never rejects for it: it returns the output (or `null`), the `error`
as `{code, message, retryable}` (or `null`), what the module wrote to stderr (up to 64 KB), and how long compiling
and running took. It's for pages that let a superuser try a module out; other code uses `run` and `call`.

The time limit covers the run; compiling comes before it (below).

`$wasm` is declared in each app's `types.d.ts` ([`wasm.d.ts`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/wasm.d.ts)), for code completion and `tsc`.

### Writing a module

A module is a plain WASI program (`wasip1`), the way you'd write a command-line tool: read stdin, write stdout, exit.
The function asked for is its first argument (`os.Args[1]`, `"run"` for `$wasm.run.async`, `--describe` for its manifest,
above). To fail, exit non-zero; if
stderr is a JSON object `{"code", "message", "retryable"}`, your code gets it as is, any other text becomes the
`message` of a `module_error`. Anything it writes to stderr on success goes to the app's log (Logs in the
dashboard), so stderr is its log.

**Go** ([`example/summary/go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/go/main.go)):

```go
//go:embed manifest.json
var manifest string // what --describe prints

func main() {
	if os.Args[1] == "--describe" {
		fmt.Print(manifest)
		return
	}
	var post struct{ Title, Body string }
	if err := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&post); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprint(os.Stderr, `{"code":"bad_input","message":"not a post"}`)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(map[string]any{"text": post.Title, "words": len(strings.Fields(post.Body))})
}
```

```sh
GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm .
```

**Rust** ([`example/summary/rust`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/rust/src/main.rs)): a binary crate, serde for JSON.

```sh
rustup target add wasm32-wasip1   # once
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/summary.wasm pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm
```

**Zig** ([`example/summary/zig`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/zig/src/main.zig)): an executable for `wasm32-wasi` (Zig 0.17). Set
`stack_size = 1 << 20` in `build.zig`: Zig's default stack is 16 MB, and every call would start with it.

Any language that builds a WASI program works the same way: [Languages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages) has a page for C
and C++, Go, TinyGo, Rust, Zig and AssemblyScript, each with a module to build, and what else runs. Try a module without an app: `echo '{"title":"Hi","body":"one two"}' | wazero run summary.pb.wasm run`.

Two things are refused when the module loads, with a message that says so:

- a library instead of a program: Go's `-buildmode=c-shared`, or any module without `_start` ("not a WASI program");
- a module that imports anything outside `wasi_snapshot_preview1`, such as an [Extism](https://extism.org) plugin
  built with its PDK, or host functions this host doesn't have.

### Which language

| Example | Module | First call (compiles) | Later calls (from the cache) | Machine code: in memory during a call, and in the cache |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C | 25 KB | 17 ms | 0.5 ms | 86 KB |
| Rust | 98 KB | 33 ms | 1.3 ms | 389 KB |
| Zig | 95 KB | 30 ms | 1.2 ms | 357 KB |
| TinyGo | 284 KB | 74 ms | 3 ms | 988 KB |
| Go | 4.3 MB | 1.05 s | 38 ms | 18 MB |

A module's first call compiles it and writes its machine code to the cache (`CacheDir`); every later call, after a
restart too, loads it from there. Running the summary itself takes under a millisecond in every language. A call
holds its module's machine code in memory only while it runs, plus the program's own memory (its stack and heap, Go's
runtime and garbage collector included), which stays under `MaxCallMemoryMB`; between calls, nothing. Measured on a
laptop (2026-11-18), one call at a time; a Go module's size varies with what it imports (one that imports `net/http`
is ~11 MB). [Choosing a language](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages) has the same numbers with how to pick.

Go calls compiling at once also slow each other down: one took +19 MB, two +38 MB, four +245 MB (2026-11-16, before
the cache; calls that load from the cache take far less). That's why the calls running at once are limited by their
modules' size, `MaxModulesMB`, and not only by their number. An admin picks the trade-off with that one number:

| `MaxModulesMB` | Go calls (4.4 MB) at once | Rust or Zig calls (~0.1 MB) | Most memory they take, measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1 | 8 (`MaxConcurrent`) | ~25 MB |
| 10 (default) | 2 | 8 | ~45 MB |
| 20 | 4 | 8 | ~250 MB |

Pick by what the module does. With the cache, every language is quick after its first call; what still differs is
memory and how many calls run at once. A Go call holds 18 MB of machine code and takes 38 ms to load it, and two run at
once with the defaults: fine for a cron job, an import or an admin action. A module on a hot path (every record save,
every request) is better in C, Rust, Zig or TinyGo (the same Go source, a module 15 times smaller), whose calls take a
few milliseconds and under 1 MB.

## Commands and APIs

Generated from the `pocketone` binary and the contracts this extension provides.

### JavaScript API

What it adds to `pb_hooks` and page code: [WASM JavaScript API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/javascript/wasm).

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) | Add it to the host's standard set and Pocker gives it to every instance it runs (Docker containers run stock images): one extension value serves them all. Each instance has its own modules, in its own `pb_hooks/`, its own call slots and limits. Each call reads the instance's module file as it is then; nothing runs between calls (below). A module change reloads just that instance, like a `.pb.js` change. |
| [Sandbox](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/sandbox) | `$wasm` is safe to give a hostile tenant: a module gets nothing but its input. A call can't be interrupted by the JS engine's time limits, so `Timeout` (and compiling) bound it instead. |
| [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) | `pocketone deploy` sends the modules with the rest of `pb_hooks/`. |
| [MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mcp) | The app's `/mcp` gets `wasm_list_modules` (superusers only): every module by name, with its manifest (functions, examples) and whether it runs. Agents connecting are told how to call a module with `$wasm`, so one working on the site knows its modules even without their sources. |

### Per-instance settings (Pocker)

Each instance can override `maxCallMemoryMB`, `maxConcurrent`, `maxModulesMB`, `timeout` (a duration, like `5s`) and
`maxPayload` in its `extensions.wasm` settings, over the Config given to `New`, key by key. `enabled: false` turns
`$wasm` off for that instance (`typeof $wasm === "undefined"` in its JS). A change restarts just that instance, on
its next request:

```yaml
instances:
  - id: abc
    extensions: { wasm: { timeout: 10s, maxCallMemoryMB: 64 } }
  - id: no-wasm
    extensions: { wasm: { enabled: false } }
```

Leave `dir` unset there: each instance then gets the `pb_hooks/` in its own folder. `MaxConcurrent` and
`MaxModulesMB` count per instance, so one instance's busy modules never make another's calls wait. A restart (new
settings, a pb_hooks change, a restore) lets calls in progress finish, and the instance's modules run as before
after it, from its folder: nothing to reload.

### Building on WASM

There's no Go API, endpoint or form for calling a module: the app's JS code (`$wasm`) is the only way in, so whatever
reaches a module went through the app's own code.

## Example

[`example/main.go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/main.go) runs one app with a `posts` collection and a hook that fills each new post's summary; its folder is laid
out like an instance (`pb_data/`, `pb_hooks/`). Build the module into `example/pb_hooks/`, then
`cd example && go run . serve --dev` and create a post.

```go
// Command example runs one app with ext/wasm and the summary module wired in from pb_hooks: a new post gets its
// summary before it's saved (pb_hooks/main.pb.js). The example folder is the app's folder, laid out like an
// instance on PocketHost: pb_data/ and pb_hooks/ side by side, the module beside the JS hooks.
//
//	cd example && go run . serve --dev
//
// Build the module into pb_hooks/ (before or after starting the app: each call reads it):
//
//	(cd summary/go && GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o ../../pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm .)
//
// Then create a post (dashboard, or the API) and look at its summary field.
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/devusers"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/extkit"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/extkit/js"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/wasm"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"
	app.OnBootstrap().BindFunc(func(e *core.BootstrapEvent) error {
		if err := e.Next(); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		return posts(e.App)
	})
	// the same extension value the standard set gives every app, standalone or an instance (set.WASM)
	w := wasm.New(wasm.Config{})
	extkit.MustRegister(app, w)
	jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{
		HooksDir: "pb_hooks",
		OnInit:   func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, w) }, // $wasm in pb_hooks
	})
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

func posts(app core.App) error {
	if _, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts"); err == nil {
		return nil
	}
	c := core.NewBaseCollection("posts")
	c.Fields.Add(&core.TextField{Name: "title"}, &core.TextField{Name: "body", Max: 100000},
		&core.TextField{Name: "summary", Max: 1000}, &core.NumberField{Name: "words"})
	return app.Save(c)
}
```

### More example modules

Each is a plain program with a `manifest.json` built in, which it prints for `--describe` (its functions and examples,
so `/wasm`-style pages and the wazero CLI can try it), built with the command in its header. They answer the usual questions about a feature like this:

| Module | Language | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| [`summary/go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/go), [`summary/tinygo`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/tinygo), [`summary/rust`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/rust), [`summary/zig`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/zig), [`summary/c`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/c), [`summary/assemblyscript`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/assemblyscript) | Go, TinyGo, Rust, Zig, C, AssemblyScript | The same module in six languages: the summary above, and how much the language matters (a Go module is ~4 MB and compiles for over a second; TinyGo ~280 KB and ~65 ms; Rust, Zig, C and AssemblyScript under 100 KB and 10–25 ms). |
| [`summary/wat`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/wat), [`summary/llvm`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/llvm) | WAT, LLVM IR | The C summary written by hand in two assembly languages, for fun: WebAssembly text calling WASI directly (1.8 KB), and LLVM IR built by clang with wasi-libc (3.8 KB). See [WAT](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/wat) and [LLVM IR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/llvm). |
| [`stats-tinygo`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/stats-tinygo) | TinyGo | State kept by the app: running statistics whose state the app stores in a record and passes in with each call ([Keeping state in JS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/guides/state)). |
| [`markdown`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/markdown), [`sanitize-html`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/sanitize-html), [`diff`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/diff), [`thumbnail`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/thumbnail), [`qrcode`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/qrcode), [`csv`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/csv) | Rust | Real libraries for real jobs (pulldown-cmark, ammonia, similar, image, qrcode, csv), each with page code in the [recipes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes). |
| [`crypto`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/crypto) | Go | AES-256-GCM encryption, with no `$os.exec`. The key comes in with each call; the module can't keep it or send it anywhere. |
| [`waflows`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/waflows) | Rust | What JS can't do: a WhatsApp Flows endpoint needs RSA-OAEP and AES-GCM with WhatsApp's key and IV. Your code keeps the JSON and HTTP; the module does only those two. |
| [`edifact-orders-rust`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/edifact-orders-rust) | Rust | A real format with a real library (edifact-rs): an EDIFACT ORDERS message, as raw text, read into an order. |
| [`order-xml`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/order-xml) | Rust | The same order from XML (roxmltree), so one route takes either format and stores one shape. |
| [`devil`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/devil) | Rust | Is it safe? It tries, in plain sight, to read the app's database and `/etc/passwd`, list folders, write a file, read the environment, run `sh -c id` and send to `attacker.example`. Every try says `refused`. |
| [`memhog`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/tree/main/ext/wasm/example/memhog) | Rust | What does it cost? It asks for more memory than `MaxCallMemoryMB`: that call fails as `crashed`, saying which limit it hit, and the app goes on. `probe` shows the limit from inside. |

Every one of them is also kept built, beside its source (`example/<folder>/<name>.pb.wasm`: the Go ones about 4.5 MB,
the rest under 1 MB), so they double as the extension's tests: every run of `go test` loads each one, checks that its
`--describe` is its `manifest.json`, and runs its examples, with no compiler and no Docker needed. A change to
`ext/wasm` that breaks a real module shows there.

They're built in Docker, never with the compilers on your machine:
[`example/toolchains/Dockerfile`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/toolchains/Dockerfile) is the build environment of every example language,
one stage each: Go 1.27.4, TinyGo 0.41.1, Rust 1.100.0 and Zig 0.17.0 (Zig, and C through `zig cc`), each image
pinned by digest and Zig's download by checksum, so a rebuild on any machine gives the same bytes. After changing a
module's source: `go test -run 'TestPrebuiltExamples/<folder>' -update`. To check every kept file is what its source
builds, byte for byte: `go test -run TestPrebuiltMatchSources -rebuild` (a few minutes). To move to a newer compiler,
change it in the Dockerfile and rebuild them all with `-update`. The Go builds use `-trimpath` and the Rust builds
remap the crates' paths to `/cargo`, so a module holds no path of the container that built it.

## What a module can't do

Modules run in [wazero](https://wazero.io) (pure Go, no cgo), in the app's process, with only the standard WASI
functions and nothing behind them:

- **No files:** nothing is mounted, not even `pb_hooks/`. `open` fails.
- **No network:** WASI preview 1 has no way to connect. (Go's `net` on wasip1 is an in-memory stand-in: a module can
  "listen", but nothing outside the program reaches it.)
- **No environment, no processes**, no arguments beyond the function name.
- **No state between calls:** every call gets a fresh instance, so nothing from one call (or one caller) reaches the
  next.
- **Bounded:** memory, time, input and output size, and how many calls run at once (see Configure).

It does get a real clock and real random numbers (crypto nonces need them). Data from the app, secrets and API
responses reach a module only as input from your code, and the result goes nowhere but back to it: the network
stays with `$http.send` in your JS.

## How it works

- Modules run only while the app serves (other commands, such as `migrate`, never read them).
- Like `node script.js`: each call reads its module's file (`<name>.pb.wasm`, once the call has room), compiles the
  module in a wazero runtime of its own (or loads its machine code from the cache), runs it, and closes it after.
  Nothing stays in memory between calls, so a folder of 100 modules costs nothing while they aren't called.
  Compiling validates the module: a broken or half-written one doesn't run. A call in progress finishes with what it
  read, whatever happens to the file meanwhile. Compiling counts toward `MaxConcurrent` and `MaxModulesMB`, so the
  memory it takes stays bounded too.
- Compiled modules are kept on disk, in wazero's compilation cache (`CacheDir`), keyed by each module's bytes: a
  changed module compiles again on its next call, and the cache lasts across restarts. Each app has its own, in its
  `pb_cache/wasm` (under Pocker, outside the instance's folder, where the instance can't write). Loading from it is 20 to 30 times faster than compiling. Calls of the
  same module compile one at a time (wazero can't load one module twice at once safely); calls of other modules
  never wait for it, and a call whose caller gives up stops waiting (`busy`). When the process first opens the cache, it
  deletes entries older than 30 days, since nothing else does: a module still in use compiles once more then. The
  process runs the cache's contents as machine code, so it belongs where only the process writes, never in `pb_data`
  or `pb_hooks`.
- WASM watches nothing itself: no watches of its own, no timer, no work between calls, however many instances there
  are. (The JS engine's, or pocker's, watch on `pb_hooks/` restarts the app when a module changes, as for a hook.)
- `$wasm.modules()` lists the folder each time. It checks each module with wazero's interpreter, which validates it
  and runs `--describe` without making machine code (~0.25 s for a Go module), and keeps only what it found
  (manifest, language, error) until the module's file changes size or time; when the app starts serving, it checks
  them all once, so the log says which ones can't run.
- A call waits for room: fewer than `MaxConcurrent` calls running, and its module's size left in `MaxModulesMB`
  (`$wasm.modules()` gives each one's `size`). Compiling takes time and memory in step with a module's size, so with
  the defaults (8 calls, 10 MB) a Rust or Zig module (~0.1 MB) runs 8 calls at once and a Go one (~4.4 MB) 2, beside
  small ones. A call goes in as soon as there's room for it, so a small call doesn't queue behind a big one that's
  waiting; under a steady stream of small calls, a big one may wait until it gives up as `busy`.
- No collection and no database use: what's in the folder, and why a module can't run, comes from the files
  (`$wasm.modules()` and the log).

# Docker

Version 0.0.5 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

Run every instance on a host in its own container, with the official PocketBase or PocketOne binary of the version
the instance asks for. One host can serve PocketBase 0.23 and 0.36 and PocketOne side by side.

Docker is one of the two runtime providers of the multi-instance [multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite). The other is
[Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker), which runs every instance inside one process. A host runs one of them.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Docker is built into `pocketone`. It needs a Docker daemon on the same machine; nothing else to install.

It's off until `pocketone.yaml` has a `multisite` and a `docker` section (below). Then `pocketone serve` runs the host
instead of a single app.

In your own Go build, add it to the host's extensions; it provides the [runtime/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/runtime/v1)
contract when `pocketone.yaml` has a `docker` section:

```go
h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath,
	Extensions: []multisite.Extension{&docker.Provider{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath}}})
```

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/docker`. Add `docker.NewCommand(...)` to your root command for the
`docker seed` and `docker update` commands.

## Configure

Add a `multisite` section (host mode) and a `docker` section to `pocketone.yaml`. Listeners (`server`), instances
(`instances`) and the firewall are the host's sections. The `docker` section makes docker the host's runtime instead of
pocker; every instance runs in a container.

```yaml
multisite: {}
docker:
  image: alpine:3.20                 # base image the binaries run in
  binaries: /var/lib/pocketbase      # release binary cache
  root: /var/lib/instances           # one folder per instance: <root>/<id>
  versions: ["pb:0.23", "pb:0.36", "p1:0.0"]
  default_version: "pb:0.36.*"
  idle_ttl: 10m
  max_concurrent_starts: 4
instances:
  file: ./instances.yaml
```

`image`, `binaries` and `root` are required.

**Versions.** An instance picks its binary with the prefix of its `version`: `pb:` is upstream PocketBase, `p1:` is
PocketOne, no prefix means `pb:`. `versions` lists the minors the host serves; the newest cached patch that matches
wins. A version that isn't listed gets a clear 503. Upstream PocketBase 0.22 and older are refused unless you lower
`min_upstream` and keep those releases in the cache yourself.

**Per instance** (`instances.yaml` or a mothership): `version`, `secrets` (passed as environment), `encryption_key`,
`dev`, and `dir` to put its folder somewhere other than `<root>/<id>`. An instance with `runtime` set to anything but
`docker` isn't served here.

**Limits and hardening** are optional: `nano_cpus`, `pids_limit`, `nofile`, `cap_drop` and `no_new_privileges`.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `docker:`

Runtime provider docker: each instance in its own container with the PocketBase (pb:) or PocketOne (p1:) binary of its version (image, binary cache and manifest, instance root, default version, idle stop, limits).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `socket` | string |  | The Docker socket. Default $DOCKER_HOST when it is unix://, else /var/run/docker.sock. |
| `image` | string |  | Base image the binaries run in, such as alpine:3.20. Required; pulled when missing. |
| `binaries` | string |  | Folder of the release binary cache and its releases.json. Required. |
| `versions` | list of string |  | The minors this host serves, such as pb:0.36 or p1:0.0 (latest patch of each, from docker update). |
| `root` | string |  | Folder with one folder per instance (<root>/<id>). Required. |
| `home` | string |  | The instance folder inside the container. Default /home/pockethost. |
| `default_version` | string |  | Version for instances that name none, such as p1:0.0.*. Empty: such instances fail. |
| `min_upstream` | string |  | Oldest upstream PocketBase release served. Default 0.23.0; lower it only for releases you cache yourself. |
| `idle_ttl` | duration |  | Stop a container after this long without requests. Default 10m. |
| `max_concurrent_starts` | int |  | Containers starting at once. Default 4. |
| `start_timeout` | duration |  | How long a container gets to answer its health check. Default 60s. |
| `nano_cpus` | int |  | CPU limit per container in billionths of a CPU (1000000000 = one CPU). 0: no limit. |
| `pids_limit` | int |  | Process limit per container. 0: Docker's default. |
| `nofile` | list of int |  | Open-file limit per container: [soft, hard]. Empty: Docker's default. |
| `cap_drop` | list of string |  | Linux capabilities to drop, such as [ALL]. |
| `no_new_privileges` | bool |  | Set no-new-privileges on every container. |
| `network` | string |  | Docker network for the containers. Default the bridge. |
| `adopt_image` | string |  | Also adopt running unlabeled containers of this image named after an instance id (taking over from another manager). |

## Use

### Fetch the binaries

```bash
pocketone docker update   # find the latest patch of each docker.versions minor, record and download it
pocketone docker seed     # download whatever is recorded but not in the cache yet
```

`update` checks upstream PocketBase releases (ganigeorgiev.com, then the archived GitHub) and PocketOne releases on
GitHub, verifies each download against the release's checksums.txt, and records the list in the cache's
`releases.json`. Run it when you want new patches. Nothing is downloaded at request time: when the host starts, any
listed release missing from the cache is downloaded in the background.

The cache layout is `<binaries>/<version>/<platform>/pocketbase` for PocketBase (PocketHost's existing layout) and
`<binaries>/p1/<version>/<platform>/pocketone` for PocketOne.

### Run the host

```bash
pocketone serve
```

- A container starts on an instance's first request and is ready when `/api/health` answers. At most
  `max_concurrent_starts` start at once.
- It stops after `idle_ttl` without requests.
- It restarts on its next request when what it runs changed (secrets, version, mounts). A change to routing only
  doesn't restart it.
- It stops when the instance is deleted or moves to another edge.
- Containers keep running when the host restarts; the next process adopts them by their labels.

### Hooks and migrations

A change in an instance's `pb_hooks` restarts its container. PocketBase's own hooks watcher stays on too, so a hook
file that fails to load is logged and skipped instead of stopping the instance. A request that arrives while the
instance restarts waits for it instead of failing; one that lost its connection mid-restart is sent once more if
it's safe to repeat (GET, HEAD or OPTIONS without a body). Migrations run when a container boots.

### Maintenance

Instance folders are ordinary folders under `root`. To work on one while nothing has it open, a host's Go code calls
`WithInstanceStopped` (below); requests for that instance wait up to 30 s, then get a 503 with `Retry-After`.
The host provides [instance.fs/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/instance.fs/v1) on its scope from the same methods
(`Runtime.Files(dir)`), so host-side code (a host's deploy or file drive) gets an instance's folder, writers' lock
and restart from the contract.

### Remote control

Containers run stock images, and a PocketBase image has no PocketOne extensions, so the host answers
[remote/v1](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/contracts/remote/v1/remote.go) for them at `/api/_c/remote/v1/` on each instance's hostname: the
`pocketone remote` commands work the same as against a Pocker instance or a single app. It answers after the host's
gates (firewall, rate limits) and blocked check, so a blocked instance's remote/v1 gets the blocked answer and the
container stays stopped.

- `GET /api/_c/remote/v1` (whoami) is public and lists `remote/v1`.
- `status`, `restart` and `logs` need a superuser token of that instance (`pocketone remote login` with a superuser
  email and password). The host asks the instance itself to check it.
- A host with its own accounts sets `docker.Provider.RemoteAuth` to decide who may call them instead (PocketHost: the
  instance owner's tokens). `remote/v1` is provided on the host's scope, so whoami also lists the other contracts the
  host provides for its instances (a host's `deploy/v1`).
- `restart` replaces the container; `logs` replays and follows the container's output, the last 1000 lines per
  instance kept by this host since it started following the container.

### Switching provider

Docker and Pocker both use `<root>/<id>`, so switching is a config change. Stop the containers first when leaving
docker, since they keep running across a host restart on purpose. Data only moves forward: an instance started on a
newer PocketBase than wrote its data is upgraded.

## Commands and APIs

Generated from the `pocketone` binary and the contracts this extension provides.

### Commands

What it adds to the `pocketone` binary ([CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli)):

| Command | |
|---|---|
| [`pocketone docker seed`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-docker-seed) | Downloads the releases docker.versions lists that the cache doesn't have yet |
| [`pocketone docker update`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-docker-update) | Finds the latest patch of each docker.versions minor, records and downloads it |

### [remote/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1)

| Operation | CLI | REST | MCP |
|---|---|---|---|
| [whoami](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1#whoami) | `pocketone remote whoami` | `GET /api/_c/remote/v1` | `remote_whoami` |
| [status](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1#status) | `pocketone remote status` | `GET /api/_c/remote/v1/status` | `remote_status` |
| [restart](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1#restart) | `pocketone remote restart` | `POST /api/_c/remote/v1/restart` | `remote_restart` |
| [logs](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/remote/v1#logs) | `pocketone remote logs --n <n>` | `GET /api/_c/remote/v1/logs` | `remote_logs` |

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) | Docker is a runtime provider of the host: the host routes by hostname, runs the listeners and gates, and hands each request to docker. |
| [Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker) | The other provider. A host runs one of them, over the same instance folders. |
| [Edge](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/edge) | For a fleet: requests for instances on another edge are forwarded there. |
| [Mothership](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mothership) | Instances (and their versions) come from a mothership instead of a file. |
| [Firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall) | Rate limits and allow lists in front of every instance. |
| [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes) | The host provides remote/v1 for every container, so the CLI's whoami, status, restart and logs work. |

### Building on Docker

- **`docker.Provider`** fields extend the provider from Go: `Container` adds mounts, environment and labels to each
  container; `Version` rewrites an instance's version before the binary is picked; `OnLog` receives container output
  (default: the debug log); `Versions` replaces the `versions` list (for example a fleet's list from a mothership);
  `MinUpstream` replaces `min_upstream`.
- **`Spec`** (what `Container` fills in): `Binds`, `Env`, `Labels`, plus `Cmd` to adjust the command (for example
  drop a flag an old release lacks) and `HealthPath` / `HealthAnyStatus` for the readiness check.
- **`VersionsSource`**: any type with `Releases(ctx)` decides which releases the host serves, each pinned to its
  download and sha256. `YAMLVersions` (the `versions` key) is the built-in one.
- **Runtime API**: `docker.New(docker.Config{...})` builds the runtime without the config file.
  `WithInstanceStopped(ctx, id, fn)` stops an instance, holds its requests and runs `fn` on its folder (for deploys
  and restores); `StartInstance` starts one now; `InstanceDir` returns its folder. `Remote(host, dir)` and `SuperuserAuth()` are the
  remote/v1 provider and the host-side auth that `Provider` wires in, for a host built by hand
  (`remotev1.W.HostHandler(host, multisite.InstanceID, rt.SuperuserAuth(), next)` in `Host.InstanceRoutes`).
- **Release helpers**: `ParseVersion`, `Pick` / `PickMin`, `LatestPatches`, `Update` and `Seed` are what the commands
  use.

## Example

A minimal docker host: instances from a YAML file, each in its own container, routed by hostname on one listener. With
a Docker daemon running, start it from this folder with
`go run ./example --instances instances.yaml --data ./instances --binaries ./bin --versions pb:0.23,p1:0.0`.

```go
// A minimal docker host: instances from a YAML file, each in its own container with the PocketBase or PocketOne
// version it asks for, routed by hostname on one listener.
//
//	go run ./example --instances instances.yaml --data ./instances --binaries ./bin --versions pb:0.23,p1:0.0
//
// instances.yaml:
//
//	instances:
//	  - { id: blog, hosts: [blog.localhost], version: "pb:0.23.*" }
//	  - { id: shop, hosts: [shop.localhost], version: "p1:0.0.*" }
package main

import (
	"context"
	"flag"
	"log/slog"
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"strings"
	"syscall"

	"pocketone.dev/ext/docker"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/multisite"
)

func main() {
	instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file")
	data := flag.String("data", "./instances", "folder with one folder per instance")
	binaries := flag.String("binaries", "./bin", "PocketBase and PocketOne binary cache")
	versions := flag.String("versions", "pb:0.23,p1:0.0", "minors to serve (latest patch each; fetched at start)")
	image := flag.String("image", "alpine:3.20", "base image")
	listen := flag.String("listen", "127.0.0.1:8090", "listen address")
	flag.Parse()

	b := &docker.Binaries{Root: *binaries}
	tracked := strings.Split(*versions, ",")
	if err := docker.RunUpdate(context.Background(), os.Stdout, docker.DefaultDiscovery(), b, tracked); err != nil {
		slog.Error("versions", "error", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	rt, err := docker.New(docker.Config{Image: *image, DataRoot: *data, Binaries: b, Versions: docker.YAMLVersions{Tracked: tracked, Root: b.Root}})
	if err != nil {
		slog.Error("docker", "error", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()
	h := &multisite.Host{Source: &multisite.YAMLSource{Path: *instances}, Runtime: rt, Listeners: multisite.Listeners{Listen: *listen}}
	if err := h.Run(ctx); err != nil {
		slog.Error("host", "error", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

## How it works

- Each instance folder is mounted at `/home/pockethost` and the binary read-only at `/home/pockethost/pocketbase`.
  The container runs `./pocketbase serve --http 0.0.0.0:8090`, plus `--dev` for dev instances and
  `--encryptionEnv=PB_ENCRYPTION_KEY` when the instance has an encryption key. Its secrets are its environment.
- The port is published on 127.0.0.1 and the host proxies to it. This is the layout PocketHost's Node edge uses, so
  its instance folders and binary cache move as they are.
- Every container carries labels: `p1.runtime`, `p1.instance`, `p1.version` (the resolved release, such as
  `pb:0.36.9`) and `p1.spec` (a hash of its configuration, used to tell when it must restart). `adopt_image` also
  adopts unlabeled containers of an image, for taking over from another manager.
- Docker is reached over its socket API directly; there's no Docker SDK dependency.

### Status

Tested against a real Docker daemon, with upstream PocketBase 0.23 and PocketOne 0.0.1 side by side, alone and as a
host's runtime. Not yet in production.

`go test ./...` runs the Docker tests when a daemon is reachable (they're skipped with `-short`). The first run
downloads an upstream release and a PocketOne release into the user cache.
