Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/c

# C and C++

C makes the smallest and fastest modules: the summary example is 25 KB, its first call compiles in about 17 ms, and later calls load it from the cache in half a millisecond. The easiest compiler is `zig cc`: Zig ships clang and wasi-libc together, so there's no SDK to install.

## Set up

```bash
brew install zig   # or download it from ziglang.org
```

Clang with [wasi-sdk](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-sdk) works too: replace `zig cc -target wasm32-wasi` below with `$WASI_SDK_PATH/bin/clang --target=wasm32-wasip1`.

## The module

[`example/summary/c`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/c/main.c) counts the words of a text and returns the first twelve. C has no JSON in its standard library, so it takes the text as it is (your code can pass a string) and prints JSON:

```c
// what `summary --describe` prints: manifest.json, built in (C23 #embed)
static const char manifest[] = {
#embed "manifest.json"
    , 0};

static void fail(const char *code, const char *message) {
  fprintf(stderr, "{\"code\":\"%s\",\"message\":\"%s\"}", code, message);
  exit(1);
}

int main(int argc, char **argv) {
  const char *function = argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "";
  if (strcmp(function, "--describe") == 0) {
    fputs(manifest, stdout);
    return 0;
  }
  if (strcmp(function, "run") != 0) fail("no_such_function", "only run");

  // read stdin, count the words, keep the first 12 ...

  fputs("{\"text\":", stdout);
  put_json_string(short_text, m);
  printf(",\"words\":%zu}", words);
  return 0;
}
```

To take JSON in, add a parser such as [cJSON](https://github.com/DaveGamble/cJSON) (one `.c` file and a header) beside `main.c` and list it on the command line.

## Build

```bash
zig cc -target wasm32-wasi -std=c23 -Os -s -Wl,-z,stack-size=1048576 \
  -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm main.c
```

- `-Os -s`: smallest code, no symbols.
- `-Wl,-z,stack-size=1048576`: a 1 MB stack. Without it, `zig cc` gives a WASI program a 16 MB stack, and every call would start with 16 MB of memory.
- `-std=c23`: for `#embed`. Without it, keep the manifest in a string instead.

## Call it

An API route that saves a post with its summary and word count:

```ts
// pb_pages/posts.ts
export async function post(ctx: any) {
  const { body } = ctx.req.body()
  const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string; words: number }>("summary", String(body ?? "")) // a string goes in as it is
  const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts"))
  record.load({ body, summary: out.text, words: out.words })
  ctx.app.save(record)
  return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id, summary: out.text, words: out.words })
}
```

## C++

`zig c++` builds C++ the same way, with `-fno-exceptions` added:

```bash
zig c++ -target wasm32-wasi -fno-exceptions -Os -s -Wl,-z,stack-size=1048576 \
  -o pb_hooks/mymodule.pb.wasm main.cpp
```

WebAssembly exception handling doesn't run here, so code that throws, the standard library's included, fails to link (`undefined symbol: __cxa_throw`) until exceptions are off. What you use of the standard library sets the size: a program that uses `std::string` and `printf` is 20 KB, one that reads stdin with iostreams 204 KB.

## Libraries

C libraries that only compute (parsers, codecs, compression, math) usually build as they are: add their `.c` files to the command. What WASI preview 1 doesn't have fails to build or fails at run time: threads, sockets, `fork`, and files (no folder is mounted, so `fopen` fails).


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/go

# Go

Go builds a module with nothing extra to install: `GOOS=wasip1` is a target of the Go you already have, and the whole standard library comes along. The cost is size. The summary example is 4.3 MB: its first call compiles it for about a second, and later calls load 18 MB of machine code from the cache in about 38 ms. That's fine off the hot path: a cron job, an import, an admin action. For a module that runs on every save or every request, build the same code with [TinyGo](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/tinygo) instead: 3 ms and under 1 MB a call.

## The module

[`example/summary/go`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/go/main.go) is a plain command-line program:

```go
//go:embed manifest.json
var manifest string // what `summary --describe` prints

func main() {
	switch os.Args[1] { // the function asked for
	case "--describe":
		fmt.Print(manifest)
		return
	case "run":
	default:
		fail("no_such_function", os.Args[1])
	}
	var post struct {
		Title string `json:"title"`
		Body  string `json:"body"`
	}
	if err := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&post); err != nil {
		fail("bad_input", "the input isn't a post: "+err.Error())
	}
	// ... the summary
	json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(map[string]any{"text": text, "words": len(words)})
}

// fail ends the program with an error your code can read (err.code / err.message).
func fail(code, message string) {
	b, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]string{"code": code, "message": message})
	fmt.Fprint(os.Stderr, string(b))
	os.Exit(1)
}
```

## Build

```bash
GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm .
```

`-ldflags="-s -w"` saves little here (about 80 KB of 4.4 MB). A Go module always says it's Go, so its manifest needs no `language`.

## Call it

An API route that saves a post with its summary:

```ts
// pb_pages/posts.ts
export async function post(ctx: any) {
  const { title, body } = ctx.req.body()
  const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string }>("summary", { title, body })
  const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts"))
  record.load({ title, body, summary: out.text })
  ctx.app.save(record)
  return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id, summary: out.text })
}
```

## Size

What you import sets the size. The summary (`encoding/json`, `strings`, `fmt`) is 4.3 MB; a module that imports `net/http` is about 11 MB, over the default `MaxModulesMB` of 10, so it can't run until that's raised. Two Go calls run at once with the defaults, and calls that compile at the same time slow each other down ([Which language](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/extension#which-language) has the numbers).

## What doesn't work

`GOOS=wasip1` programs get no files, no network and no environment here. `net` builds but reaches nothing outside the program, and goroutines run, one at a time. A library (`-buildmode=c-shared`) isn't a program and is refused when it loads.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/tinygo

# TinyGo

[TinyGo](https://tinygo.org) compiles Go for small targets. The same source as the [Go](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/go) summary builds to a 284 KB module instead of 4.3 MB. Its first call compiles in about 74 ms instead of a second, and later calls load it from the cache in 3 ms instead of 38, holding under 1 MB of machine code instead of 18 MB. It's the way to write Go for a module on a hot path.

## Set up

```bash
brew install tinygo
```

TinyGo supports a range of Go versions (TinyGo 0.41: Go 1.19 to 1.26) and uses the `go` on your `PATH`. With a newer Go installed, TinyGo stops with `requires go version 1.19 through 1.26`. The go command can fetch a supported one for it:

```bash
export PATH="$(GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.0 go env GOROOT)/bin:$PATH"
tinygo version
```

## The module

[`example/summary/tinygo`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/tinygo/main.go) is the Go summary, unchanged: `encoding/json`, `os.Args`, stdin and stdout work as they do in Go. Its manifest says `"language": "TinyGo"`, since a TinyGo module doesn't say it itself.

## Build

```bash
tinygo build -target=wasip1 -opt=z -no-debug -scheduler=none -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm .
```

- `-opt=z`: smallest code.
- `-no-debug`: no debug information.
- `-scheduler=none`: no goroutine scheduler. A module is one call that reads, computes and exits, so it rarely needs one, and leaving it out takes the summary from 481 KB to 284 KB. A program that starts a goroutine doesn't build with it; leave the flag off then.

## Call it

The page code is the same as for Go:

```ts
const { title, body } = ctx.req.body()
const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string }>("summary", { title, body })
```

## What's different from Go

- **Most of the standard library works**, `encoding/json`, `strings`, `math`, `sort`, `time`, `crypto/*` and `encoding/*` included. Packages that lean hard on reflection or on the operating system may not build; [TinyGo's package list](https://tinygo.org/docs/reference/lang-support/stdlib/) says which.
- **Memory starts small:** a TinyGo module starts with 128 KB and grows as it needs, where a Go one starts with 3 MB.
- **Third-party packages** build when they stay inside what TinyGo supports. Try the build: TinyGo says which import it can't compile.

[Keeping state in JS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/guides/state) builds a second TinyGo module, with two functions and the state held by the app.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/rust

# Rust

Rust makes small, fast modules (the summary is 98 KB: about 33 ms for its first call, which compiles it, and 1.3 ms for later ones), and most crates that only compute build for WASI as they are. It's the best choice when you need a library: a parser, a codec, a format. The [recipes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes) are all Rust for that reason.

## Set up

```bash
rustup target add wasm32-wasip1
```

## The module

[`example/summary/rust`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/rust/src/main.rs) is a binary crate with serde for JSON:

```rust
fn fail(code: &str, message: &str) -> ! {
    eprint!("{}", serde_json::json!({ "code": code, "message": message }));
    std::process::exit(1)
}

fn main() {
    match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() {
        Some("--describe") => {
            print!("{}", include_str!("../manifest.json"));
            return;
        }
        Some("run") => {}
        other => fail("no_such_function", other.unwrap_or("")),
    }
    let post: Post = serde_json::from_reader(std::io::stdin())
        .unwrap_or_else(|e| fail("bad_input", &format!("the input isn't a post: {e}")));
    // ... the summary
    serde_json::to_writer(std::io::stdout(), &Summary { text, words: words.len() }).unwrap();
}
```

Keep the release profile small:

```toml
[profile.release]
opt-level = "z"
lto = true
strip = true
codegen-units = 1
```

## Build

```bash
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/summary.wasm pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm
```

`strip = true` also drops what tells `$wasm.modules()` the module is Rust, so the manifest says `"language": "Rust"`.

## Call it

```ts
const { title, body } = ctx.req.body()
const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string }>("summary", { title, body })
```

## Crates

A crate works when it only computes. One that needs threads, sockets, files or a C library built for another target won't build or won't run: `rayon`, `tokio`'s runtime, `reqwest`, `openssl`. Turn off default features you don't need (`image = { version = "0.25", default-features = false, features = ["png"] }`); it keeps the module small and leaves out code that can't build for WASI. A panic ends the call as `crashed`; return an error with `fail` instead when the input is wrong.

Don't build for `wasm32-wasip2` or with `cargo component`: those make a component, which doesn't run here.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/zig

# Zig

Zig makes small, fast modules (the summary is 95 KB: about 30 ms for its first call, which compiles it, and 1.2 ms for later ones) and needs nothing but Zig: WASI is one of its targets. Its standard library has JSON, so a module reads and writes JSON with no packages.

## Set up

```bash
brew install zig   # Zig 0.17
```

Zig's standard library changes between versions. The example is written for Zig 0.17, where I/O goes through `std.Io` and `main` takes `std.process.Init`.

## The module

[`example/summary/zig`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/zig/src/main.zig):

```zig
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const allocator = init.arena.allocator();
    var out_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;

    const args = try init.minimal.args.toSlice(allocator);
    const function: []const u8 = if (args.len > 1) args[1] else "";
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, function, "--describe")) {
        try out.writeAll(@embedFile("manifest.json"));
        return out.flush();
    }
    if (!std.mem.eql(u8, function, "run")) fail(io, "no_such_function", function);

    var in_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdin = std.Io.File.stdin().readerStreaming(io, &in_buf);
    const input = try stdin.interface.allocRemaining(allocator, .unlimited);
    const post = std.json.parseFromSliceLeaky(Post, allocator, input, .{ .ignore_unknown_fields = true }) catch
        fail(io, "bad_input", "the input isn't a post");
    // ... the summary
    try std.json.Stringify.value(.{ .text = text.items, .words = words.items.len }, .{}, out);
    try out.flush();
}
```

Flush the writer before returning: output still in its buffer is lost when the program exits.

## Build

In [`build.zig`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/zig/build.zig), target WASI, make the manifest importable, and set the stack:

```zig
const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{
    .default_target = .{ .os_tag = .wasi, .cpu_arch = .wasm32 },
});
// ...
mod.addAnonymousImport("manifest.json", .{ .root_source_file = b.path("manifest.json") });
const exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "summary", .root_module = mod });
exe.stack_size = 1 << 20; // Zig's default stack is 16 MB: every call would start with 16 MB of memory
```

```bash
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall
cp zig-out/bin/summary.wasm pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm
```

A Zig module never says it's Zig, so the manifest says `"language": "Zig"`.

## Call it

```ts
const { title, body } = ctx.req.body()
const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string }>("summary", { title, body })
```

## C libraries

Zig compiles C as well: add C files to the module with `mod.addCSourceFiles(...)` and link libc (`mod.link_libc = true`), and a Zig module can use a C library directly. For C alone, see [C and C++](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/c).


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/assemblyscript

# AssemblyScript

[AssemblyScript](https://www.assemblyscript.org) looks like TypeScript and compiles straight to WebAssembly, so it's the closest you can get to writing a module in the language your page code is in. Its modules are tiny: the summary example is 10 KB, its first call compiles in about 13 ms, and later calls load it from the cache in half a millisecond.

It looks like TypeScript, but it isn't: types are WebAssembly's (`i32`, `f64`, `u8`), there's no `any` and no union types, and npm packages written for JavaScript don't work in it. Only packages written for AssemblyScript do.

## Set up

AssemblyScript builds for the browser by default. [`@assemblyscript/wasi-shim`](https://github.com/AssemblyScript/wasi-shim) makes it build a WASI program instead, with `process.argv`, `process.stdin`, `process.stdout` and `process.exit`:

```bash
npm install --save-dev --save-exact assemblyscript @assemblyscript/wasi-shim
```

`asconfig.json` extends the shim's settings and sets the release build:

```json
{
  "extends": "./node_modules/@assemblyscript/wasi-shim/asconfig.json",
  "targets": {
    "release": {
      "outFile": "summary.pb.wasm",
      "optimizeLevel": 3,
      "shrinkLevel": 2,
      "noAssert": true,
      "runtime": "stub"
    }
  }
}
```

- **The shim is required.** Without it, a module imports `env.abort` from the browser's world, and it's refused when it loads.
- **`"runtime": "stub"`** leaves out the garbage collector: a call reads, computes and exits, so nothing needs collecting, and the module is smaller. A module that builds large data in a loop can use `"incremental"` instead.

## The module

[`example/summary/assemblyscript`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/assemblyscript/assembly/index.ts) counts the words of a text and returns the first twelve. AssemblyScript's standard library has no JSON, so, like the [C](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/c) example, it takes the text as it is (your code can pass a string) and prints JSON:

```ts
// what `summary --describe` prints: AssemblyScript can't embed a file, so the manifest is a string here
const manifest = `{ "description": "Summarizes a text: its first words, and a word count", ... }`

function fail(code: string, message: string): void {
  process.stderr.write(`{"code":"${code}","message":"${message}"}`)
  process.exit(1)
}

const fn = process.argv.length > 1 ? process.argv[1] : ""
if (fn == "--describe") {
  process.stdout.write(manifest)
} else if (fn != "run") {
  fail("no_such_function", "only run")
} else {
  const text = readStdin() // process.stdin.read() into a growing buffer, then String.UTF8.decode
  // ... split into words, keep the first 12
  process.stdout.write(`{"text":${jsonString(short)},"words":${words.length}}`)
}
```

To take JSON in, add a JSON package written for AssemblyScript, such as [json-as](https://github.com/JairusSW/json-as).

## Build

```bash
npx asc assembly/index.ts --target release
cp summary.pb.wasm pb_hooks/
```

The manifest says `"language": "AssemblyScript"`, since the module doesn't say it itself.

## Call it

An API route that saves a post with its summary and word count:

```ts
// pb_pages/posts.ts
export async function post(ctx: any) {
  const { body } = ctx.req.body()
  const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string; words: number }>("summary", String(body ?? "")) // a string goes in as it is
  const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts"))
  record.load({ body, summary: out.text, words: out.words })
  ctx.app.save(record)
  return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id, summary: out.text, words: out.words })
}
```


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/wat

# WebAssembly text (WAT)

WAT is WebAssembly's assembly language: the instructions a module is made of, written as text. Writing a module in it means no compiler, no runtime and no libc, only the module and the WASI functions it imports. The summary example is 1.8 KB, the smallest module here: its first call compiles in about 9 ms, later calls load it from the cache in under half a millisecond.

It's for fun and for learning what's under every other page here. For real work, any other language is less code: the summary takes about 200 lines of WAT.

## Set up

```bash
brew install wabt   # wat2wasm, wasm2wat, and friends
```

## The module

[`example/summary/wat`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/wat/summary.wat) takes a text on stdin, like the [C](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/c) one, and prints `{"text", "words"}`. It does by hand what libc and a compiler do for the other languages:

- **It imports WASI directly:** `args_sizes_get` and `args_get` for the function asked for, `fd_read` for stdin, `fd_write` for stdout and stderr, `proc_exit` to fail.
- **It lays out its own memory:** fixed addresses for its strings, the arguments and the manifest, and the input from 64 KB up, growing memory with `memory.grow` as the input needs it.
- **It exports `_start`**, the function a WASI program runs.

```wat
(module
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "fd_read" (func $fd_read (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "fd_write" (func $fd_write (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "proc_exit" (func $proc_exit (param i32)))
  ;; ...
  (memory (export "memory") 2)
  (data (i32.const 160) "{\22code\22:\22no_such_function\22,\22message\22:\22only run\22}")

  ;; end the program with an error your code can read (err.code / err.message)
  (func $fail (param $ptr i32) (param $len i32)
    (call $write (i32.const 2) (local.get $ptr) (local.get $len))
    (call $proc_exit (i32.const 1)))

  ;; space, tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return
  (func $space (param $c i32) (result i32)
    (i32.or (i32.eq (local.get $c) (i32.const 32))
            (i32.lt_u (i32.sub (local.get $c) (i32.const 9)) (i32.const 5))))

  (func $main (export "_start")
    ;; read argv[1], print the manifest for --describe, read stdin, count the words,
    ;; write {"text": ..., "words": ...}
  ))
```

The manifest is a data segment, the compacted `manifest.json` with its quotes written `\22`. WAT can't include a file, so the tests check the two say the same thing.

## Build

```bash
wat2wasm summary.wat -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm
```

`wasm2wat` turns any module back into text, which is a good way to see what a compiler made: `wasm2wat pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm | less`.

## Call it

```ts
const { body } = ctx.req.body()
const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string; words: number }>("summary", String(body ?? "")) // a string goes in as it is
```

## What to know

- **A trap is a crash.** An out-of-bounds load, a division by zero or `unreachable` ends the call as `crashed`. The example uses `unreachable` when memory can't grow.
- **Only WebAssembly 2.0 runs**, so instructions from later proposals (tail calls, GC, exceptions, threads) fail when the module loads. `memory.copy` (bulk memory) and SIMD are fine.
- **The manifest's `language`** is up to you; a WAT module says nothing about itself. The example says `"WAT"`.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/llvm

# LLVM IR

LLVM IR is the language Clang, Rust, Zig and Swift translate your code into before LLVM turns it into machine code, or here, WebAssembly. It reads like a portable assembly language: typed values, basic blocks, branches. Written by hand, it gets LLVM's optimizer and wasi-libc for free. The summary example is 3.8 KB; its first call compiles in about 7.5 ms, later calls load it from the cache in half a millisecond.

Like [WAT](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/wat), it's here for fun and to show what compilers produce. Seeing your C or Rust as IR is the useful part: `clang -S -emit-llvm` or `rustc --emit=llvm-ir`.

## Set up

Nothing new if you have Zig: `zig cc` is clang, and it reads `.ll` files as well as `.c` ones.

```bash
brew install zig
```

## The module

[`example/summary/llvm`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/summary/llvm/summary.ll) does what the [C](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/c) summary does, in IR, and calls wasi-libc's `read`, `write`, `malloc` and `exit` like C would:

```llvm
target datalayout = "e-m:e-p:32:32-p10:8:8-p20:8:8-i64:64-i128:128-n32:64-S128-ni:1:10:20"
target triple = "wasm32-unknown-wasip1-unknown"

@err_nsf = private constant [48 x i8] c"{\22code\22:\22no_such_function\22,\22message\22:\22only run\22}"

declare i32 @write(i32, ptr, i32)
declare void @exit(i32) noreturn

; space, tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return
define internal i1 @space(i8 %c) {
  %is.sp = icmp eq i8 %c, 32
  %d = sub i8 %c, 9
  %is.ctl = icmp ult i8 %d, 5
  %r = or i1 %is.sp, %is.ctl
  ret i1 %r
}

; main(argc, argv): on WASI, C compilers name it __main_argc_argv
define i32 @__main_argc_argv(i32 %argc, ptr %argv) {
  ; ...
}
```

Two things hand-written IR has to get right that a compiler would do for you:

- **The datalayout and triple** must be wasm32-WASI's. Get them from clang: `zig cc -target wasm32-wasi -S -emit-llvm -o - x.c | head`.
- **`main` is called `__main_argc_argv`.** For WASI, clang renames a C `main(argc, argv)`, and wasi-libc's `_start` calls it by that name. Name it `main` and it isn't the function libc calls with the arguments.

The example keeps its locals in `alloca` stack slots, which is easier to write than SSA with `phi` nodes; `-Os` turns them into registers.

## Build

```bash
zig cc -target wasm32-wasi -Os -s -Wl,-z,stack-size=1048576 -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm summary.ll
```

The flags are the [C](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/c) ones: smallest code, no symbols, a 1 MB stack instead of 16 MB.

## Call it

```ts
const { body } = ctx.req.body()
const out = await $wasm.run.async<{ text: string; words: number }>("summary", String(body ?? "")) // a string goes in as it is
```


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/others

# Other languages

Any language works when it builds a **WASI preview 1 program**: a module with a `_start` function that imports nothing but `wasi_snapshot_preview1`, and uses only WebAssembly 2.0 (no GC, no exception handling, no threads). Load it and `$wasm.modules()` says at once whether it runs: a module that needs anything else shows an error that says what.

The languages below weren't tried for these docs. What's said of each is what its own tools document.

| Language | Fits? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Swift | Yes | The Swift SDK for WASI (`swift build --swift-sdk wasm32-unknown-wasi`) builds WASI preview 1 programs. Foundation makes modules several MB, so a first call compiles for a long time and every call holds more memory. |
| C# / .NET | Likely too big | .NET's WASI build carries its runtime: tens of MB, over the default `MaxModulesMB`. |
| Nim, Odin, D | Through C or LLVM | Each can target `wasm32-wasi`, through C (`zig cc`) or its own LLVM backend. |
| Grain, MoonBit | Check the target | Both build WebAssembly; a module runs here only if their WASI output is preview 1 with no other imports. |
| Kotlin/Wasm, Dart, Java (WasmGC) | No | They need WebAssembly GC. |
| Python, Ruby, JavaScript | Not as interpreters | An interpreter built for WASI (CPython, Ruby, QuickJS) needs its standard library as files, and no folder is mounted. A tool that bundles the script and interpreter into one preview 1 program (Javy's static mode for JavaScript) can work, at a few MB per module. For JS, your page code is already JavaScript. |

To check a module without an app, run it with the [wazero CLI](https://wazero.io), which runs it with the same engine:

```bash
wazero run mymodule.wasm --describe
echo '{"text":"hi"}' | wazero run mymodule.wasm run
```

Then copy it to `pb_hooks/<name>.pb.wasm` and look at `$wasm.modules()`: a module that can't run says why there.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/guides/state

# Keeping state in JS

Every call gets a fresh module: nothing a call leaves in memory reaches the next one. That's what makes a module safe to share, and it means a module that works on a series (running totals, a rate, a game, a parser that resumes) can't keep its own state. The app keeps it instead:

1. Your page code loads the state: from a record, or from memory.
2. It passes the state in with the call.
3. The module returns the new state, and your code saves it.

The module stays a pure function, `(state, input) → new state`, which also makes it easy to test: each example in its manifest is one step.

## The module

[`example/stats-tinygo`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/stats-tinygo/main.go) keeps running statistics of a series of readings: count, mean, standard deviation, min and max. It uses [Welford's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_calculating_variance#Welford's_online_algorithm), so the state is five numbers however many readings it has seen. It has two functions:

- `add`: `{"state": <state or null>, "values": [...]}` → the new state
- `report`: a state → `{count, mean, stddev, min, max}`

```go
// State is everything the module needs to go on where the last call stopped. The app stores it as JSON.
type State struct {
	Count int     `json:"count"`
	Mean  float64 `json:"mean"`
	M2    float64 `json:"m2"` // the sum of squared distances from the mean
	Min   float64 `json:"min"`
	Max   float64 `json:"max"`
}

func main() {
	switch os.Args[1] {
	case "--describe":
		fmt.Print(manifest)
	case "add":
		var in struct {
			State  *State    `json:"state"`
			Values []float64 `json:"values"`
		}
		decode(&in)
		s := State{}
		if in.State != nil {
			s = *in.State
		}
		for _, v := range in.Values {
			// ... update count, mean, m2, min, max
		}
		encode(s)
	case "report":
		// ... stddev = sqrt(m2 / count)
	default:
		fail("no_such_function", os.Args[1])
	}
}
```

Build it with [TinyGo](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/tinygo):

```bash
tinygo build -target=wasip1 -opt=z -no-debug -scheduler=none -o pb_hooks/stats.pb.wasm .
```

It's 283 KB. Its first call compiles it (about 80 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 3 ms.

## State in a record

Give the collection a JSON field for the state: here, a `sensors` collection with `name` (text) and `stats` (JSON). An API route takes new readings, runs them through the module with the sensor's state, and saves the new state on the record:

```ts
// pb_pages/sensors/[id]/readings.ts
// POST /sensors/{id}/readings {"values": [21.5, 22]}: adds readings to the sensor's running statistics
type Stats = { count: number; mean: number; m2: number; min: number; max: number } // the module's state
type Report = { count: number; mean: number; stddev: number; min: number; max: number }

export async function post(ctx: any) {
  const sensor = ctx.app.findRecordById("sensors", ctx.params.id)
  const { values } = ctx.req.body() as { values: number[] }

  try {
    const state: Stats | null = JSON.parse(sensor.getString("stats")) // null until the first readings
    const next = await $wasm.call.async<Stats>("stats", "add", { state, values })

    sensor.set("stats", next)
    ctx.app.save(sensor)
    return ctx.res.json(await $wasm.call.async<Report>("stats", "report", next))
  } catch (err) {
    const w = err as WasmError
    if (w.name !== "WasmError" || w.retryable) throw err
    return ctx.res.json(400, { code: w.code, message: w.message }) // bad_input, bad_value: the caller's mistake
  }
}
```

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:8090/sensors/<id>/readings -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"values":[21.5,22]}'
# {"count":2,"max":22,"mean":21.75,"min":21.5,"stddev":0.25}
```

The record now holds the state, `{"count":2,"m2":0.125,"max":22,"mean":21.75,"min":21.5}`, and the next readings start from it.

- **An empty JSON field reads as `"null"`**, so `JSON.parse` gives `null` the first time, and the module starts a new series.
- **The module's errors come back as `WasmError`**, with its own `code`. Answer the caller's mistakes (`bad_input`) yourself, and let the rest (`busy`, `timeout`) fail the request.
- **Two requests at once for the same sensor** can both read the same state, and the second save drops the first one's readings. If that matters, send a sensor's readings one at a time, or save them as records and fold them into the state from a cron job.

## State in memory

State the app can lose on a restart (a cache, a count since start) can stay in memory instead, in `$app.store()`. It's the app's own key-value store, shared by all its code, and it holds the module's output as it is:

```ts
const store = ctx.app.store()
const next = await $wasm.call.async<Stats>("stats", "add", { state: store.get("load") || null, values: [1] })
store.set("load", next)
```

Each app (each instance, under a host that runs many) has its own store, and a restart empties it: a change in `pb_hooks/` restarts the app.

## Why not keep it in the module?

A module can't: each call starts from the module's file, with fresh memory, and nothing outlives the call. That's on purpose. One caller's data never reaches another's call, a module that crashes takes nothing with it, and a folder of modules costs nothing between calls. Keeping state in the app also puts it where the app's other tools reach it: the dashboard shows it, backups keep it, and the API rules decide who reads it.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes

# Recipes

A module can't reach the database, files or network, so what it's good for is computing: turning one thing into another. Each recipe here is a module built on a library from another language, with page code that uses it. Every module is kept built in the repository and checked by the extension's tests.

All of them are Rust: it has the most libraries that build for WASI as they are (see [Rust](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/rust)). Copy a module's `.pb.wasm` from its folder into your `pb_hooks/`, or build it from its source, and call it from your page code.

## Content

| Recipe | Library | Module | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Markdown to HTML](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/markdown) | pulldown-cmark | 258 KB | Renders a Markdown field to HTML when a record is saved. |
| [Sanitize HTML](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/sanitize-html) | ammonia | 803 KB | Cleans HTML users wrote, so it's safe to show. |
| [Text diffs](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/diff) | similar | 130 KB | Keeps a revision history of a text field as unified diffs. |

## Files and data

| Recipe | Library | Module | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Image thumbnails](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/thumbnail) | image | 448 KB | Makes a PNG thumbnail of each uploaded photo. |
| [QR codes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/qrcode) | qrcode | 109 KB | Draws a QR code as SVG, for a ticket or a check-in link. |
| [CSV import](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/csv) | csv | 108 KB | Reads a CSV file, quoted fields and all, into records. |

## From the extension's examples

These came with the extension, to answer real questions. Each is kept built beside its source, in [`example/`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/main.go)'s folders.

### Orders from EDIFACT and XML

[`edifact-orders-rust`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/edifact-orders-rust/src/main.rs) reads an EDIFACT ORDERS message (raw text, as trading partners send it) into an order: parties, lines, prices and allowances, with the message's own counts checked. [`order-xml`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/order-xml/src/main.rs) reads the same order from XML into the same JSON. So one route takes either format and stores one shape:

```ts
// pb_pages/orders.ts: the raw message is the request body, as text: a string goes in as it is
export async function post(ctx: any) {
  const raw = toString(ctx.req.event.request.body)
  const module = raw.trimStart().startsWith("<") ? "order-xml" : "edifact-orders-rust"
  const order = await $wasm.run.async<{ number: string; lines: object[] }>(module, raw)
  const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("orders"))
  record.load({ raw, number: order.number, lines: order.lines })
  ctx.app.save(record)
  return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id })
}
```

### Crypto JS doesn't have

[`waflows`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/waflows/src/main.rs) does what a WhatsApp Flows endpoint needs and the JS runtime can't: RSA-OAEP to unwrap the request's key, and AES-GCM with WhatsApp's key and IV. Your page code keeps the JSON, the base64 and the HTTP; the module does only those three steps, with bytes as base64:

```ts
type Data = { data: string } // what each waflows function gives: bytes as base64
const body = ctx.req.body() // in the endpoint's post handler
const { data: key } = await $wasm.call.async<Data>("waflows", "rsa-decrypt", { privateKey, data: body.encrypted_aes_key })
const { data: request } = await $wasm.call.async<Data>("waflows", "gcm-open", { key, iv: body.initial_vector, data: body.encrypted_flow_data })
// ... answer the request, then seal the answer with the flipped IV
const flipped = Buffer.from(body.initial_vector, "base64").map((b) => ~b).toString("base64")
const { data } = await $wasm.call.async<Data>("waflows", "gcm-seal", { key, iv: flipped, data: Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(answer)).toString("base64") })
```

[`crypto`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/crypto/main.go) (Go) is AES-256-GCM with a key your code passes in: `encrypt` takes `{key, text}`, `decrypt` takes `{key, data}`. The module can't keep the key or send it anywhere. Built with Go it's 4 MB: its first call compiles for about a second, and later calls load it in about 40 ms. The same source built with [TinyGo](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages/tinygo) is 348 KB: about 75 ms the first time, a few ms after.

## Write your own

A recipe is a module like any other: a program that reads stdin and writes stdout. Pick the library first, then the language it's in, and check it builds for WASI: one that needs threads, sockets or files won't run (password-strength checking with zxcvbn, for one, reads the browser's clock and fails here). [Choosing a language](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/languages) has the costs, and [Keeping state in JS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/guides/state) covers modules that work on a series.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/markdown

# Markdown to HTML

## What it's for

Your users write posts, docs or product descriptions in Markdown, and your pages show HTML. Render it once, when the
record is saved, and keep the HTML beside the Markdown: pages then show it with no work per view. The module is
[pulldown-cmark](https://crates.io/crates/pulldown-cmark), the CommonMark parser behind rustdoc and mdBook, with
tables, strikethrough and task lists on.

## The route

A `posts` collection with a `body` text field (the Markdown) and an `html` text field:

```ts
// pb_pages/posts.ts: posts are written in Markdown; html is what your pages show
async function renderPost(markdown: string): Promise<string> {
  const html = (await $wasm.run.async<string | null>("markdown", markdown || "")) ?? ""
  return (await $wasm.run.async<string | null>("sanitize-html", html)) ?? "" // users wrote it: keep only safe HTML
}

export async function post(ctx: any) {
  if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in to post")
  const { body } = ctx.req.body()
  const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts"))
  record.load({ body, html: await renderPost(body) })
  ctx.app.save(record)
  return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id })
}
```

A route that saves an edit sets `html` the same way, from the new body, before it saves.

CommonMark passes raw HTML through, so `<script>` in a post would reach your pages. The second call runs the result
through [sanitize-html](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/sanitize-html), which keeps the formatting and drops scripts, event handlers and
`javascript:` links. Leave it out only for Markdown you wrote yourself.

`?? ""` is there because an empty output comes back as `null`.

## The module

The Markdown is the module's stdin, as text, and the HTML is its stdout
([`src/main.rs`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/markdown/src/main.rs)):

```rust
let mut input = String::new();
if let Err(e) = std::io::stdin().read_to_string(&mut input) {
    fail("bad_input", &format!("the input isn't UTF-8 text: {e}"));
}
let opts = Options::ENABLE_TABLES | Options::ENABLE_STRIKETHROUGH | Options::ENABLE_TASKLISTS;
let mut out = String::with_capacity(input.len() * 3 / 2);
html::push_html(&mut out, Parser::new_ext(&input, opts));
std::io::stdout().write_all(out.as_bytes()).unwrap();
```

Other options (footnotes, heading ids, smart punctuation) are one more flag each.

## Build

```sh
cd ext/wasm/example/markdown
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1   # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/markdown.wasm pb_hooks/markdown.pb.wasm
```

## Cost

258 KB. The first call compiles it (about 60 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 2.5 ms and render a
short post in under 1 ms. With sanitize-html after it, a save takes under 10 ms more than without, once both are in
the cache.

## Limits

- Input and output are each at most 4 MB (`MaxPayload`).
- Each call still loads and starts the module (a few ms), so render on save, not on every page view.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/sanitize-html

# Sanitize HTML

## What it's for

A comment box with a rich text editor, an import of HTML from somewhere else, the output of [Markdown](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/markdown):
any HTML a user controls can carry a `<script>`, an `onerror=` or a `javascript:` link. Showing it as is lets one
user run code in another's browser. [ammonia](https://crates.io/crates/ammonia) parses the HTML the way a browser
does (html5ever) and keeps only an allow list of tags and attributes. Links get `rel="noopener noreferrer"`.

## The route

A `comments` collection with an `html` text field, cleaned before it's saved:

```ts
// pb_pages/comments.ts: comments arrive as HTML from a rich text editor
export async function post(ctx: any) {
  if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in to comment")
  const { html } = ctx.req.body()
  const comment = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("comments"))
  comment.set("html", String((await $wasm.run.async<string | null>("sanitize-html", html || "")) ?? ""))
  ctx.app.save(comment)
  return ctx.res.json(201, { id: comment.id })
}
```

Clean edits too if comments can be edited: the route that saves an edit makes the same call.

`String(...)` is there because a module's output comes back parsed when it's JSON: a comment that's just `42` comes
back as the number 42.

What it does to a hostile comment:

```html
<p onclick="steal()">Hi <a href="javascript:alert(1)">there</a><script>alert(1)</script></p>
```

```html
<p>Hi <a rel="noopener noreferrer">there</a></p>
```

## The module

The whole program is one call to ammonia's defaults ([`src/main.rs`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/sanitize-html/src/main.rs)):

```rust
let mut input = String::new();
if let Err(e) = std::io::stdin().read_to_string(&mut input) {
    fail("bad_input", &format!("the input isn't UTF-8 text: {e}"));
}
let clean = ammonia::clean(&input);
std::io::stdout().write_all(clean.as_bytes()).unwrap();
```

For your own rules (allow `class` on `<code>`, drop images), build an `ammonia::Builder` in its place.

## Build

```sh
cd ext/wasm/example/sanitize-html
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1   # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/sanitize-html.wasm pb_hooks/sanitize-html.pb.wasm
```

## Cost

803 KB, most of it a full HTML parser. The first call compiles it (about 120 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 5 ms and clean a comment in under 1 ms.

## Limits

- Input and output are each at most 4 MB (`MaxPayload`).
- `style` attributes are removed, not filtered; allow them only with your own CSS rules in the builder.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/diff

# Text diffs

## What it's for

A wiki page, a contract, a blog post: when people edit text, you want to see who changed what, and maybe roll back.
Storing a diff of each edit shows exactly the lines that changed, the way `git diff` does. The module compares two
texts line by line with [similar](https://crates.io/crates/similar) and returns a unified diff and how many lines were
added and removed.

## The route

A `pages` collection with a `body` text field, and a `revisions` collection with `page` (text or a relation), `diff`
(text), `added` and `removed` (numbers):

An API route saves an edit of a page's body (`PUT` with `{"body": "..."}`) and keeps it as a diff:

```ts
// pb_pages/wiki/[id].ts: every edit of a page's body is kept as a diff in revisions
interface Diff {
  changed: boolean
  unified: string
  added: number
  removed: number
}

export async function put(ctx: any) {
  if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in to edit")
  const page = ctx.app.findRecordById("pages", ctx.params.id)
  const { body } = ctx.req.body()
  const d = await $wasm.run.async<Diff>("diff", { old: page.getString("body"), new: body })
  page.set("body", body)
  ctx.app.save(page)
  if (d.changed) {
    const rev = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("revisions"))
    rev.load({ page: page.id, diff: d.unified, added: d.added, removed: d.removed })
    ctx.app.save(rev)
  }
  return ctx.res.json({ changed: d.changed, added: d.added, removed: d.removed })
}
```

The old body is read before the page changes. The revision is saved after the page, so only once the page itself is
saved.

What an edit gives:

```json
{"old": "Pocket\nbase\n", "new": "Pocket\nOne\nrocks\n"}
```

```json
{"unified": "--- old\n+++ new\n@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@\n Pocket\n-base\n+One\n+rocks\n", "added": 2, "removed": 1, "changed": true}
```

## The module

[`src/main.rs`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/diff/src/main.rs):

```rust
let diff = TextDiff::from_lines(&input.old, &input.new);
// count the inserted and deleted lines...
let unified = diff
    .unified_diff()
    .context_radius(input.context.unwrap_or(3))
    .header("old", "new")
    .to_string();
```

`context` in the input sets how many unchanged lines show around each change (3 by default, as in `git diff`).

## Build

```sh
cd ext/wasm/example/diff
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1   # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/diff.wasm pb_hooks/diff.pb.wasm
```

## Cost

130 KB. The first call compiles it (about 35 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 1.6 ms and diff a page in under 1 ms.

## Limits

- Both texts together are at most 4 MB (`MaxPayload`), as JSON.
- It's a line diff: a change inside a long line shows as the whole line removed and added.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/thumbnail

# Image thumbnails

## What it's for

A gallery, a product list or a profile page shows many images small. Sending each one full size is slow on a phone.
PocketBase can make thumbnails of a file field on request (`?thumb=100x100`); a module lets you make your own when the
file is uploaded: a fixed size, a PNG whatever came in, kept in its own field you can query and send anywhere. The
module uses the [image](https://crates.io/crates/image) crate, built with PNG and JPEG only.

## The route

A `photos` collection with two file fields, `image` (what the user uploads) and `thumb`. An API route takes the
upload (a multipart form with an `image` field) and saves the photo with its thumbnail:

```ts
// pb_pages/photos.ts: an uploaded photo is saved with a 256 px PNG thumbnail in its thumb field
export async function post(ctx: any) {
  if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in to upload")
  const [file] = ctx.req.files("image")
  if (!file) throw ctx.httpError(400, "No image")
  const reader = file.reader.open()
  let bytes: Uint8Array
  try {
    bytes = new Uint8Array(toBytes(reader))
  } finally {
    reader.close()
  }
  const thumb = await $wasm.run.async<{ width: number; height: number; png: string }>("thumbnail", bytes)
  const photo = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("photos"))
  photo.set("image", file)
  photo.set("thumb", $filesystem.fileFromBytes(Array.from(Buffer.from(thumb.png, "base64")), "thumb.png"))
  ctx.app.save(photo)
  return ctx.res.json(201, { id: photo.id })
}
```

`ctx.req.files` gives the files uploaded with this request, ready for a record field. A `Uint8Array` goes to the module
as raw bytes. The module answers with JSON, `{width, height, png}`, the PNG as base64; `$filesystem.fileFromBytes`
takes the bytes as a plain array, hence `Array.from`.

## The module

[`src/main.rs`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/thumbnail/src/main.rs) reads the image, scales it to fit, and writes a PNG:

```rust
let size = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() {
    Some("run") => 256,
    Some("small") => 64,
    // ...
};
let img = image::load_from_memory(&input)
    .unwrap_or_else(|e| fail("bad_image", &format!("not a PNG or JPEG image: {e}")));
let thumb = if img.width() > size || img.height() > size { img.thumbnail(size, size) } else { img };
```

`run` fits the image in 256×256 and `small` in 64×64, kept in proportion (`$wasm.call.async("thumbnail", "small",
bytes)` for the small one). It also takes the image as base64 text, which is how its manifest's examples pass one.

## Build

```sh
cd ext/wasm/example/thumbnail
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1   # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/thumbnail.wasm pb_hooks/thumbnail.pb.wasm
```

## Cost

448 KB. The first call compiles it (about 110 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 4.5 ms. Decoding is most of the run: a 1280×853 JPEG takes about 230 ms, a
1920×1280 one about 460 ms, a 2560×1706 one about 780 ms (2026-11-18, a laptop).

## Limits

- The decoded image has to fit in the call's memory, 32 MB by default (`MaxCallMemoryMB`): 3 bytes a pixel, so up to
  about 2560×1706 with the defaults. A 4000×2666 photo fails with `crashed` and a message naming the limit; raise
  `MaxCallMemoryMB` (and the timeout) for big camera photos.
- The upload is at most 4 MB (`MaxPayload`).
- PNG and JPEG only. WebP, GIF and others are one Cargo feature each on the `image` crate, and make the module bigger.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/qrcode

# QR codes

## What it's for

Event tickets, check-in links, a table's ordering page, a Wi-Fi login: a QR code your users scan from a screen or
paper. The module draws one as an SVG image from any text, with the
[qrcode](https://crates.io/crates/qrcode) crate. SVG stays sharp at any size and prints well.

## The route

An API route that gives a ticket's owner their ticket's QR code. `tickets` has a `code` text field and an `owner`
relation to `users`:

```ts
// pb_pages/tickets/[id]/qr.ts: a ticket's QR code, for its owner, as SVG
export async function get(ctx: any) {
  if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in first")
  const ticket = ctx.app.findRecordById("tickets", ctx.params.id)
  if (ticket.get("owner") !== ctx.auth.id) throw ctx.httpError(403, "Not your ticket")
  const svg = await $wasm.run.async<string>("qrcode", `https://example.com/check-in/${ticket.get("code")}`)
  return ctx.res.json({ svg })
}
```

A plain `<img src>` doesn't send the user's PocketBase token, so fetch the SVG with it (the JS SDK's `pb.send`)
and show it from a blob URL (`new Blob([svg], { type: "image/svg+xml" })`). Or draw it once, when the ticket is created, and save it in a protected file field:
then an `<img>` with a [file token](https://pocketbase.io/docs/files-handling/#protected-files) shows it.

## The module

The text is stdin; the SVG is stdout ([`src/main.rs`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/qrcode/src/main.rs)):

```rust
let code = QrCode::with_error_correction_level(&input, EcLevel::M)
    .unwrap_or_else(|e| fail("too_long", &format!("can't encode it: {e}")));
let image = code.render::<svg::Color>().min_dimensions(200, 200).build();
std::io::stdout().write_all(image.as_bytes()).unwrap();
```

Error correction `M` survives about 15% of the code being damaged or covered. Change the colors with
`.dark_color(svg::Color("#1d4ed8"))`.

## Build

```sh
cd ext/wasm/example/qrcode
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1   # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/qrcode.wasm pb_hooks/qrcode.pb.wasm
```

## Cost

109 KB. The first call compiles it (about 30 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 1.3 ms and draw a code in about 2 ms.

## Limits

- A QR code holds at most 2,331 bytes at level `M`; longer text fails with `too_long`.
- An empty input fails with `empty_input`.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm/recipes/csv

# CSV import

## What it's for

Customers, products, price lists: the data people already have is in a spreadsheet, and the easiest way out of one is
CSV. Splitting lines on commas works until a field holds a comma, a quote or a line break, which real files do. The
module reads CSV properly with the [csv](https://crates.io/crates/csv) crate (quotes, `""` inside quotes, CRLF line
ends, Excel's UTF-8 BOM) and gives back one JSON object per row, keyed by the header line.

## The route

An API route a superuser posts a file to, which imports it into `contacts` (`name` text, required; `email` email):

```ts
// pb_pages/import/contacts.ts: superusers import contacts from a CSV file (the request body)
interface CsvImport {
  rows: Array<{ name: string; email: string }> // one object per row, keyed by the header line
  errors: Array<{ line: number; message: string }>
}

export async function post(ctx: any) {
  if (!ctx.auth?.isSuperuser()) throw ctx.httpError(403, "Superusers only")
  const csv = new Uint8Array(toBytes(ctx.req.event.request.body))
  const { rows, errors } = await $wasm.run.async<CsvImport>("csv", csv)
  const contacts = ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("contacts")
  ctx.app.runInTransaction((txApp: any) => {
    for (const row of rows) {
      const contact = new Record(contacts)
      contact.load({ name: row.name, email: row.email })
      txApp.save(contact) // an invalid row throws: nothing is imported
    }
  })
  return ctx.res.json({ imported: rows.length, skipped: errors })
}
```

```sh
curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" --data-binary @contacts.csv http://127.0.0.1:8090/import/contacts
```

The file is the request body, sent as it is; `ctx.req.event` is PocketBase's request event, and its `request.body` is the raw body. In a transaction, the import is all or nothing: a row the collection
refuses (a blank `name`, a bad email) stops it with that row's error, and nothing is saved. A row with the wrong
number of fields doesn't stop it; it's skipped and listed with its line number:

```json
{"imported": 2, "skipped": [{"line": 4, "message": "CSV error: record 3 (line: 4, byte: 64): found record with 1 fields, but the previous record has 2 fields"}]}
```

## The module

[`src/main.rs`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/wasm/example/csv/src/main.rs):

```rust
let mut reader = csv::ReaderBuilder::new().delimiter(delimiter).from_reader(data);
for result in reader.records() {
    match result {
        Ok(record) => { /* one object: column name -> value */ }
        Err(e) => { /* {line, message} into errors */ }
    }
}
```

`run` reads comma-separated files, `tsv` tab-separated and `semicolon` semicolon-separated, which is what spreadsheets
save in many European locales: `$wasm.call.async("csv", "semicolon", csv)`. Every value comes back as a string, as it
is in the file; convert numbers and dates in your page code, or let the collection's field types do it.

## Build

```sh
cd ext/wasm/example/csv
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1   # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/csv.wasm pb_hooks/csv.pb.wasm
```

## Cost

108 KB. The first call compiles it (about 30 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 1.5 ms and read a small file in under 1 ms.

## Limits

- The file and the JSON that comes back are each at most 4 MB (`MaxPayload`). The JSON repeats the column names on
  every row, so it's bigger than the file: keep files to about 2 MB, or split them.
- Spreadsheet formulas come through as their saved values, if the file has them; CSV has no types or formatting.

# New in PocketOne

PocketOne does everything PocketBase does, and adds the features below. They're all built into the `pocketone`
binary, and most are on by default. There's nothing to install.

Three of them set PocketOne apart: hooks with `async`, `import` and TypeScript,
async pages in TSX, and hundreds of apps running as isolates in one process.

## Modern JavaScript on the server

**[Hooks with async, import and TypeScript](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs).** Your `pb_hooks` run on QuickJS with the same JS API you
already use, plus:

- `async` handlers and `await`. The app keeps serving other requests while a handler waits on the database or an HTTP
  call.
- ES modules: `import` and `export` between your files, and packages from `node_modules`.
- TypeScript: write `.pb.ts` files and they run as they are.
- Globals shared by every handler, and memory and time limits that stop a runaway script instead of the app.

```ts
// pb_hooks/orders.pb.ts
import { total } from "./lib/pricing.mjs"

routerAdd("GET", "/api/orders/{id}/total", async (e) => {
  const order = await e.app.findRecordById.async("orders", e.request.pathValue("id"))
  return e.json(200, { total: total(order) })
})
```

**[Pages in TSX, TypeScript or EJS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/sites).** Put a `.tsx`, `.jsx`, `.ejs` or `.md` file in `pb_pages`
and it's a server-rendered page, with your records a function call away. Components `import` each other, and a page's
code and endpoints are `.ts` files beside them. Every part of a page can `await`: loaders, handlers, middleware, EJS tags and
`async` components, and sibling components render at the same time. esbuild is built into the binary: no Node, no
`npm install`, no build step.

```tsx
// pb_pages/products/[id].tsx
import Price from './_private/Price'

export default async function Product({ ctx }: any) {
  const product = await ctx.app.findRecordById.async('products', ctx.params.id)
  return (
    <article>
      <h1>{product.getString('name')}</h1>
      <Price cents={product.getInt('price')} />
    </article>
  )
}
```

## Hundreds of apps in one process

**[PocketBase isolates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/isolates).** One `pocketone` process runs hundreds of PocketBase apps as
isolates, routed by hostname. Each is a complete app with its own data, hooks and dashboard. It starts on its first
request in tens of milliseconds, costs about 3 MB while it runs, and is sandboxed from the others: its own memory cap,
time limits, files, SQL and secrets. No container per app, no idle memory to pay for.

```yaml
# pocketone.yaml: every hostname you ask for becomes its own app (dev mode)
multisite: {}
instances: { dev: true }
pocker: { root: ./pb_root }
```

## Everything new at a glance

| | What you get |
|---|---|
| [QuickJS hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs) | `async`/`await`, ES module `import`, TypeScript, shared globals and hard limits, on the same JS API |
| [Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/sites) | Server-rendered pages in TSX, JSX, TypeScript, EJS or Markdown, with `await` everywhere and no build step |
| [PocketBase isolates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/isolates) | Hundreds of apps in one process, each starting in tens of ms, about 3 MB each, sandboxed |
| [Point-in-time restore](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/restore) | Every change recorded; restore to any second in the last 72 hours, and undo the restore |
| [Deploy and live sync](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/deploy) | `pocketone deploy` uploads only what changed; `pocketone dev` syncs a folder both ways and streams logs |
| [Remote CLI](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/remote) | Admin commands against any app, from your terminal, a script or an agent |
| [API tokens and OAuth](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/tokens) | Named, scoped tokens you revoke one by one; your app is an OAuth server |
| [MCP for AI agents](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/mcp) | `/mcp` on every app, with OAuth sign-in and your own tools from `pb_hooks` |
| [Bulk mail](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/bulk-mail) | Campaigns from the dashboard, with unsubscribes, suppression and pacing |
| [Desktop apps](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/desktop) | The same folder builds into native macOS, Windows and Linux apps with `pocketone desktop build`, each user's data on their machine (preview) |
| [pocketone.yaml](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml) | One config file, with every extension's options and a `.env` for secrets |

Each page shows the feature in the dashboard, from your terminal and from an agent. For how a feature works or how to
build on it, follow its **How it works** links to the [extension](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/all) pages.

## Also built in

Smaller additions you'll notice without a page of their own:

- **Mail you can see in dev mode:** with `serve --dev` and no SMTP settings, mail is caught and shown at
  `http://127.0.0.1:8025` instead of being sent ([Mail Trap](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mailtrap)).
- **S3 redirects:** files kept in S3 download straight from the bucket through short-lived signed links
  ([S3 Redirect](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3redirect)).
- **Restylable sign-in pages:** copy the OAuth sign-in screens into your app with `pocketone template eject` and edit
  them ([Templates](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/templates)).
- **Settings and cache:** one settings screen and one shared memory budget for every feature
  ([Settings](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/settings), [Cache](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/cache)).

Coming from PocketBase? [What stays the same, and how each feature compares](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketbase).

# Pages: sites in TSX, TypeScript or EJS

Put a `.tsx`, `.jsx`, `.ejs` or `.md` file in a `pb_pages` folder next to `pb_data`, and your app serves it as a web
page. Each file is a route. Components `import` each other, a `.ts` file runs (a page's code beside it, or an endpoint), and
page code reads and writes your records directly. Every part of a page can `await`, and the app keeps serving other
requests while it waits. This is Pages, built into PocketOne.

esbuild is built into the `pocketone` binary, so TSX and TypeScript compile the first time a page is used: no Node, no
`npm install`, no bundler, no build step. It's on for every PocketOne app whenever a `pb_pages` folder exists. No folder,
no pages.

## A product page in TSX

The page is an `async` component: it awaits its record, then renders it with another component.

```tsx
// pb_pages/products/[id].tsx
import Price from './_private/Price'

export default async function Product({ ctx }: any) {
  const product = await ctx.app.findRecordById.async('products', ctx.params.id)
  return (
    <article>
      <h1>{product.getString('name')}</h1>
      <Price cents={product.getInt('price')} />
    </article>
  )
}
```

```tsx
// pb_pages/products/_private/Price.tsx
export default ({ cents }: { cents: number }) => <span class="price">${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}</span>
```

`/products/<id>` now answers with `<article><h1>Mug</h1><span class="price">$12.50</span></article>`. Edit any of the
files and reload: the change shows up with no restart.

## await anywhere

`.async` twins of Go functions (`findRecordById.async`, `countRecords.async`, ...) do their work
outside the JS VM, so the app serves other requests while a page waits.

- **Components:** any component can be `async`. Sibling components run at the same time, so these two counts load in
  parallel:

  ```tsx
  async function Count({ collection }: { collection: string }) {
    const n = await $app.countRecords.async(collection)
    return <b>{n}</b>
  }

  export default () => <p><Count collection="orders" /> orders, <Count collection="users" /> users</p>
  ```

- **Loaders and handlers:** `load`, `get`, `post` and the rest in a page's `.ts` or an endpoint, and `+middleware`
  can be `async`.
- **EJS:** a tag can `await`: `<% const n = await ctx.app.countRecords.async('orders') %>`.
- **Sync stays free:** a page without `await` runs exactly as before.

[Loading data](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/loading-data#async-loading), [EJS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/ejs#await) and
[JSX and TSX](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/jsx#async-components) have the details.

JSX renders to plain HTML on the server. There's no virtual DOM and no client-side React, so pair it with htmx,
Datastar or plain `<script>` tags for interactivity. TypeScript types are stripped, not checked; run `tsc --noEmit` or
rely on your editor. [JSX and TSX](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/jsx) has the details.

## Prefer EJS? Hello world

1. Make a folder for your app with a page in it:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p myapp/pb_pages && cd myapp
   echo '<%= `Hello, world!` %>' > pb_pages/index.ejs
   ```

2. Create a superuser, then start the app:

   ```bash
   pocketone superuser upsert you@example.com <password> --dir ./pb_data
   pocketone serve --dir ./pb_data
   ```

3. Open http://127.0.0.1:8090. You see `Hello, world!`

Edit the file and reload the browser. Changes show up right away, with no restart.

To start from something bigger, `pocketone pages starters` lists the starter kits and
`pocketone pages create myapp --starter <kit>` makes a new app from one.

## What's covered

- **Files are routes:** `pb_pages/about.ejs` serves `/about`, and `pb_pages/blog/index.ejs` serves `/blog`.
- **Templates:** TSX, JSX, EJS and Markdown, mixed freely (an EJS page can sit in a TSX layout), with layouts,
  partials, middleware and JSON routes. A route's code is a `.ts` file (`about.ts` beside `about.ets`, or an endpoint like `feeds/rss.ts`); `.js` files are served to the browser.
- **Leftovers go on:** a URL no page matches goes on to `pb_public`, then to PocketBase. URLs under `/api/` and `/_/`
  always belong to PocketBase.
- **Errors:** in dev mode you get detailed error pages. Otherwise visitors see a plain error page and the details go to
  the log.
- **Not with `--jsvm goja`:** pages run in PocketOne's own JS engine, so they're off when you serve with PocketBase's.

To send your pages to a running app, see [Deploy and live sync](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/deploy).

## Change it

To serve pages from another folder, pass `--pagesDir` to `pocketone serve`, or set `server.pages_dir` in
`pocketone.yaml` ([pocketone.yaml reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference)). Settings for the site itself, such as which
Pages plugins to load, go in `pb_pages/+config.js` ([+config.js](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/config)).

## Learn more

The full Pages docs:

- [Installation](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/installation) and [starter kits](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/starter-kits)
- [JSX and TSX](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/jsx)
- [Creating a page](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/creating-a-page) and [routing](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/routing)
- [Loading data](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/loading-data)
- [Layouts and slots](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/layouts)
- [Authentication](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/authentication)
- [Going live](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/deploying)

## How it works

- [Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/extension) serves the `pb_pages` folder and adds the `pages create` and
  `pages starters` commands. Page code runs in your app's JS engine.
- [Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages) is the home of its docs, guides and plugins.

# Advanced installation

[Installation](https://pocketone.dev/docs/installation) covers the usual way on each system: Homebrew, Scoop or the install script. This
guide covers the rest.

## Install script settings

The [install script](/install.sh) reads these environment variables. With `curl | sh`, put them before `sh`:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://pocketone.dev/install.sh | POCKETONE_VERSION=<release tag> sh
```

| Variable | What it does |
|---|---|
| `POCKETONE_VERSION` | Install this release tag instead of the newest one. |
| `POCKETONE_INSTALL_DIR` | Where the binary goes when no package is used. Default `/usr/local/bin`; a folder you own, such as `$HOME/.local/bin`, needs no `sudo`. |
| `POCKETONE_NO_PACKAGE=1` | On Linux, install the plain binary, never a package. |

## Windows without Scoop

Releases include 64-bit Windows builds: the zip ending in `_windows_amd64.zip` for most PCs, `_windows_arm64.zip` for
ARM ones. The executable inside is `pocketone.exe`. Download one from
[Releases](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/releases), then in PowerShell, from the folder you downloaded it to:

```powershell
$dir = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\pocketone"
Expand-Archive pocketone_*_windows_amd64.zip -DestinationPath $dir -Force
Unblock-File "$dir\pocketone.exe"
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";$dir", "User")
```

This puts PocketOne in a folder of your own, so it needs no administrator rights, and adds that folder to your user
`PATH`. Open a new terminal and check it with `pocketone --version`.

`Unblock-File` clears the "downloaded from the internet" mark. The executable isn't code-signed, so if you start it
from File Explorer instead, SmartScreen may stop it: choose **More info**, then **Run anyway**. `pocketone` commands
are the same in PowerShell and in Command Prompt.

## Download a release

Download the zip for your platform from [Releases](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/releases), unzip it, and
put `pocketone` somewhere on your `PATH`. Each release's `checksums.txt` lists the SHA-256 of every file.

PocketOne's Linux builds are static binaries for `amd64`, `arm64`, `armv7` (32-bit ARM, such as older Raspberry Pis),
`ppc64le` and `s390x`, so they run on any distribution. Releases also have `.deb`, `.rpm` and `.apk` packages
([install one by hand](https://pocketone.dev/docs/guides/linux-server#or-install-a-package-by-hand)).

## Build from source

With [Go](https://go.dev) installed:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone.git
cd pocketone/examples/pocketone
go build -o pocketone .
```

## Upgrade

A binary from a release zip or `go build`, or the plain binary the install script put in `/usr/local/bin`, upgrades
itself with `pocketone upgrade` (with `sudo` if its folder is root's). It keeps the old one beside it as
`pocketone-<version>`, never deleted, so you can go back.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest/authentication

# Authentication API

Auth endpoints are per [auth collection](https://pocketone.dev/docs/authentication), at `/api/collections/{collection}/...`. A sign-in
answers a token and the record; send the token as the `Authorization` header from then on.

```json
{
  "token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9...",
  "record": { "collectionName": "users", "id": "0slkeutr0bxpw3v", "email": "ada@example.com", "verified": true }
}
```

That's the answer of every sign-in below. With multi-factor auth on, the first sign-in answers `401` with
`{"mfaId": "..."}` instead; pass that `mfaId` to the second sign-in.

## Sign-in methods

`GET /api/collections/{collection}/auth-methods`

Which methods the collection allows, for building a sign-in form. Anyone may call it.

```json
{
  "password": { "enabled": true, "identityFields": ["email"] },
  "oauth2": { "enabled": true, "providers": [{ "name": "google", "displayName": "Google", "state": "...", "authURL": "https://accounts.google.com/...", "codeVerifier": "...", "codeChallenge": "...", "codeChallengeMethod": "S256" }] },
  "mfa": { "enabled": false, "duration": 0 },
  "otp": { "enabled": true, "duration": 300 }
}
```

## Password

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/auth-with-password`

| Body | |
|---|---|
| `identity` | the email (or another identity field's value) |
| `password` | the password |
| `identityField` | optional: which identity field `identity` is |

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/users/auth-with-password \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"identity": "ada@example.com", "password": "a long password"}'
```

## One-time code

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/request-otp` with `{"email": "..."}` emails a code and answers `{"otpId": "..."}`
(also for an email with no account, so it doesn't reveal which exist).

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/auth-with-otp` with `{"otpId": "...", "password": "<the code>"}` signs in.

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/users/request-otp \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email": "ada@example.com"}'
# {"otpId": "8xk1r4t2y0p9q3z"}

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/users/auth-with-otp \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"otpId": "8xk1r4t2y0p9q3z", "password": "47201956"}'
```

## OAuth2

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/auth-with-oauth2`

After the user signs in at the provider (`authURL` from `auth-methods`) and comes back to your redirect URL with a
`code`, exchange it:

| Body | |
|---|---|
| `provider` | the provider's name (`google`) |
| `code` | the code the provider sent back |
| `codeVerifier` | the `codeVerifier` from `auth-methods` |
| `redirectURL` | the redirect URL you sent the user to the provider with |
| `createData` | optional: fields for the record, when this sign-in creates it |

The answer also has `meta`: the provider's profile (name, avatar, email). A first sign-in creates the record, if the
collection's create rule allows it.

The JS SDK's `authWithOAuth2` does all of this in a popup, through a redirect URL every app serves for that purpose:
`GET /api/oauth2-redirect` (and `POST /api/oauth2-redirect`, for providers that post back). Register
`https://<your app>/api/oauth2-redirect` with the provider.

## Refresh

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/auth-refresh`

With a valid token, answers a fresh one (and the current record). Use it to keep a session going, and to check that a
token is still good.

## Verify an email

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/request-verification` with `{"email": "..."}` emails a link (answers `204`).

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/confirm-verification` with `{"token": "..."}`, the token from the link, marks the
record `verified` (answers `204`).

## Reset a password

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/request-password-reset` with `{"email": "..."}` emails a link (answers `204`).

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/confirm-password-reset` with `{"token": "...", "password": "...",
"passwordConfirm": "..."}` sets the new password (answers `204`) and signs the record out of its other sessions.

## Change an email

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/request-email-change` with `{"newEmail": "..."}`, signed in, emails a link to the
new address (answers `204`).

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/confirm-email-change` with `{"token": "...", "password": "..."}` changes it
(answers `204`).

## Impersonate

`POST /api/collections/{collection}/impersonate/{id}` (**superusers**)

| Body | |
|---|---|
| `duration` | optional: how long the token lasts, in seconds (default: the collection's auth token duration) |

Answers a sign-in for that record: a token that can't be refreshed. For support: see the app as a user does.

## Next

- [Authentication](https://pocketone.dev/docs/authentication): sign-in methods, settings and the signed-in user in your code.
- [Records API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest/records): create a record in an auth collection to sign up.

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest/backups

# Backups API

A backup is a zip of the app's `pb_data`, kept in `pb_data/backups` or in S3 (**Settings → Backups**). All endpoints are
for **superusers**. PocketOne also records every change for [point-in-time restore](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/restore), which
these full backups sit beside.

## List backups

`GET /api/backups`

```json
[{ "key": "pb_backup_20261123030000.zip", "size": 1048576, "modified": "2026-11-23 03:00:01.000Z" }]
```

## Make a backup

`POST /api/backups` with an optional `{"name": "before-migration.zip"}` (default: a timestamped name). Answers `204`
when it's done, which takes a while for a big app. One backup or restore runs at a time.

## Download a backup

`GET /api/backups/{key}?token=...`

Takes a superuser's file token in the URL, from [`POST /api/files/token`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest/files#protected-files), so a
browser can download it directly.

## Upload a backup

`POST /api/backups/upload`, `multipart/form-data` with the zip in `file`. Answers `204`.

## Delete a backup

`DELETE /api/backups/{key}` (`204`).

## Restore a backup

`POST /api/backups/{key}/restore`

Replaces `pb_data` with the backup and restarts the app (answers `204` before the restart). Everything since the backup
is gone, so make a backup first.

## Next

- [Backups and restore](https://pocketone.dev/docs/features/restore): point-in-time restore, and undoing a restore.
- [Settings API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest/settings): the backup schedule and S3.

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest/batch

# Batch API

`POST /api/batch`

Runs several record writes in one database transaction: if any fails, none of them is kept. Each one is checked like
the same request on its own (the collection's rules, your hooks).

Batch requests are off until you turn them on: **Settings → Application → Batch API**, or `PATCH /api/settings` with
`{"batch": {"enabled": true, "maxRequests": 50, "timeout": 3}}`.

| Body | |
|---|---|
| `requests` | the writes, in order: each a `method`, a `url` (a Records API path), and its `body` (and optional `headers`) |

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/batch \
  -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "requests": [
      {"method": "POST", "url": "/api/collections/orders/records", "body": {"total": 42}},
      {"method": "PATCH", "url": "/api/collections/products/records/p4x8m2k1z9q0w3e", "body": {"stock-": 1}},
      {"method": "DELETE", "url": "/api/collections/carts/records/c7n2b5v8x1z4q6r"}
    ]
  }'
```

It answers one result per request, in order:

```json
[
  { "status": 200, "body": { "collectionName": "orders", "id": "o1a2b3c4d5e6f7g", "total": 42 } },
  { "status": 200, "body": { "collectionName": "products", "id": "p4x8m2k1z9q0w3e", "stock": 9 } },
  { "status": 204, "body": null }
]
```

If one fails, the whole batch answers `400`, with the failed request's index and error in `data`.

The urls may only be the Records API's create, update, upsert (`PUT /api/collections/{collection}/records`, which
creates or updates by the body's `id`) and delete. To upload files in a batch, send `multipart/form-data` with the
JSON in a `@jsonPayload` field and each file as `requests.N.fieldName`.

## Next

- [Records API](https://pocketone.dev/docs/rest/records): the requests a batch is made of.
- [Records](https://pocketone.dev/docs/records#transactions): transactions in your own code.
